News.title: Miss Universe host hits out at pageant on stage after contestants wore indigenous dress during competition
News.content:
A PAGEANT host has slammed two Miss Universe Canada contestants after they wore Indigenous-inspired outfits during the competition.

The controversy erupted during the national costume segment, when former winner Ashley Callingbull broke from the script to call out what she described as cultural appropriation.



Callingbull, a Plains Cree woman from the Enoch Cree Nation, interrupted her co-host and said: “Sometimes there are mistakes that are made.

“It’s 2026. We should know better, but most importantly, a part of reconciliation is that we educate and learn and understand and move on from these things in a good way.”



She took issue with one contestant who wore a fur dress and boots, while another appeared on stage wearing a feathered headdress.

Speaking to CBC Indigenous, Callingbull said: “My jaw just dropped on the floor.



“This cannot be real. I just couldn’t get over that this was happening. Who allowed this on stage? Who approved this?

“Anything traditional or sacred should not be allowed. I was very, very upset.”



One of the controversial costumes, worn by Karisa Haverkemp, featured a feathered headdress traditionally associated with highly respected Indigenous leaders in North America.

She also had a red handprint painted across her face – a symbol of solidarity with the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG) movement.

In a statement, Miss Universe Canada said: “If any costume caused offense, hurt or misunderstanding, please know it was never our intention.”

Haverkemp later took to Instagram to acknowledge her mistake.

She wrote: “I acknowledge and recognise that my outfit for the national costume caused hurt and offence to people in the Indigenous community.



“I appreciate what I have learned from this experience.”

The other contestant, Jasleen Kaily, wore a costume titled “Arctic Beauty”.

It featured an all-fur dress, fur boots known as mukluks, and two braids.



Kaily also apologised on social media, saying: “My intention was never to disrespect or misrepresent Indigenous culture” but rather to “recognise and celebrate one of the First Peoples of Canada”.

According to the Miss Universe Canada website, the national costume segment is “a celebration of Canadian culture and heritage, combined with creativity”.

It states: “Each delegate must showcase a unique costume, dress, or outfit inspired by Canada’s traditions, symbols, and history.”

The organisation has now said it will introduce a “comprehensive costume guide” to “establish clear guidelines and standards for all future pageant cycles to ensure every presentation is thoughtful and respectful”.

Pageant director Sonny Borrelli said he has also invited Callingbull to be the costume segment’s official liaison.



It is not the first time the Miss Universe Canada competition has faced criticism over cultural appropriation.

In 2015, the organisation said there had been a “misunderstanding” over entrant Paola Nunez Valdez, who wore a totem pole costume during the national costume segment.

Both Valdez and the organisation said the outfit was intended to represent her Dominican heritage.

News.title: Britain’s so hot that woman in Dorset has grown BANANAS – as UK on course for warmest summer on record
News.content:
BRITAIN’S blistering summer will see temperatures hit 38C tomorrow — with bananas among the few things growing.

Health warnings were issued, with householders told to close the curtains for extra shade during a fifth successive heatwave.



Experts predicted shortages of some foods in shops and higher prices as drought-hit farms battle to keep crops alive during what is set to be the hottest summer on record.

More expensive grain for animal feed will push up meat costs, and milk output has fallen as cows struggle in the heat and grass turns brown.



NFU president Tom Bradshaw added: “It does feel like there are going to be some shortages of food product.”

Analysts Shore Capital called it Britain’s “worst food security challenge in decades”.



But in Poole, Dorset, Pam Woodall found bananas growing on her garden fruit trees for the first time since she moved in 13 years ago.

The fruit typically grows in tropical climates in Asia and South America.

But Pam said she was shocked to see a bunch on her tallest 10ft plant.

She said: “I was walking around the garden and thought, ‘What’s that?’ It looks amazing but I’ll wait to see if the bananas ripen.”



Tomorrow’s 38C high would equal this year’s top temperature, recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk on June 26.

Extreme amber heat warnings have been issued for large swathes of England, including London, parts of the South East and East, the Midlands, and Yorkshire.

People are advised to keep out of the sun, drink lots of fluids — and close curtains.



The Met Office also warned the hot weather is likely to bring travel chaos and damage to heat-sensitive infrastructure — potentially causing power cuts in places.

Chief forecaster Chris Bulmer said: “High pressure is now becoming dominant and temperatures will build day-by-day. Southerly and south-easterly winds will also tap into the hot conditions over Europe.”

Up to 27million people are under hosepipe bans as reservoirs and rivers dry up, with increased risk of wildfires.

News.title: PC Andrew Harper’s mum says she’s been ‘turned inside out’ after Government’s chaotic U-turn over killers’ early release
News.content:
THE mother of PC Andrew Harper has said she had been “turned inside out” after a chaotic Government U-turn over the early release of his killers.

After days of confusion, Andy Burnham said he was “increasingly confident” a way could be found to prevent thugs Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole being allowed out of jail.



But the PM stopped short of confirming how, or whether the pair will remain locked up.

Officials had spent days briefing that it was proving too hard to stop the duo’s early release without tipping crowded prisons into chaos.



PC Harper’s mum, Debbie Adlam, blasted the “gut-wrenching” confusion as she revealed Downing Street had called her to claim the PM was doing “everything he can”.

She told ITV’s Good Morning Britain: “I just don’t know how to think, how to feel. It’s turned me inside out.” Separately, she said: “It feels like a hash . . . a rush job.



“It feels like nobody’s put enough effort into actually look for reasons or ways. We are having to push on every level. They [Bowers and Cole] weren’t given extreme sentences.

“I’m only asking for them to do what they were given.”

Claire Waxman, Victims’ Commissioner for England and Wales, accused the PM of “flip-flopping” over early release. She said: “I’m not really sure what to call it other than “flip-flopping”.

“From a victim’s perspective, the position appears to keep changing.”



Thames Valley Police Federation chairwoman Aileen O’Connor, who started the petition calling for Bowers and Cole to be kept inside, said that Labour had “sent a deeply troubling message” about the value it placed on police officers.

Ms O’Connor, whose petition had last night been signed by more than 915,000 people, said: “Their actions so far have been totally demoralising for all police officers.”

She accepted, however, that there was now a “glimmer of hope”.



Newly-married PC Harper died after getting caught up in a strap attached to the rear of a car.

He was dragged more than a mile as the killers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berks, in 2019. Bowers and Cole, both 17 at the time of the crime, got 13 years in 2020 after being convicted of manslaughter.

They are due for release next year after completing half of their sentences but before this year’s Sentencing Act they would have served two-thirds.

Hopes were raised for PC Harper’s family when the PM ordered a review of the scheme.

Changes were made including preventing rapists and paedophiles from being let out early — but not include those convicted of manslaughter like Bowers and Cole.



The PM has said he does not want any lags let out early and has asked for three areas to be examined with a view to this aim.

He wants to increase the rate at which foreign criminals are sent back to their country of origin.

He is also looking to fix the dispute over Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences — abolished in 2012 — under which more than 2,300 people are indefinitely detained or trapped in a cycle of lifelong recall, and the release of lower-risk offenders.



Another possibility is the use of female jails for male criminals.

Mr Burnham said: “I’ve heard the depth of concern felt across the country about the potential release of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

“Obviously I feel for the family and the anguish they’re going through. What I’ve done since I came into office is push the system every single day to go further.

“I’ve not accepted it’s impossible to do more. I believe there is more that can be done.”

Communities Secretary Angela Rayner said the PM was “really clear” the plan would keep the worst offenders in jail.



Justice Secretary Alex Norris will draw up plans ready for Parliament’s return from its summer break.

Victims’ Commissioner Ms Waxman added: “While I understand the new Prime Minister is finding this new sentencing legislation very difficult, it’s legislation that got passed and came in in January.

“If he doesn’t like it then it doesn’t commence — but that means we’ll run out of spaces in prison.



“But he’s got to make a decision. And he should have done when he announced the outcome of the review last week.

“I think we’re losing sight of the thousands of people that this is impacting across the country.

“Bereaved families they want clarity and certainty about what lies ahead. Continued uncertainty is only adding to their distress.”

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: “Andy Burnham and Labour are re-traumatising victims and their families with their constant U-turns.

“It’s clear that good vibes and a snazzy T-shirt do not make for competent government.



“Mr Burnham is letting down victims and their families every day. It’s not good enough.”

Meanwhile, probation officers have voted overwhelmingly in favour of potential strike action in protest against the early release scheme.

Ninety per cent of the members of Napo, the probation union, said the system was already struggling to cope, and that a bigger workload will put public safety at risk.

The Ministry of Justice said it was “disappointed” at the outcome of the indicative ballot after they agreed a pay increase earlier this year.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Napo national chair Ben Cockburn said: “This ballot wasn’t about members being too busy.



“It was professionals warning they cannot protect the public properly when there are not enough people to do the work.”

News.title: Nigel Farage says he’d STILL take £5m crypto donation despite investigation ahead of by-election
News.content:
NIGEL Farage said he would still take the controversial £5million donation from a cryptobillionaire even now — as he prepares to fight a by-election tomorrow.

The Reform UK leader insisted he had no regrets accepting it and will need protection for the rest of his life.



Before resigning as an MP and forcing a fresh contest in his constituency of Clacton, Essex, he was under investigation by Parliament’s ethics watchdog for failing to declare the money from Christopher Harborne.

That could reopen upon his likely return to Parliament. And it will force him to fight another by-election if it finds him in major breach of Commons rules.



Speaking to The Sun at Clacton yesterday, Mr Farage said: “If I get the result I want, if Standards decide that they want to do it again, well, I think they’d look rather silly.”

He has argued he did not need to declare the £5million as it was gifted to him before he became an MP when he had no intention of returning to frontline politics.

It has been the source of relentless criticism and scrutiny on his finances in recent months.

And Mr Farage is also mindful of his security in the wake of the death in her own home of Reform spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe.



Asked if he would still have taken the money if he knew of the subsequent hassle, he said: “Oh yes. Ann Widdecombe was 78 years old.

“She was murdered. She had nothing apart from CCTV.

“She had no personal protection whatsoever. I’m going to need it till the day I die. You can see that around me now.”

During our interview with the Sun, a pair of hecklers began yelling at Mr Farage about the £5million row and were kept back by his security.

He is the overwhelming favourite to win re-election to Parliament tomorrow after rival parties refused to partake in what they described as a “stunt”.



Instead his main opponent is the comedy candidate Count Binface who has emerged as the vehicle for anti-Farage voters.

Branding his rival the “Establishment candidate”, Mr Farage said: “I’m hoping for a big thumping vote, and that’ll be a message back to an Establishment that’s done its best over the last few months, not to give us an even break, literally on anything.”

News.title: World erupted when Wacko Jacko dangled baby off balcony, but somehow it’s OK for tot to be chucked on death-trap dinghy?
News.content:
WHEN Michael Jackson dangled his baby son over a hotel balcony in Berlin, the world rightly lost its mind.

Yet when an asylum seeker in a puffa jacket and life vest dangles a tiny baby dressed in just a flimsy Babygro, no one bats an eyelid as they clamber aboard a potential death-trap dinghy to make the perilous crossing to the UK.



Not least the French police who, despite being paid millions by us to supposedly stop these boats, appear to be se moquer — aka taking the piss — and doing ­nothing.

Wacko Jacko and the migrant boats ­crisis might be two very different ­scenarios, but they are identical in presenting danger to a small child.

Thanks to luck, good weather, and the French coastguard following to make sure it didn’t sink, the small boat arrived safely in the UK.



But this Russian roulette of desperate people cannot go on. The following day, the biggest-ever Channel migrant boat — carrying an astonishing 230 people — arrived here too.

That number of people could have filled a Ryanair plane but, of course, they wouldn’t be able to board without documents

So why the hell are they being allowed to dodge passport control and board an equivalent-sized boat to get here?

It’s a reasonable question that no Government minister seems able to answer.

Yesterday, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner was asked about it and filled the allotted airtime with word salad platitudes like, “You’re absolutely right, more needs to be done” and “Nobody wants to see babies and toddlers washed ashore” and “We’re in constant dialogue with the French”. Blah blah blah.



But a coherent policy on how they’re going to stop people-smuggling in these dangerously flimsy vessels wasn’t forthcoming.

Nor was it when Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood came on Loose Women in June and I asked her why, as we have a £660million deal with France, we don’t pick the boats up in the Channel and escort them back there?

Not least because it would act as an obvious deterrent against getting in one of these boats in the first place.

She replied that once the migrants get to the mid-line of the Channel, they are in our waters and therefore become our responsibility.

To take them back, she said, “you have to have an agreement”.



She added: “What we’re paying for is law enforcement activity and I have seen that working for myself.”

Well, it doesn’t appear to be working this week and, with photos of this mega-boat circulating on social media and another heatwave looming, there will soon be plenty more risking their lives to get here.

The reality, one suspects, is that France is more than happy for them to become our problem and not theirs.

So the Decathlon at Dunkirk-sur-Mer flogs life vests in bulk to the people- smugglers, the gendarmes frequently turn a blind eye, and the French coastguard escorts them safely to the “mid-line” where either our Navy, Border Force or the RNLI taxi them to their chosen destination of good old Blighty.

And doubtless nothing will change until more children die. How utterly tragic.



‘PROF’ NEEDS FAMILY

THE famous maxim of journalism is “who is this bastard and why are they lying to me?”

Yet when I appeared on Laura Kuenssberg’s ­Sunday morning show in March last year, my fellow newspaper reviewer was a man so admirably humble about his many academic achievements that my bulls**tometer remained dormant.

It was Jason Arday, “Cambridge’s youngest black professor,” an accolade all the more incredible because, he told me, he’d been mute until the age of 11 and unable to read and write before he was 18.

Incredible indeed. Turns out that most of the professor’s claims were, at best, exaggerated, at worst utter bunkum.



Someone forwarded me a round robin email he’d sent to “friends” at the time, saying that a “two-year campaign” by other academics accusing him of plagiarism “has now reached The Times, who want to publish a piece academically discrediting me”.

He was asking for signatories to an open letter he’d drafted himself to then-Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson, saying: “The integrity of the Academy [i.e academia itself] is at risk from right-wing extremists if we do not take a stand and speak out against the racist attempts to erase black scholarship.”

We now know that the only risk to the integrity of anyone involved in this unholy mess is Jason himself, who cried “racism” to try to shut down scrutiny.

Look, no one died and, if anything, he’s done academia a favour by exposing its weaknesses.

So I hope he’s OK and getting support from his “wife and two children” – ­ assuming they exist.



JUST two weeks into his premiership, our new PM Andy ­Burnham sparked outrage by going on holiday with his family.

Give him a break. (Er, isn’t he already on one? – Ed). After all, it was ­probably booked before he knew he would waltz into No10 off the back of 25,000 votes in Makerfield. Like as far back as, ooh, June maybe.

SYDNEY’S SIMPLY THE BUST FOR BLOKES

SCIENTISTS in Japan have conducted a study among men to ask what they find physically attractive in a woman.

The conclusion is a large bust and small waist – in other words, Sydney Sweeney.



I can’t imagine why.

Next week, a survey reveals that bears s**t in the woods.

AS any social ­etiquette expert will tell you, wearing white to a friend’s wedding isn’t the done thing.

Yet Geri “only wears white” Horner pitched up at fellow Spice Girl Mel C’s nuptials in a floor-length outfit that only just ­teetered on the edges of acceptability thanks to a smattering of flowers.



Mel laughed it off, ­probably just grateful she didn’t wear that Union Jack mini dress.

And let’s face it, you don’t always have to wear white to pull focus from the bride.

As ably demonstrated by wedding guest Kendall Jenner, when, in 2021, her risque frock at a friend’s big day, prompted the question: “What bride?”

NOT A PRIVATE MIATTA



ENERGY Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh was a big fan of Labour slapping VAT on private school fees.

But she’s now been accused of “classic champagne socialism” after it has been revealed that all three of her children are privately educated at a probable bare minimum cost of £50,000 a year.

I have no issue with politicians of any party persuasion educating their kids at fee-paying schools.

It’s just when they make it difficult for others to do so that it grates.

Ms Fahnbulleh is married to a hedge-funder so, with their joint income, the extra 20 per cent on fees is a mere drop in the ocean.



But a lot of the “working people” her Government purports to be a champion of don’t have that kind of money.

So they scrimp, save and borrow to educate their kids privately, and the extra demand is a tipping point.

Hence why independent schools have lost 30,000 pupils since the rise and around 100 of them have closed.

What a dumb policy.

News.title: Masked thug, 28, hotwires tractor and drives it ‘full throttle’ into family home smashing huge hole through front window
News.content:
A MASKED thug who hotwired a tractor and smashed into a family home at full speed is now facing time behind bars.

Nathan Blagg, 28, ploughed the vehicle into a terrace house in Middlesborough just after 1am on May 9.



Footage shows the red Massey Ferguson backing away from the property unsteadily, after smashing a hole through the terrace’s front window.

Locals who witnessed the incident reported hearing the tractor barge into the terrace, as neighbours were forced to evacuate.



One resident, who filmed the crash, said: “I heard it and felt it, it reversed into a car and drove back again.

“They were all in balaclavas and hoodies. It was the most insane thing I’ve ever seen.”





Blagg, of Addlington Drive, Middlesborough, appeared at Teesside Crown Court on August 4, where he admitted aggravated vehicle taking and criminal damage.

He had previously pleaded guilty before magistrates to affray and another count of aggravated vehicle taking.

Judge Clews said: “It seems to me that the sentence you will ultimately receive will be a custodial sentence and of some length.

“Nevertheless a pre-sentence report may be of some assistance.”

The family was not in the property at the time of the crash due to an alleged break-in weeks before, which had a left the interiors “smashed up”.



Following the collision, farmer Ian Tate arrived to find his tractor still lodged in the front wall with its engine whirring.

“There was no key in the ignition,” he told The Mail on Sunday.

“This was a good ten hours after the crash.

“I don’t know if they can hotwire these modern tractors or not.”

He added that the machines were “complicated to handle” and that the user had to “know what they were doing”.



The vehicle was later removed from the property on May 12.

Blagg remains in custody until his next appearance.

News.title: When will it rain? Latest Met Office weather forecast with UK heatwave predicted this week
News.content:
IT has been a hot, dry summer for much of the UK, which looks set to continue for many regions this week.

The Met Office says another heatwave is developing, with temperatures expected to peak on Thursday as the mercury soars yet again.



An amber heat health alert has been issued for much of England, where the forecaster predicts that temperatures could reach 36C or 37C.

And following an extended period of dry conditions, nearly three-quarters of England, and the entirety of Wales, are experiencing drought – here’s when to expect rain to return.



When will it rain in the UK?

While it is dry and sunny across much of the UK currently, Northwest Scotland and western Northern Ireland are notable exceptions.

The Met Office is forecasting outbreaks of light rain in these regions on Tuesday.



Showers will then return to western Scotland and western Northern Ireland on Wednesday, becoming heavy at times.

Elsewhere, the next couple of days are expected to be hot, dry and sunny across much of England and Wales, with heatwave conditions likely for many areas.

It is then forecast to remain largely dry from Thursday into the weekend, with northern areas seeing some showers arriving on Saturday.

The Met Office says Atlantic weather systems are likely to approach or move across the UK later from Sunday into the start of next week, which will bring some wetter conditions.



These could bring rain to some areas, perhaps heavy at times, while there is also a risk of thunderstorms in the south early next week.

But the forecasting service expects high pressure to become more dominant towards the end of next week, bringing drier conditions back to many areas.

When will the heatwave start?

The Met Office said a widespread heatwave is expected across England and Wales, with temperatures climbing day by day as high pressure builds.

Southerly and south-easterly winds are also drawing in hot air from Europe, helping temperatures rise further.

Thursday is expected to be the hottest day, with the amber heat health warning in force from 9am until 11.59pm.



It covers parts of the East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands, Yorkshire and Humber, London and the South East.

If temperatures reach or exceed these daily limits for three full days in a row, an official heatwave is declared for that area.

The Met Office predicts that the heatwave should begin to ease after Thursday’s peak.

Some warmth will remain across the south and southeast on Friday before cooler air spreads south from the northwest on Saturday, bringing a lower temperatures more widely.

What is a heatwave?

The Met Office defines an official heatwave as when temperatures in a certain area meet or exceed a specific threshold for three consecutive days.
