News.title: Dozens of police chiefs urge PM Andy Burnham to prevent PC Andrew Harper killers' early prison release
News.content:
Dozens of police chiefs urge PM Andy Burnham to prevent PC Andrew Harper killers' early prison release

Andy Burnham is 'increasingly confident' the killers of PC Andrew Harper will not be released early, but an open letter has demanded drastic changes and stronger protections

View 4 Images Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Stephen Watson is one of dozens to sign the letter (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

An open letter signed by 50 police and law enforcement leaders from across Britain has demanded PC Andrew Harper's killers remain locked up.

In an unpresented move, dozens of high-ranking officers have written to the Prime Minister with three key demands, as Andy Burnham comes under increasing pressure from victims' families not to allow Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers - sentenced to 13 years for the cop's manslaughter in 2020 - to be freed in January.

The new PM has ordered an urgent review into the controversial plan. A change was expected to sentencing rules from October 1, meaning most adults serving a standard prison sentence would be released earlier than the date originally set. Prisoners convicted of less serious offences were also expected to leave jail after a third of their sentence.

4 View 4 Images PC Andrew Harper was killed back in 2019 (Image: Thames Valley Police/PA Wire) 4 View 4 Images Andy Burnham is 'confident' the killers will remain behind bars (Image: Sean Hansford | Manchester Evening News)

Should the early prisoner release scheme be paused? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

Andy Burnham confident release of PC Harper's killers will be blocked READ MORE :

Mr Burnham said he is “increasingly confident” the killers of PC Harper will not be released early, but that hasn't stopped the open letter being published. Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Stephen Watson and Commissioner Pete O’Doherty were just two of the officials to put their name to it.

They asked the Government to consider three measures, and wanted every lawful option examined to determine whether the earlier release of those responsible for the PC's death could be prevented.

Article continues below

They also wanted additional public protection safeguarding to be established in cases involving the most serious offenders whenever future changes to sentencing on release arrangements are considered.

Thirdly, they demanded victims and bereaved families must be "properly considered" whenever significant changes are made to sentencing or release arrangements.

View 4 Images The PM is under intense public pressure regarding the potential early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers (Image: Thames Valley Police/PA Wire)

Justice Secretary Alex Norris has been tasked by Mr Burnham with finding ways to keep the serious offenders in prison.

The letter read: "Dear Prime Minister, We welcome your intervention regarding the potential earlier release of those responsible for the death of PC Andrew Harper, and your instruction to the Justice Secretary to examine what can lawfully be done.

"When the state asks people to run towards danger on behalf of the public, they should be able to trust that the justice system will stand behind them when the worst happens. PC Andrew Harper's case also raises a wider question.

"When someone is sentenced for an exceptionally serious offence, how much confidence can victims, bereaved families and the public place in that sentence if subsequent changes to release arrangements result in an offender being released significantly earlier than originally anticipated? This question extends far beyond policing.

"Families across the country are now facing the distress of learning that offenders may be released earlier than they understood when sentence was passed. We do not suggest that the grief of a police family is greater than that of any other bereaved family, nor that the life of an emergency worker has greater value.

"Our concern is for all victims and families affected by serious offending sentencing changes. PC Andrew Harper lost his life while protecting the public and serving his community. Following his death, Lissie Harper campaigned for a change in the law, leading Parliament to establish Harper's Law, recognising the exceptional risks emergency workers take while protecting others.

"Police officers and staff see first-hand the impact serious crime has on victims and their families. They support people through some of the most difficult moments of their lives and ask them to place their trust in the justice system. That trust is vital and should not be weakened.

"We are also collectively concerned that an approach to early release which does not sufficiently distinguish the most serious offending risks undermining public safety, victim confidence and wider confidence in the criminal justice system."

Article continues below

All those who have signed the letter

News.title: Pub giant announces major shake-up as 65 locations hit the market
News.content:
Pub giant announces major shake-up as 65 locations hit the market

Brewer and pub operator Greene King is putting around 65 pubs up for sale as part of a massive shake-up dubbed Project Portico

View 2 Images The chain owns pubs across the UK (Image: Mail News Media Ltd)

Around 65 Greene King pubs are due to be put up for sale as the pub giant says it is currently reviewing dozens of sites for potential sale.

‌



The latest shake-up of Greene King’s massive property empire will see venues put up for sale either individually or as part of larger groups, the brewer and pub operator said.

‌



The sale will include around 65 predominantly “wet-led” pubs across the UK – meaning they focus mainly on selling drinks rather than food, according to industry publication Propel.

‌



Potential buyers could reportedly snap up the entire portfolio, smaller groups of pubs or individual venues. However Greene King has not yet revealed which pubs are included in the package.

A Greene King spokesperson said: “As part of our pub estate strategy announced earlier this year, we identified a number of pubs for potential sale in the medium term.

View 2 Images About 65 pubs are due to come up for sale

‌



“As a result, we are reviewing each pub to determine the most appropriate route to market, which may involve an open sales process or a targeted off-market approach.

“In either case, prospective purchasers may seek to acquire individual or multiple sites.”

No closures have been announced in connection with the move, with pubs that are sold not necessarily due to close. Pubs with a similar operational focus had been presented collectively to prospective buyers, the company said.

‌



The sell-off, known internally as Project Portico, is part of a wider shake-up announced by Greene King in March.

Around 300 managed pubs, identified as potentially being “better suited to different operating models” will become leased, tenanted or franchised as part of Greene King’s Pub Partners scheme.

The remaining 150 are being evaluated for potential sale with the cash reinvested into Greene King’s core pub estate, the company previously said.

‌



In April, Greene King put 13 freehold pubs and hotels on the market, with a total of 420 bedrooms. They included Ye Olde Talbot in Worcester, the Cromwell Lodge Hotel in Banbury and the Bear Hotel in Havant.

Another 10 freehold managed pubs went onto the market in May. Eight had a combined asking price of around £9.4million, while offers were invited for the remaining two. Six were still trading when they went on the market, while four had already closed.

Greene King operates around 2,500 pubs, including approximately 1,000 leased, tenanted and franchised venues.

Article continues below

Its latest financial results showed revenue climbed 3.6 per cent to £2.539billion, while adjusted operating profit rose 9.8 per cent to £217.4million.

News.title: 'Bigger boats crossing the Channel are a warning sign that people smugglers will keep adapting'
News.content:
'Bigger boats crossing the Channel are a warning sign that people smugglers will keep adapting'

"Break the supply of boats and engines, disrupt the money, identify the organisers and work with our European partners to stop launches before desperate migrants are packed aboard"

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

The emergence of so-called mega dinghies in the Channel shows just how quickly the criminal smuggling gangs change tactics when pressure is put on them.

‌



That is why Britain cannot simply wait for these boats to reach the French coast. British intelligence is already working with foreign agencies to trace where the vessels are made, how they are moved across borders, where they are assembled and who is behind the networks supplying them.

‌



That is exactly where this battle has to be fought. Break the supply of boats and engines, disrupt the money, identify the organisers and work with our European partners to stop launches before desperate migrants are packed aboard.

‌



There are encouraging signs. Crossings are down by more than 40 per cent, and gangs are being dismantled.

But these bigger boats are a warning that the smugglers will keep adapting. The answer is relentless international pressure, intelligence-sharing and enforcement.

Smash the supply chain, and you smash the trade in human lives.

‌



Real leadership

Andy Burnham inherited a prison system in crisis and legislation risking early release for serious offenders.

He did not inherit the public anger that followed, but he has listened. The outrage over the possible early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, convicted of killing PC Andrew Harper, was understandable.

Andrew's family have suffered enough without watching them walk free early. Mr Burnham shares that concern and is acting.

‌



The Justice Secretary has been ordered to find extra prison capacity, speed up deportations and keep serious criminals behind bars. Governments cannot always control the problems they inherit. They can control how they respond.

Here, the Prime Minister heard the public and changed course. It is what leadership should look like.

No red card yet

After 62 seasons and more than 5,000 matches, Ken Wright still refuses to blow time on a remarkable refereeing career.

Article continues below

At 78, the world’s longest-serving man in black is back for another season in Swansea. Some refs lose the crowd. Ken has outlasted several generations of them.

Clearly, he still loves the shrill.

News.title: Should the early prisoner release scheme be paused? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Should the early prisoner release scheme be paused? Take our poll and have your say

Despite claims the government has U-turned on the early prisoner release scheme over rising pressure, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said 'nothing has changed'

View 3 Images The Prime Minister is facing his first major hurdle as the pressure grows to scrap the plan (Image: Corbis via Getty Images)

The early prisoner release scheme has already suffered a number of significant set-backs after the new Prime Minister ordered an urgent review in a dramatic intervention.

‌



From October 1, a change was expected to sentencing rules, meaning most adults serving a standard prison sentence would be released earlier than the date originally set. Prisoners convicted of less serious offences were also expected to leave jail after a third of their sentence.

‌



After Andy Burnham said the controversial idea would be paused, many are calling for a longer delay - with some suggesting it should be scrapped altogether and more ideas put forward to ease prison overcrowding.

‌



View 3 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham has paused the programme (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/POOL PA via AP)

The scheme drew criticism from survivors and victims' families, including the widow of PC Andrew Harper, who described the possibility of his killers Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers being released early as "deplorable".

Mr Burnham admitted he wanted to go even further and ban other offenders from having their time in prison shortened, as Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the pause aimed to "give victims and survivors certainty" and the government wanted to make sure it got "the implementation of this policy right".

‌



Today, Mr Burnham vowed to press "every single day to go further” on limiting the number of inmates who will be set free.

Downing Street previously said it was “not possible” to exempt “one or two offenders” convicted of manslaughter from the early release scheme, only for the PM to order his Justice Secretary to look again at the issue.

‌



In a statement Mr Burnham said he is “increasingly confident” that plans to increase headroom in prisons will mean the number of criminals being released early, including two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers, can be reduced.

He said: "I have asked the Justice Secretary [Alex Norris] to fast-track the development of a plan for presentation to Parliament early next month to create more headroom within the prison system.

View 3 Images The government is under intense public pressure regarding the potential early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers (Image: Thames Valley Police/PA Wire)

‌



“It will be based on a range of options including the three strands of further work I asked him to initiate last week: increasing the rate of removal of foreign national offenders from the prison estate to their country of origin; finding an early resolution to the long-running injustice of IPP sentences, which could allow for the release of lower-risk prisoners; and making greater use of the entire prison estate including using the female estate for male offenders.

“I am increasingly confident that a more focused approach along these lines will allow us to reduce the number of people released early and, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC Harper, prevent their early release altogether.

“In advance of the Justice Secretary’s proposals being presented to Parliament, we will seek to engage other political parties in discussions with the aim of gaining the widest possible public and political consensus on the approach being taken.

Article continues below

"However, I recognise that, even with all these changes, there will be concerns from many victims about who will still be released early for other offences. I am doing all I can, but it is simply not possible to prevent all offenders from being released early without the prison system collapsing.”

News.title: Mum who had winning lottery ticket thrown in the bin finally bags £12million Lotto jackpot
News.content:
Mum who had winning lottery ticket thrown in the bin finally bags £12million Lotto jackpot

After her winning Lotto ticket was inadvertently thrown away by a shopkeeper, mum-of-two Kath Main faced a hellish four-week wait to see if she would scoop the life-changing sum

View 2 Images Kath Main only realised she had a winning ticket hours after the bin had already been emptied (Image: Kath Main/Facebook)

A mum who endured an excruciating 30-day wait to find out if she had won £12million after her lottery ticket was thrown in the bin by a shopkeeper will scoop the lot.

‌



Kath Main, 46, discovered the June 6 Lotto jackpot had remained unclaimed and recognised the winning numbers 10, 26, 30, 35 and 42, remembering they corresponded with the identical combination she has played for more than 20 years.

‌



However, the ticket had been thrown away after she took it to a Londis store in Abercynon, south Wales, to be verified after she was supposedly informed it was not a winner. The National Lottery operator Allwyn has been examining the allegation ever since an appeal was lodged.

‌



Over a month later, she found out the good news and now she's planning what to do with the cash. A spokesman for the operator confirmed the pay-out, saying: "We are the only major lottery which is able to look to pay a winner even if they have lost their ticket.

View 2 Images When she realised the prize had gone unclaimed, she had to double check (Image: Kath Main/Facebook)

Bin men spent TWO DAYS searching through rubbish after woman threw away winning lotto ticket READ MORE :

"The investigation we conduct is designed to ensure any claim is from the rightful ticketholder. We are then able, at our discretion, to pay that player once the claim period has expired 180 days after the draw. We are proud to pay out millions of prizes as well as raising over £33million for Good Causes each week."

‌



Kath, a mother-of-two who serves as a rugby club treasurer, hasn't yet spoken about her win, but said last month that the uncertainty left her struggling to manage.

"I just feel sick all the time, it's the not knowing and waiting," she said. "I saw there was an unclaimed lottery ticket and checked the numbers and realised they were mine.

"I rang my mother and said, 'You did put the lottery on?' and she said 'Yeah'. I said, 'Well we've won the lottery,' and she said, 'I checked and there was no winners'. I said 'No, it's a winner, we've won'."

‌



When Kath enquired about the ticket's whereabouts, she was informed it had been thrown away. When the worker accepted the ticket for verification, they stated the machine failed to generate the customary alert and the shop assistant informed her no winning prize had been displayed.

The Londis shop didn't have CCTV because it was being refurbished. Proprietor Karan Kumar said: "The machine could have been playing up. Now they are doing an investigation. It would be amazing if she won."

Kath revealed that one ambition would be to travel to New Zealand for the Lions rugby tour in 2029.

Article continues below

Some previous players have also managed to secure big prizes after initially misplacing their tickets. Builder Andrew Clarke claimed £76million in 2018 despite losing his ticket for six weeks.

He said at the time: "It almost feels like some magical Christmas story, the man who nearly lost £76 million!"

News.title: 'My son, 7, had six teeth removed after inhumane wait for treatment'
News.content:
'My son, 7, had six teeth removed after inhumane wait for treatment'

EXCLUSIVE: Children under 18, or under 19 and in full-time-education, can get free NHS dental appointments and treatment but there is a shortage of NHS practices

View 2 Images Hayley Bramhall, from Macclesfield, said it was "devastating" to see her son Philip in agony (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

A mum whose seven-year-old autistic son had six teeth removed due to a dental abscess has said it was "inhumane" he had to suffer a four-month wait in intense pain.

‌



Hayley Bramhall, from Macclesfield, said it was "devastating" to see her son Philip in agony. During the wait for "urgent" treatment, his abscess grew leading to the need for him to have teeth taken out.

‌



She said her non-verbal son has been holding his mouth and avoiding toothbrushing in a particular area since his surgery in July and she fears they might have to face another long and painful battle if he has another dental problem.

‌



Speaking about him having six teeth removed, Hayley said: "Eating's become more challenging because of that. He's a lot more irate and upset. As a family and for me, it's traumatic. It's frustrating. It makes you feel angry - angry at the lack of services.

Children waiting over a year in agony for tooth extractions READ MORE :

View 2 Images Nearly 10,000 children were admitted to hospital for rotting teeth last year, damning figures show. (Image: Getty Images)

"Frustrated at the fact that, for example, now I need to start the process again because I think he's got toothache. Although I don't know whether it's because he was in pain for four months, which is just inhumane in itself."

‌



Hayley has launched a petition on the Parliament website calling for a maximum 12-week wait for children with special educational needs requiring urgent dental care under sedation or general anaesthetic.

She said her son needs sedation and general anaesthetic just for check up, which can mean long waits that result in the problem getting worse.

"I think the pressure and the wait just for that is exceptional, never mind the wait for someone in extreme pain," she said. "It's devastating as a parent seeing him in pain all the time."

‌



Nearly 10,000 children admitted to hospital for rotting teeth last year, grim study shows

Nearly 10,000 children were admitted to hospital for rotting teeth last year, damning figures show.

In 2025, 8,930 under 18s were admitted for tooth decay, slightly up from 8,925 the year before, analysis by the Liberal Democrats shows.

Children under 18, or under 19 and in full-time-education, can get free NHS dental appointments and treatment but there is a shortage of NHS practices. Around 14 million people – or well over one in four of England’s adult population – were unable to access NHS dental care in 2025.

‌



The study found 470 dental practices have pulled out of the NHS and handed back their contracts since 2020 as ‘dental deserts’ spread across the country.

The research also found particular damage in rural areas, with higher numbers of dentists approaching retirement and a higher proportion leaving the profession.

Elsewhere, researchers found local Education Authorities have shelled out over £2.5million for school-aged pupils since 2020, including on toothbrush kits and on public health initiatives.

‌



Tooth decay remains the number one reason for hospital admissions among young children. The British Dental Association says some kids are waiting years to have teeth extracted because the surgery is competing with other operations on the NHS waiting list for operating theatre time.

Children usually require going under general anaesthetic for tooth extractions so this has to be done in hospital.

Lib Dem primary care spokeswoman Helen Maguire said: “Thousands of young children are being forced into hospital beds just to have their rotting teeth pulled out, millions are trapped in expanding 'dental deserts' unable to get an appointment, and local councils are being forced to shell out millions to patch up a broken system.”

‌



The Liberal Democrats have demanded a £750million Dental Rescue Package to revive access to local NHS appointments and guarantee regular checkups for children. It is also calling for emergency dental A&Es in every community across the country that provide walk-in urgent care seven days a week to ensure that nobody is left in agony.

The British Dental Association welcomed the commitment to new money and criticised a lack of new investment from the Labour Government. The Mirror has launched the Dentists for All campaign with the BDA calling for a return to universal access to NHS dentistry for everyone who needs it.

Eddie Crouch, BDA chair, said: “When millions of people have no options, it’s refreshing to see serious proposals to invest in expanding access to NHS dental care. The real threat to NHS dentistry has always been a poverty of ambition. Rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic won’t help.”

‌



More than 40,000 people have signed a petition launched by 38 Degrees calling on Andy Burnham to make NHS Dentistry a priority, amid a crisis of people being forced to carry out DIY Dentistry and pull out their own teeth.

Veronica Hawking, Campaigns Director at 38 Degrees, said: "Nobody in modern Britain should be pulling out their own teeth because they can't get an NHS dentist.

"The Government has the public firmly on side - now it needs to properly fund NHS dentistry, so no one else is forced to take matters into their own hands."

Article continues below

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "This government is fixing NHS dentistry after a decade of decline. We have improved access to urgent dental treatment by prioritising patients with the greatest need, and millions of additional courses of treatment have been delivered, including a significant amount for children.

“But there is still more to do - especially to increase the dentistry workforce - and that is why we’re rolling out more dentistry school training places in areas which need them, and cutting red tape to allow qualified dentists to practise.”

News.title: Major nuclear power station shut down by millions of invading jellyfish
News.content:
Major nuclear power station shut down by millions of invading jellyfish

The massive Gravelines nuclear power plant just 30 miles from Britain has been forced to close down in order to avoid disaster after a swarm of jellyfish got sucked into the cooling system on Monday

View 2 Images Jellyfish on the shore near the Gravelines nuclear power plant in Gravelines, northern France (file photo) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Western Europe’s biggest nuclear power station has been shut down after it was invaded by millions of jellyfish.

‌



EDF’s Gravelines plant near Dunkirk, just 30 miles from Britain, was forced to shut down in order to avoid disaster on Monday as the sea creatures swarmed into the plant.

‌



EDF revealed how the jellyfish had been filter drums at the seawater pumping stations, used to cool the giant nuclear reactors at the heart of the plant.

‌



The company was forced to take emergency measures, with reactors two, three and four taken offline, while output from reactor one was halved.

“This situation has no impact on the safety of the facilities, the safety of our personnel, or the environment,” a statement from EDF said.

Only reactor six was operating at full power on Tuesday, with reactor five previously taken offline for scheduled works.

‌



View 2 Images A massive influx of jellyfish into seawater pumping stations has caused chaos at the Gravelines nuclear powe (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The massive Gravelines plant has six reactors and pumps out 5,400 megawatts of juice, supplying around 70 per cent of the power in northern France’s Hauts-de-France region each year.

The jellyfish invasion comes exactly a year after another swarm of the creatures took the French nuclear site offline for two days.

‌



An invasive species of jellyfish, called the Asian Moon Jellyfish, have been making themselves at home in the English Channel and North Sea in 2020.

The species, usually native to the Pacific, is thought to have been brought here in the ballast tanks of supertankers and dumped into the seas around France and Britain.

Nuclear plants in China, Japan and India, which also rely of seawater for cooling, have previously been thrown into chaos by the slimy sea creatures. And last year power production at Gravelines came to a standstill after the jellies caused chaos.

Article continues below

The plant installed cameras monitoring the seawater intake and filters after last year’s fiasco and set up a warning system to give advanced notice of swarms heading their way.

The system saw fishing boats sent out of saturday with trawler nets in an attempt to thin the numbers of the invasive jellyfish. This helped to limit the latest invasion, the engineer said.

Meanwhile vacuum trucks are sucking out the jellyfish already trapped inside the plant. The engineer said that since no new jellies are arriving the plant will hopefully be back on line soon.

News.title: Mum reveals how son survived head-on motorway crash as car ‘drove wrong way’
News.content:
Mum reveals how son survived head-on motorway crash as car ‘drove wrong way’

Craig Fox, 22, miraculously walked away from a head-on collision on the M50 after he was hit by what is believed to be a stolen Toyota Yaris carrying eight underage teens as travelling 100mph.

View 2 Images The scene of the crash near junction 12 of the M50 (Image: © 2026 COLLINS PHOTO AGENCY)

A shocked mum has spoken of the moment she arrived at the scene of a crash involving her innocent son and a car allegedly carrying eight underage teenagers.

‌



The devastating collision took place as Sarah Jane Fox's son, Craig, 22, was driving on the M50 in Dublin when a reportedly stolen Toyota Yaris crashed into his Skoda Fabia head-on. The Toyota was travelling the wrong way down an off-ramp near junction 12 of the motorway at Firhouse around 5.30am on Sunday.

‌



It has been reported that eight teenagers, all under 16, were in the Toyota, including a 13-year-old boy who suffered critical, life-threatening injuries. Craig and the other seven teenagers were also taken to hospital, with the 22-year-old suffering internal bleeding.

‌



Still, he stepped out of his car to check on the teenagers in the other vehicle, with Ms Fox saying "there were guardian angels" watching over her son, who remains in shock in hospital after the crash.

"There were guardian angels with my child on Sunday morning," Ms Fox told the Neil Prendeville Show. "It's the only thing I can tell you how he walked out of that car."

She said Craig managed to get out of the wreckage before sitting down around 10 feet away. "But he walked out of that car and checked on the other kids. He was asking how they were."

‌



Ms Fox said Craig suffered internal bleeding following the crash but was able to avoid surgery. "Craig is doing well at the moment. He's stable," she said. "He had some internal bleeding yesterday, but it stopped without surgery, which was a relief.

"He's sitting up, talking, but he is sore all over, which is expected. He was hit head-on at 100 kilometres an hour so he's in shock as well."

View 2 Images Sarah Jane Fox believes 'guardian angels' were responsible for her son's survival (Image: Image: Mick O'Neill/Daily Mirror/Irish Daily Star.)

‌



Craig called his mother from a police officer's phone just after 5.30am to inform her of the incident. This was due to his own phone being thrown from the car during the crash, the Irish Mirror reports.

Ms Fox said: "Craig rang me at 5:32 from a police officer's phone. He couldn't find his phone. We realised then it had flown out of the car when it was spinning.

"He rang me from the police officer's phone, and I got into my car and was across the M50 as quickly as I could." Emergency services were on the scene within minutes, the mother said.

‌



"Craig said it was no more than two minutes before the police were jumping the barrier on the M50 because they came down the correct side of the road and came across to him," she said. The mother said she was particularly distressed after learning that those in the other vehicle were under 16.

"I'm not going to get into that part of it, but I have a feeling that another word isn't being used," she said. Asked about the ages, she confirmed: "Yeah, under 16."

Ms Fox said she had seen TikTok videos involving the young people and struggled with the circumstances surrounding the crash. "The TikTok videos show children in that car, and I keep saying the word children because that's all they are," she said.

‌



She said she had heard that the group had allegedly been in a stolen car for several hours before the collision, but stressed that this information was second-hand and that she could not confirm it. "Apparently, this is what I'm hearing, and again, it's I'm hearing it second-hand, so I can't confirm it," she said. "But they were out prior to hitting my child for a number of hours in a robbed car."

Despite her anger and heartbreak, Ms Fox repeatedly stressed that she was not looking to blame the children. "I don't blame the children for this. I'm not going to place blame on anyone," she said.

"It's after happening. My child is alive and he's lucky, but there has to be consequences for someone for what's happened."

‌



She added: "What they've done is wrong. I'm not taking or minimising what they've done is wrong. What I'm saying is, I'm not going to start placing hate and anger after the families. I hope they make it up for the justice system."

The crash has also left Craig without the car he relies on for his electrical apprenticeship. "My child has no car now. He's a third-year electrician, and he's no car for work now," Ms Fox said.

"And he's not going to have a car for a while." She said she was also worried about whether her son would be able to get behind the wheel again.

‌



"And the other thing is, is my child going to get back in a car after what's happened?" she said. Craig remembers the crash, according to his mother.

"Every bit of it,” she said when asked if he could recall what happened. "That's why, at the moment, he's still in shock. It's going to cause issues, I think."

Ms Fox described her son as a hard-working 22-year-old who secured his electrical apprenticeship himself and had been working since before he left school. "He's a good kid. He's a kind, caring, loving young fella that's gone out. He's been working since before he left school," she said.

‌



"He got his apprenticeship off his own back. He used his initiative. He got it all off his own back." She said Craig had been looking forward to finishing his apprenticeship and travelling.

"He goes to his gym. He has his girlfriend. He has his pals there - normal 22-year-old young fella," she said. "And his dream is that when he finishes electrical apprenticeship, that he goes travelling." For Ms Fox, however, the memory of the crash scene remains deeply distressing.

"Once I knew my child was okay, I could look at something else," she said. "But if you were at that crash site and you'd seen what I saw at that crash site - it was like a clown car with eight children coming out of it."

‌



She said emergency crews were treating those involved as the young people emerged from the vehicle. "Those kids that came out of it, were on the ground. Ambulance men everywhere," she said. "And that's, I think, why I have this reaction, because I saw the crash site."

For now, her focus is on Craig's recovery and the lasting impact the collision may have on his life. She is grateful her son survived, but believes what happened cannot simply be left without consequences.

"My child is alive and he’s lucky, but there has to be consequences for someone for what’s happened."

Article continues below

The State’s policing watchdog has launched an independent investigation into the incident. In a statement on Monday, Fiosrú, which investigates incidents involving contact with Gardaí where a member of the public has died or been seriously injured, confirmed it received a referral regarding the incident.

It said a team of investigators attended the scene and an independent investigation is ongoing.

"A referral does not necessarily mean a garda or gardaí have been accused of wrongdoing. Instead, it means that Fiosrú should independently investigate the incident to ascertain whether or not the act or omission of a garda or gardaí may have resulted in the death of, or serious harm to, a person," it said.

News.title: Summer 2026 on course to be UK's hottest on record, says Met Office
News.content:
This summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, according to the Met Office.

Only average conditions are needed for the remainder of August to surpass the record set just last year.

Provisional Met Office statistics show that the UK's mean temperature for meteorological summer so far (1 June to 10 August) currently stands at 16.48C (61.66F), which is 1.88C above the 1991-2020 average.

In summer 2025, the mean temperature across the country - which includes overnight lows as well as daytime highs - was 16.10C (60.98F).

It is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change.

News.title: Burnham 'confident' early release of PC Harper's killers can be halted
News.content:
Andy Burnham says he is "confident" PC Andrew Harper's killers can be excluded from the government's early release scheme, as outcry over the case grows.

The prime minister has now ordered the justice secretary to find a way to bar Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were jailed for 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, from early release.

It marks a shift from last week, when he said there was "nothing more" he could do without risking the collapse of the prison system.

The move comes after days of pressure to exclude Harper's killers from the scheme, which is aiming to free about 5,000 offenders in England and Wales to make space in overcrowded jails.

Harper's mother, Debbie Adlam, told the BBC she was in "turmoil" following conflicting reports about whether two of her son's killers would be released from prison early, describing the handling of the situation as a "hash".

Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp accused Burnham and Labour of "re-traumatising victims and their families with their constant U-turns".

On Tuesday evening, an open letter signed by 50 chief constables, commissioners and law enforcement leaders called on Burnham to examine "every lawful option" to determine whether the earlier release of Harper's killers can be prevented.

They welcomed the prime minister's intervention, adding: "This provides an opportunity not only to examine every lawful avenue in PC Andrew Harper's case, but to ensure similar concerns do not arise again."

Burnham said a new plan to prevent more prisoners from being freed long before the end of their sentences would be presented to Parliament in September.

It comes after he initially announced some prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sex and other grooming offences would be barred from early release, after a review of the scheme he ordered after he became prime minister.

In an article published last week, external, Burnham said he had "wanted to go even further" but had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

He added: "I know I can look people in the eye and say to them there is nothing more I could have asked for without risking the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing within months."

But on Tuesday, Burnham insisted he had never accepted "there was nothing more that could be done" to prevent the early release of more offenders, including Harper's killers.

"I came into office and started pushing on this issue, and I have pushed every single day in office," he added.

Burnham said he would seek to hold talks with other political parties to build "consensus" on the approach to early releases.

News.title: Eclipse chasers scramble for glasses as stocks run low
News.content:
At a bakery in central London, stock has been flying off the shelves.

"I've sold, like, 100 this morning," a staff member tells the BBC. But it's not baked goods driving queues out of the door - customers are here to buy eclipse glasses.

They are among those hoping to catch a safe glimpse of Wednesday's solar eclipse - the UK's most significant since 1999 - but struggling to get their hands on the right gear.

Experts have urged eclipse enthusiasts not to look directly at the Sun - with even brief exposure causing lasting damage - and to seek out specialist glasses instead.

But online, pairs that meet safety specifications have all but sold out. Those still available either require a hefty next-day delivery fee or simply cannot arrive on time.

Even the Royal Museums Greenwich - recommended as a reputable retailer by UK health officials - has sold out, citing an "unprecedented volume" of orders.

Meanwhile, eclipse glasses have been turning up for sale in unexpected places as retailers try to capitalise on the demand.

"I Googled 'where can I get eclipse glasses but not through the post', because I realised I was too late," one customer waiting to buy three pairs at the bakery on Monday tells BBC Radio 4's PM programme.

"People have been struggling to find them all over," says another.

News.title: Watch: Was Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck?
News.content:
Donald Trump secretly switched planes when he was returning from a Nato meeting last month in order to avoid a threat to his life from Iran, US media has reported.

The president boarded Air Force One in Ankara, Turkey, on 8 July before being transported to another aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said.

He was then seen disembarking Air Force One in the UK, before boarding his newer, Qatari-gifted jet and returning to the US.

Trump spoke to journalists during his flight to the US but did not say whether he had been moved to a different plane.

The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Paul Adams explains.

News.title: The Office actress Lucy Davis says she has 'incurable' cancer
News.content:
Lucy Davis, who played Dawn Tinsley in the original UK version of The Office, has revealed she has "incurable" breast cancer.

Davis, the daughter of comedian Jasper Carrott, starred as the office receptionist in the groundbreaking sitcom, which ran from 2001 to 2003.

A post from the 53-year-old actress on Instagram, external on Tuesday said: "I wanted to share something with you all that I've kept to myself for a while but for various reasons would like to share now.

"A year-and-a-half ago I was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer, which has metastasized [spread] to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo."

News.title: Wealthy areas must play their part in housing asylum seekers, Burnham suggests
News.content:
Labour has pledged to stop using asylum hotels, a costly form of accommodation that has become a focal point for anti-migrant protests.

The government has sought to house migrants at military sites across the country instead, announcing in June that it planned to open three more including the site in Bicester, Oxfordshire.

The plans have prompted protests there, with residents of nearby Piddington voting to stage a symbolic referendum on leaving the UK.

Burnham said on Tuesday that he would listen to and address the concerns being raised.

"I don't know the issue yet in detail, but in some ways, as I understand it, it is about creating secure space," he said.

"We understand people's concerns and I will look into the issues raised by the good people of Piddington."

But he added: "I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part."

After winning the Makerfield by-election in June, Burnham promised to end "HMO Britain" and said he would change Britain's asylum accommodation system.

HMOs, or houses in multiple occupation, have been widely used by government contractors to house asylum seekers, often in lower income, urban areas.

Last week, there were anti-immigration demonstrations in the town of Thetford, Norfolk, with protesters attempting to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living.

In response to Burnham's interview, Philp reiterated the Conservatives' policy of leaving the European Convention on Human Rights in order to deport migrants to their country of origin or a safe third country.

"Andy Burnham just doesn't get it," he wrote on X.

"Illegal immigrants should all be deported within a week of arrival - to their country of origin or a safe third country like Rwanda."

Government statistics, external showed there were 97,519 people in receipt of asylum support at the end of March, with 20,885 in hotel accommodation.

The figures added that 72,768 people were in other accommodation, including "dispersal accommodation" - which normally means houses in the community.

The remaining 3,866 people were in receipt of subsistence support only, according to the government.

The regions and nations with the highest number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support included 19,578 in the north-west of England, 13,687 in London, 11,969 in the West Midlands and 8,635 in Yorkshire and the Humber.

The Home Office said the regions with the most supported asylum seekers as a proportion of their overall population were the north-east and north-west of England, with 26 and 25 supported people per 10,000 residents respectively.

It added the local authorities with the highest numbers of supported asylum seekers within them were Glasgow city (3,870), Birmingham (2,142), Liverpool (2,053), Coventry (1,712) and Belfast (1,607).

Burnham, during his time serving as the mayor of Greater Manchester, threatened to block the region from housing any more asylum seekers in 2018.

He complained about the government's dispersal system and said Greater Manchester's public services could not continue to support "disproportionate" numbers of people compared with elsewhere in the country.

Burnham at the time said the north-west of England was hosting 25% of the national population of asylum applicants who require housing and support - with Greater Manchester housing 70% of the region's numbers.

The then-Home Secretary Sajid Javid replied by promising to work towards a fairer distribution.

News.title: Luigi Mangione murder trial to have anonymous jury and overflow seating
News.content:
The judge overseeing the state trial of Luigi Mangione, accused of killing UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson, has laid down the ground rules for court public and media access to the high-profile case.

Mangione returned to court on Tuesday ahead of his murder trial, which begins next month in New York. Dressed in a charcoal grey suit with his hair clipped short, Mangione sat silently at the defence table while his attorneys conferred with the judge.

In Tuesday's hearing, Judge Gregory Carro decided that the 12-person jury would remain anonymous to the public due to the spotlight on the case, and that there would be an overflow room to meet media demand.

The case has attracted national attention, and has also created an online frenzy, with both his backers - many of whom see Mangione as a symbol of the backlash against US healthcare costs - and his critics analysing everything from his intentions to his appearance.

The spectacle is likely to intensify when jury selection for the trial begins on 8 September.

Mangione, if found guilty, could face decades behind bars. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including second-degree murder and weapons-related offences.

He faces a separate federal trial next year, in which he has also pleaded not guilty.

Much of what is expected at the state trial â the prosecutor's case, Mangione's defence, and obstacles both parties face â were previewed in months of court filings and arguments.

Here's what to know about the upcoming trial, and what questions remain.

News.title: Criticism as thousands of seats empty at Europeans Athletics Championships
News.content:
Nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships on Monday evening.

A crowd of 13,623 watched as Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt stormed to her first senior international title, in a stadium that has a capacity of 23,000.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with some describing them as "extortionate", while BBC commentator Steve Cram commented that spectator numbers were a "little disappointing".

But Birmingham 2026 organisers said they were "delighted" with ticket sales, which have "far surpassed" their targets with "Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions approaching sell-out, with several other sessions close to capacity".

On Monday, Category A tickets for the home straight cost Â£150 with no concessions for juniors.

For the men's 100m final on Tuesday, those same seats cost Â£110, again with no concessions - while a similar ticket for the same final in Rome two years ago was 88 euros (Â£75).

It is Britain's first time hosting the championships in their 92-year history.

News.title: Man guilty of harassing MP Stella Creasy on Tube train
News.content:
A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP for Walthamstow after preventing her from leaving a Tube carriage and behaving in an "abusive and aggressive" manner.

Clifford Wilby, from east London, targeted Stella Creasy on a Victoria line train between Walthamstow Central and Finsbury Park on 15 July last year.

Westminster Magistrates' Court heard how Wilby spoke to Creasy about knife crime and her "failings as a Member of Parliament" before filming her, leading to members of the public intervening.

Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

Wilby and Creasy first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 as part of her role as an MP.

She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else's case.

Creasy said he had "made a series of very serious allegations", became abusive and "referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath".

The meeting was stopped because of Wilby's behaviour.

News.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
News.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to block new betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and for many people, the high streets they grew up with are "unrecognisable".

He said the plans were "shaped" by a series of BBC News investigations which exposed organised crime on high streets, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes, vapes, cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco for up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least Â£1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham told the BBC that the changes would make it "easier for police to close a vape shop and have it closed for longer".

He said: "At the same time we're changing the planning regime... which should stop the proliferation of vape shops on our high streets."

The prime minister added that Operation Vulcan in Cheetham Hill, Greater Manchester, cleared the area of counterfeits and crime and "proved" what could be achieved.

"When I look at police reform across England, I will be asking for a similar approach to be taken," he said. "I want the strongest possible neighbourhood policing, with all agencies involved, to rip out criminal behaviour that is pulling places down."

Burnham said he did not accept the decline of the high street as "inevitable".

"I don't see why anywhere should have to accept they have empty shops, vape shops and the challenges that come with that."

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday that many people were frustrated at vape and gambling outlets "popping up even near schools and some of them are linked to illegal activity and crime".

News.title: Man dies after punch from security guard in Turkey bar, inquest hears
News.content:
A rugby player was punched in the head by a security guard while on holiday in Turkey and died after he returned home, an inquest has heard.

Scot James, from Maesteg, Bridgend county, had been in hospital since he suffered head and brain injuries in an alleged bar assault on 5 July.

He fell and hit his head during a "verbal exchange", Pontypridd Coroner's Court was told on Tuesday.

The 34-year-old was repatriated to the UK and died on 26 July at the Royal Glamorgan Hospital in Llantrisant, Rhondda Cynon Taf.

A provisional cause of death was given as blunt head injury.

James' family described him as a "loving father, son, grandson and partner" in tributes following his death.

Maesteg Celtic RFC said he was an "outstanding player and a great character".

Coroner Rachel Knight said a full inquest was necessary as there was reason to suspect the death may have been unnatural.

She said that as police in Turkey would potentially be investigating James' death, the next inquest hearing would be scheduled for later this year.

Knight said it may be necessary to pause inquest proceedings pending the outcome of any criminal investigation and confirmed the court would liaise with Turkish authorities.

Police in Turkey are understood to be investigating the death, with assistance from the Foreign Office.

In a statement, James' family said he "had a warm heart, a great sense of humour, and a natural ability to bring people together".

"We are heartbroken by his loss," they said.

"No words can truly express the pain we are experiencing or the void his passing has left in our lives."

Maesteg Celtic RFC said: "Everyone at the club is devastated by this news and our thoughts go out to his family and friends at this difficult time."

News.title: England set to be one of the first countries to eliminate hepatitis C
News.content:
Hepatitis C is spread through contact with blood infected with the virus, such as by sharing needles with someone who has it.

Donor blood is already screened for it.

It is a silent disease, meaning people often have no symptoms until much later.

Untreated, it can cause serious and potentially life-threatening liver damage.

NHS England says that since 2015, more than 100,000 people have been diagnosed and treated for hepatitis C, meaning the country is already meeting that target.

Another goal - a 65% reduction in hepatitis C-related mortality compared with 2015 levels - has yet to be met, but might be before the 2030 target date.

Around 50,200 adults are living with hepatitis C, figures for England in 2024 suggest.

Estimates indicate 84.6% of those living with hepatitis C have been diagnosed - just short of the 90% target.

The Hepatitis C Trust says England is "on the cusp" of one of the most significant public health achievements in our country's history.

Prof Frankie Swords, NHS national medical director, added: "England is now leading the world in the mission to eliminate this disease and on course to beat the WHO's 2030 target, but we are determined to keep up the momentum and finish the job.

"We are committed to finding and treating everyone who needs support and would urge those at greater risk to come forward by ordering a free and confidential home-testing kit online."

Adults born in Ukraine, Romania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Albania, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Czechia or Slovakia are particularly urged to test, as some may have been infected through medical or dental procedures before 1991.

People can order a free, confidential NHS home self-testing kit, external without needing to speak to a GP.

News.title: YouTube couple's donkey sanctuary plans approved
News.content:
A famous YouTube couple have been allowed to build a donkey sanctuary behind their West Sussex home.

Earlier this year, Zoella - real name Zoe Sugg - and her fiancÃ© Alfie Deyes applied for permission to develop a five-acre field they had bought next to their property near Hassocks.

They were warned by Mid Sussex District Council (MSDC) that there could be potential Roman, Anglo-Saxon or even prehistoric remains buried there.

MSDC approved their application at a planning meeting on Friday, having recommended that work cannot begin until archaeologists conduct an investigation.

Zoella, 36, who made her name with make-up videos before moving on to books and her own range of products, applied for planning back in May.

Included were proposals to create an enclosure for the animals, stables, three shepherd huts, parking for tractors and a pond.

However, an earlier excavation across the road had uncovered items from the Roman period, with MSDC's archaeological adviser previously stipulating that no groundwork should take place until a programme of archaeological monitoring was approved.

Locals also voiced concerns about how the development might impact the views of the surrounding area, increase traffic and impede access to nearby bridleways and public footpaths.

They complained that a gate and fences have already gone up at the site.

"We also don't like the gates and would rather they were not there," said one resident, who did not want to be named.

"Once you have gates up, it's not the same.

"There are paths and bridal ways all around here and people use them for walks all the time."

On the gate is a poster from Sugg and Deynes which reads: "We've lived here for nine years with our garden backing onto this field, and we have always worried about it one day being developed into new houses.

"After many years of trying to purchase it, last year we managed to do so.

"This means not only is the view from our house and many others nearby protected, it also helps keep this area the lovely walking spot it is for so many people each day.

"If you live in this area and are also keen to keep as much green space thriving as possible, please head over to the council's planning website and leave a positive comment to help encourage the approval of other projects like ours - thank you."

News.title: Golfer left shaking by 411-yard hole in one
News.content:
An amateur golfer was left "frozen" and "could not stop shaking" after hitting a hole in one from 411 yards (376 metres) - a one-in-six-million chance, according to one estimate.

Matthew Vigurs, from Droitwich in Worcestershire, narrowly missed out on claiming a Guinness World Record when he sank the shot during a league match at Great Barr Golf Club on 25 July in Sandwell near Birmingham.

The record sits with Robert Mitera, external who in 1965 at Miracle Hills Golf Course in Nebraska, USA,, external hit a hole in one from 447 yards (408 metres).

But despite being 36 yards (33 metres) short, 32-year-old Vigurs said: "I got married last year so obviously that's number one but this is definitely up there as a close second best moment of my life."

England Golf, external, the national governing body for amateur golf, believes Vigurs' achievement could be a national record, but that is yet to be confirmed.

But for any golfer a hole in one is a moment to remember and due to its rarity, Vigurs admitted he felt "stupid" even looking for his ball near the hole.

"We all hit good shots but I didn't expect it to go anywhere close to the green and I didn't know it had until we got up there," he said.

"We were looking for the balls but mine was missing.

"Everyone else was about 40 yards short of the green and we even had a look over the back of the green.

"I just double checked the hole and unbelievably I froze for about 10 seconds when I noticed the ball in the bottom.

"I rolled it over and saw my markings and we all went mad. It was surreal."

News.title: Antisemitism towards Jewish children 'shocking', government expert tells BBC
News.content:
Headteachers of some Jewish schools are spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than on educational matters, a review into antisemitism in schools and colleges has found.

Sir David Bell, speaking for the first time about his ongoing government-commissioned independent review, told the BBC he had been struck by how many leaders of Jewish faith schools had told him security was their main concern - and that "sometimes education takes second place to that".

The extent of antisemitism directed at children and young people was "shocking" he said.

The report, due this autumn, examines experiences of Jewish pupils and staff in faith and secular schools and colleges in England.

Sir David said he found that pupils were "subject to regular harassment and abuse".

He said Jewish children and young people "are facing a pressure - and indeed one might say even a crisis - that is not the experience of other communities in this country".

The review is likely to recommend dedicated training for all teachers and improved education about antisemitism for pupils, the BBC has been told.

The BBC has spoken to several headteachers and staff at Jewish schools. All asked not to be named because of concerns over their security and that of their schools.

One headteacher said: "In recent years [security] has become an overwhelming priority and increased a significant amount. There have been weeks where approximately 90% of my time has been spent on security-related matters.

"Security concerns can become one of the many things that headteachers carry with them beyond the school day and, quite literally, can be among the things that keep me awake at night."

News.title: Girl, 6, dies and another child hurt in A12 crash
News.content:
A six-year-old girl was killed and another child was injured in a collision that shut part of the A12 on Monday, police have said.

The crash, involving a lorry and a car, happened at about 10:30 BST on the northbound carriageway near the Colchester United football stadium.

The road was shut in both directions and an air ambulance landed, while vehicles caught in the closure were turned around.

Det Insp Mark Fraser, of Essex Police, said the lorry driver had passed all road-side tests and was due to be interviewed in the coming days.

The injured child suffered a leg injury and was recovering in hospital, the force added.

The collision led to parts of Colchester being gridlocked throughout the day, while A12 queues stretched back to Marks Tey.

Cristiano Ronaldo has married his long-term partner Georgina Rodriguez in a civil ceremony in Portugal.

The pair, who first met in Madrid and have been together since 2016, shared a photograph on Instagram displaying their rings.

Ronaldo, 41, tied the knot just four days prior to his club Al Nassr opening their 2026-27 Saudi Pro League season.

The service took place in Cascais, a coastal resort town situated approximately 20 miles west of Lisbon, the Portuguese capital, with their five children present.

The post on Instagram was captioned with the letters ‘C’ and ‘G’, with a love heart in between them.

Ronaldo has scored close to 1,000 goals across a career representing Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus, Al Nassr and Portugal.

He recently featured in his sixth World Cup, sharing the record alongside Argentina’s Lionel Messi for most appearances in the men’s finals.

The couple first revealed their relationship in 2017 after appearing together at the Best FIFA Football Awards in Zurich, Switzerland, before posting each other on social media for the first time later that year.

In June 2017, they welcomed their first set of twins, Eva Maria and Mateo, via surrogate, and then welcomed their daughter Alana, in November 2017.

Ronaldo also has a son, Cristiano Jr., from a previous relationship.

A few years later, the model and the soccer player announced the death of their twin son, Ángel, in April 2022, as they revealed that their twin daughter, Bella, had been born.

Ronaldo and Rodríguez shared the news of their son’s passing in a joint social media post at the time. “It is with our deepest sadness we have to announce our baby boy has passed away. It is the greatest pain that any parents can feel,” they wrote. “Only the birth of our baby girl gives us the strength to live this moment with some hope and happiness.”

The couple also took the opportunity to express their gratitude to the doctors, nurses and medical staff for “all their expert care and support.”

“We are all devastated at this loss and we kindly ask for privacy at this very difficult time,” they wrote. “Our baby boy, you are our angel. We will always love you.”

News.title: US employers are increasingly relying on ‘disposable’ workers - and the public pays a price
News.content:

When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a part-timer with no career prospects in that job.

When my best intentions to eat well are for naught and I gorge on Doritos, I remember that the tasters PepsiCo hires to test the chips’ addictiveness are contractors.

These are all examples of what I call “disposable jobs.” People who have them work at an employer’s site, but their employer makes no commitment to them regarding career prospects or job security. My research shows that employers treat more than 1 in 3 U.S. workers as disposable. That comes to just under 57 million full- or part-time workers out of the nation’s workforce of 162 million.

I am a labor economist. In my new book, Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment, I explain why this is happening, what forms it takes, how common it is, what the consequences are for people and for society, and what can be done about it.

Employing part-time workers costs less than having full-timers on the payroll ( Getty Images )

Three different varieties

To learn more, I commissioned a nationally representative survey of over 6,000 people in late 2022. I also interviewed nearly 100 workers, employers and policymakers.

I found that there are three categories of disposable workers.

Contractors who are employed by a staffing firm but work at a client’s site. Examples include temporary office workers, building cleaners and security guards. Many of these people are poorly paid, but some, such as travel nurses, are highly compensated. My survey shows that these contractors account for 13% of the workforce. Freelancers who work for companies, organizations or agencies without being employees. Examples include Uber and Lyft drivers, food delivery drivers, computer programmers and freelance journalists. In my survey, organizational freelancers represent 5% of the workforce. I don’t include in this category freelancers who work for individual people, such as most dog-walkers and handymen, because my focus is on how employers treat their employees. Marginal workers who are employed by companies, organizations or agencies. They lack career opportunities, and their jobs have high turnover built in. Marginal workers account for 17% of the workforce in my survey.

Marginal work is important due to its magnitude and because although those jobs look standard, they are designed to be disposable.

Who are marginal workers?

Staff attorneys are quintessential marginal employees. They’re hired by law firms as employees, but the central feature of their jobs is that they are not on the promotion ladder to partner. Unlike their career-track counterparts, they have no job security. They are often hired to do the grunt work on a specific case, with the understanding that there is no commitment to keep them on if business lags or the project ends.

Adjunct professors are another good example. This group includes part-timers who teach a small number of courses and full-time contract faculty, but in both cases they lack job security and aren’t on track to obtain permanent, tenured, academic jobs.

In 1970, people with tenure or tenure-track jobs constituted 73% of those teaching at colleges and universities. By 2021 only 32% had that status, and the rest were adjunct instructors or contract faculty.

Part-time marginal workers

Another example of marginal work is part-timers.

Employing part-time workers costs less than having full-timers on the payroll. Part-time jobs pay an hourly wage that is nearly 20% below what workers with full-time jobs earn after age, education, occupation and industry are taken into account. When benefits are considered, the gap rises by another 5%.

A second advantage of part-timers from the employer’s perspective is higher turnover, which provides an easy path to be able to adjust the size of the workforce and which enables them to avoid investing in career development.

When a team of researchers led by professor Susan Lambert interviewed 88 employers that pay low wages, they found that many use part-time work to make their workforces more “flexible.” One manager explained that high churn of part-timers gave the company so much flexibility that they didn’t need temp workers.

“Temp workers: We don’t need them,” he said. “Wait a day for turnover.”

About the author Paul Osterman is a Professor Emeritus, MIT Sloan School, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

Evidence that employers try to maximize the number of people working for them part time instead of full time and with benefits arose after the Affordable Care Act fully took effect in 2014.

The ACA requires that employers with 50 or more employees either provide them with health insurance or pay for them to buy it, but only for people who work 30 or more hours a week. Otherwise they pay, as of 2026, a penalty of US$3,340 per uninsured employee.

Another team of researchers compared trends in part-time work in three low-wage industries – retail, hotels and restaurants, before and after the ACA rolled out. They found that the use of part-timers increased by 500,000 in the years after the Affordable Care Act was implemented. This suggests that companies add to their part-time ranks to save on the health insurance costs of standard employment.

Forces behind this trend

Why do employers want many of their workers to be disposable? A primary motive is to save money. Employing freelancers and contractors means they can avoid mandatory benefits such as Social Security contributions and, for larger employers, contributing to the cost of health insurance.

Marginal workers, to be sure, do receive these benefits. But the high turnover built into their jobs means that their employers can invest less in their training and avoid the management costs otherwise associated with layoff severance and fair treatment on the job.

An additional motive for many employers is a lack of respect for what front-line employees can contribute. A 2023 report from the McKinsey consulting firm illustrated this tendency when it asserted that 5% of employees deliver 95% of “an organization’s value.”

This claim, which I believe is inaccurate, still speaks volumes about the attitude of McKinsey and the firms they interviewed regarding the other 95% of workers. They see those employees as disposable.

Less pay and job satisfaction

My survey showed that contractors, freelancers who work for employers and marginal employees all earn less than regular workers do.

In addition, the survey found that contractors and marginal workers are notably less satisfied with their jobs compared with regular workers, whereas freelancers, due to their ability to choose where and when to work, are more satisfied.

The public also pays a price for the use of disposable workers. As examples, researchers have found that hospital infection rates rise when cleaners are contract workers and that the use of contractors leads to a higher rate of industrial accidents.

Thousands of homes and businesses have been left with no water or low pressure after pipes burst in London and Essex as a fifth heatwave looms.

Thames Water said 14 postcodes were involved and the BBC estimated that 10,000 homes were affected.

All of England has been issued with a rare amber heat warning, with the risk of temperatures reaching 38C this week.

The Met Office says this summer is set to be the UK’s hottest since records began.

Only average conditions are needed for the remainder of August for the month to surpass the record which was set only last year.

July was the busiest month on record for wildfires, statistics show, after firefighters attended 458 cases last month.

In the first 10 days of August, crews have been called out to 185 wildfires, including a large blaze in the New Forest which has burned for three days.

Met Office experts warned of a risk of travel delays, adverse health effects and potential power cuts. The warning covers large parts of England from 9am to midnight on Thursday.

Some 45 million people have been plunged into drought conditions as dry and hot weather continues. The National Drought Group has declared 71.3 per cent of England is now suffering a “flash” drought.
