World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia
World.content:
At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:51 UTC Full article

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead

At least 132 people were killed and 570 injured by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday, according to the latest report submitted by the Colombian Association of Capital Cities at 7:00 p.m. local time. Authorities warned the figure is preliminary and that rescue work is continuing.

The quake struck at 07:34, with its epicenter near the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, at a depth of more than 80 kilometers, according to the Colombian Geological Service. It is the strongest recorded in the country in the past decade.

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead. Departmental tolls released by governors and mayors correspond to different cutoff times and do not match one another: Chocó governor Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi reported 12 dead and 84 injured in that department, while the mayor of Manizales confirmed two deaths. Fatalities were also reported in Valle del Cauca and Antioquia.

| URGENTE: Momento del derrumbe de un edificio de 3 pisos tras el terremoto de magnitud 7,4 en Pereira, Colombia. pic.twitter.com/r3v2lW5pU3 — Alerta News 24 (@AlertaNews24) August 10, 2026

The government put the number of damaged homes at more than 1,500, with 37 destroyed and 61 buildings completely collapsed, along with damage to 18 health centers, 52 schools, 17 community centers and 18 roads. The civil aviation authority suspended operations at seven air terminals: Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.

Damage to the hospital network is among the most critical. In Cali, the Hospital Universitario del Valle partially collapsed and seven large health care institutions were closed and evacuated because of structural damage. Valle del Cauca governor Dilian Francisca Toro said at least five intensive care patients were trapped under rubble. Cali mayor Alejandro Eder reported at least twenty collapsed structures with people trapped inside and requested rescue teams from Bogotá and Medellín. The capital's mayor, Carlos Fernando Galán, dispatched a hundred rescue workers.

De la Espriella agreed to declare a national disaster situation and is leading a unified command post at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, with additional posts in Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry is coordinating international cooperation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was ready to provide assistance.

The Colombian Geological Service reported two aftershocks, of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8. The agency also recorded an emission of ash and gases from the Puracé volcano, in Cauca department, on orange alert since July, coinciding in time with the earthquake.

World.title: Colombia and Venezuela quakes are unconnected despite similar magnitude, experts say
World.content:
Colombia and Venezuela quakes are unconnected despite similar magnitude, experts say

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:11 UTC Full article

“The Venezuelan earthquakes are shallower and involve a different mechanism, a strike-slip mechanism. This one is deeper, a subduction earthquake,” a seismologist stressed

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday has a different tectonic origin from the earthquakes recorded in Venezuela in June, despite comparable magnitudes, said Viviana Dionisio, a seismologist with Colombia's National Seismological Network.

“It was a tectonic earthquake associated mainly with a subduction mechanism,” the specialist said. That process occurs when the Nazca plate, beneath the Pacific Ocean, slides under the South American plate, on which Colombia's mainland territory sits. Energy accumulated at the contact between the two can be released in large earthquakes, of the kind historically recorded around the Pacific Ring of Fire.

The Venezuelan earthquakes of June 24, of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.4, responded to a different mechanism. According to Dionisio, they originated in the interaction between the Caribbean and South American plates through lateral displacement, known as strike-slip faulting. “The Venezuelan earthquakes are shallower and involve a different mechanism, a strike-slip mechanism. This one is deeper, a subduction earthquake,” she stressed.

Depth is the factor explaining why two earthquakes of similar magnitude can cause very different damage. The focus of the Colombian quake was located at around one hundred kilometers, according to revised data from the Colombian Geological Service, which in its first bulletin had placed it at 82. In shallow earthquakes, waves travel a shorter distance and reach areas near the epicenter with greater intensity; in deep ones they pass through more material and lose energy along the way. The seismologist warned, however, that depth alone does not determine the extent of damage, which also depends on the vulnerability of buildings and ground conditions.

The epicenter was located in San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, on the boundary with Risaralda and Valle del Cauca. Dionisio said it is not unusual for an earthquake of these characteristics to originate in that region, given the tectonic dynamics of western Colombia.

The Colombian Geological Service has recorded more than thirty aftershocks, the strongest of magnitude 4.8. “An earthquake of this magnitude generates a certain number of aftershocks that generally decrease in frequency and magnitude over the following days or weeks,” the seismologist said.

Rodrigo León, of the Geosciences Department at Universidad de los Andes, noted that earthquakes cannot be predicted, nor is it possible to anticipate when an aftershock will occur or to rule out larger movements. He also considered that, given the magnitude of the event, the damage could have been worse. The provisional toll exceeds 130 dead.

World.title: American Airlines resumes its seasonal Montevideo-Miami route in December
World.content:
American Airlines resumes its seasonal Montevideo-Miami route in December

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:00 UTC Full article

The operation is not the restoration of a discontinued route but the reopening of a service the company suspends each year outside the tourist season

American Airlines will restart its seasonal service between Carrasco International Airport and Miami International Airport on December 3, once again becoming the only carrier offering nonstop flights between Uruguay and the United States during the peak summer season.

The operation is not the restoration of a discontinued route but the reopening of a service the company suspends each year outside the tourist season. The change from the previous cycle is the extension of the daily-frequency stretch: in 2025-2026 daily flights ran until February 11, while this season they will continue until March 2, 2027, some three weeks longer.

From that date, the connection will operate three times a week, on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays, until March 28, 2027, when the scheduled season ends.

The route will be flown by a Boeing 787-8 with capacity for 234 passengers, in a configuration of 20 Business class seats, 28 in Premium Economy and 186 in the main cabin. According to the itinerary released by the airline, flights from Miami will depart at 22:55 and arrive in Montevideo at 10:10 the following day. In the opposite direction, departures from Carrasco are set for 22:30, landing in Miami at 05:45. Times are local and subject to change. The journey takes approximately nine hours.

“After nearly three decades of dedicated service to Uruguay, we are delighted to resume our daily seasonal flights in Montevideo for the busiest period of the summer,” said Pascual Álvarez, the company's managing director of operations for South America, Central America and the Caribbean. He said the route targets both international travelers visiting Uruguay and Uruguayan passengers connecting from Miami to other destinations.

Miami is the airline's main international connecting hub, with more than 400 daily flights in peak season to over 200 destinations, according to company figures.

At Aeropuertos Uruguay, the concession holder for the Carrasco terminal, commercial director Matías Carluccio said the reactivation “strengthens Uruguay's access to the United States and broadens travel options for passengers seeking to connect our country with new international destinations.” He added that the company would continue working to support the growth of air connectivity.

American Airlines has operated in Uruguay for close to thirty years. The Miami connection is the only direct route between the South American country and US territory, and its calendar coincides with the busiest tourist season in the River Plate.

World.title: Lacalle Pou's return reopens the debate over opposition leadership in Uruguay
World.content:
Lacalle Pou's return reopens the debate over opposition leadership in Uruguay

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 09:56 UTC Full article

Lacalle Pou spoke for around half an hour before more than a thousand party members in Montevideo's Plaza Matriz, after several months of keeping a low profile

The first public appearance by former Uruguayan president Luis Lacalle Pou since leaving office, at Sunday's ceremony marking the Partido Nacional's 190th anniversary, drew contrasting readings within the governing Frente Amplio and reopened discussion of his role in the opposition.

Lacalle Pou spoke for around half an hour before more than a thousand party members in Montevideo's Plaza Matriz, after several months of keeping a low profile. He described himself as an “old militant” and said that, after taking stock of his administration, he feels “at ease, satisfied, but not content.” He acknowledged “successes and mistakes” and called for unity: “It is not about healing wounds, it is about not inflicting them.” He made no electoral statements and did not announce a candidacy. Those present chanted “we are going to return” and cheered him with shouts of “President.”

The most discussed passage was a distinction between power and authority, which he attributed to a period of introspection begun months before his term ended. He defined power as something formal that originates in the vote, and authority as something built on intellectual, moral and emotional bonds. “You cannot exercise power well if you do not first have authority. You cannot govern a country well if you do not know it,” he said.

Party figures and some analysts read those words as aimed at President Yamandú Orsi. Political scientist Antonio Cardarello described them as a measured criticism of the government. Orsi dismissed the reading on Monday: “No, not at all, not at all. It is not for a president to comment on what other leaders say.” He noted that his government had granted the Partido Nacional national radio and television airtime to mark the anniversary.

Former vice president Lucía Topolansky, of the Movimiento de Participación Popular, praised the former president's composure and described his speech as that of a statesman. She read his call to avoid giving offense as a message directed at Parliament as a whole, in the midst of debate on the annual budget accounts, and not only at his own party's lawmakers. It was a rebuke delivered with dignity, she told El País.

Socialist senator Gustavo González offered a more critical assessment: he welcomed the fact that the former president did not attack the government, but called the speech very vague and said he had not spoken as a statesman, since he did not address the international situation. Senator Daniel Caggiani called the tone republican and sensible, though he saw a contradiction between it and the opposition's parliamentary strategy. Frente Amplio president Fernando Pereira said Orsi “probably does not look as good on the platform,” but “governs better on the pitch.”

Uruguay bars immediate re-election but allows non-consecutive terms, meaning Lacalle Pou could run in the 2029 elections.

World.title: Burnham's Labour edges ahead of Reform UK in a YouGov poll for the first time
World.content:
Burnham's Labour edges ahead of Reform UK in a YouGov poll for the first time

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 09:44 UTC Full article

The survey, conducted on August 9 and 10 among 2,417 respondents, puts Labour on 24%, two points higher than in the August 3 poll, while Reform UK falls one point to 22%

The Labour Party of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has moved ahead of Reform UK, the right-wing party led by Nigel Farage, in a voting intention survey by YouGov published on Tuesday by The Times. It is the first time this has happened in that pollster's series since Reform took the lead in early 2025.

The survey, conducted on August 9 and 10 among 2,417 respondents, puts Labour on 24%, two points higher than in the August 3 poll, while Reform UK falls one point to 22%. The two-point gap sits at the edge of the sample's margin of error, so the change of position is not statistically conclusive.

Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party, the main opposition force, rises two points to 21%. The Greens fall one point to 12% and the Liberal Democrats one point to 11%. All five parties are above the 10% threshold, a structural feature of the current British political landscape.

YouGov's recent sequence shows a less linear movement than the latest figure suggests. In Burnham's first week in Downing Street, Labour and Reform were tied on 22%; in the August 3 poll, Reform regained the lead with 23% against Labour's 22%. An earlier More in Common survey had already placed Labour ahead, on 28% against 24%.

Burnham took office on July 20, replacing Keir Starmer, who announced his resignation in June after his party's results in the May local and regional elections, in which Reform UK made significant gains. The new prime minister devoted his early weeks to cost-of-living measures, including a cut to VAT on energy bills.

YouGov's head of elections and political data, Patrick English, qualified the scale of the improvement. He noted that Burnham leads the favourability ratings among the leaders being measured, but that voters still believe the government is not addressing their concerns over the cost of living and immigration, and will want to see tangible improvements before rewarding Labour at the ballot box.

The poll appears two days before the Clacton by-election in southeast England, where Farage is seeking to win back the seat he vacated in July to trigger the vote. His resignation came amid an investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner into an alleged undeclared gift of five million pounds, on which no findings have been reached. The next general election must be held by August 2029 at the latest.

World.title: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for crimes against humanity
World.content:
Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for crimes against humanity

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 09:21 UTC Full article

Russia granted asylum to Assad and his brother, making enforcement of the sentence unfeasible while they remain in that country

A criminal court in Damascus sentenced former Syrian president Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia on Tuesday for premeditated murder, torture, arbitrary detention and crimes against humanity. Assad was ousted in December 2024 and is living in exile in Moscow. It is the first public sentence handed down against the man who governed Syria for more than two decades.

Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Uryan, of criminal court number 4, also sentenced eight other people to death, among them Maher al-Assad, the former president's brother, and Atef Najib, maternal cousin of both and the only defendant present in the courtroom. Najib heard the ruling in the defendants' cage, wearing a prison uniform, under heavy security.

“The contribution of the criminal Bashar al-Assad to the crimes was that of the ultimate decision-maker, who mobilized state institutions to commit them,” the judge said as he read the verdict. The court found him guilty of the intentional killing of more than one person and of children, as well as of torture and arbitrary detention.

The ruling came during the hearing against Najib, a brigadier general who headed the Political Security Branch in the southern province of Daraa between 2008 and April 2011. He is accused of ordering the detention and torture of a group of minors who painted anti-government slogans on a school wall, an episode that triggered the first protests of the Syrian uprising.

The judge said investigations and witness testimony established his involvement in the interrogation of detainees and that the branch under his command, together with other security services, stormed the Omari mosque in Daraa. The mosque was the main gathering point for the March 2011 demonstrations, and security forces raided it on several occasions, killing dozens of protesters.

Najib was transferred to Idlib after the protests began and went into hiding from mid-2011. That same year he was sanctioned by the United States and the European Union. He was captured on January 31, 2025, in a raid in rural Latakia.

The six remaining defendants, all fugitives, were sentenced for premeditated murder and torture resulting in death. The hearing was attended by Attorney General Hasan al-Turbeh, the head of the Transitional Justice Commission, Abdulbaset Abdullatif, representatives of international legal and humanitarian organizations, and relatives of victims.

The proceedings, which began on April 26 and ran to nine hearings, are the first of the transitional justice phase opened after the fall of Assad's government, when forces led by current interim president Ahmed al-Sharaa entered Damascus. The war lasted fourteen years and left an estimated half a million dead. Russia granted asylum to Assad and his brother, making enforcement of the sentence unfeasible while they remain in that country.

World.title: Kast rules out backing bill that ties abortion access to hearing the fetal heartbeat
World.content:
Kast rules out backing bill that ties abortion access to hearing the fetal heartbeat

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 09:18 UTC Full article

“It is legitimate for lawmakers to introduce their bills and for a debate to be generated around that, but we are not going to move forward on this matter,” the president said

Chilean President José Antonio Kast said on Monday that his government would not push forward a bill introduced by lawmakers from his own coalition that would condition access to legal abortion on a woman agreeing to hear the fetus's cardiac activity.

“It is legitimate for lawmakers to introduce their bills and for a debate to be generated around that, but we are not going to move forward on this matter,” the president said in an interview with T13 Radio. He recalled that his campaign centered on an emergency government focused on the economy, security and social issues, and that he would not promote measures that generate tension.

Kast also drew a distinction about the text itself. “In other countries, the heartbeat is voluntary. The difference with the parliamentary bill in Chile is that it was made compulsory,” he said.

The initiative, named “Escucha su corazón,” was introduced in July by lawmaker Cristóbal Urruticoechea of the Partido Nacional Libertario, with signatures from members of that party and of the Partido Republicano, founded by Kast. It would amend the Health Code so that when a woman requests an abortion, the physician informs her whether cardiac activity is detectable and offers her the chance to hear it. If she declines the offer, the practitioner would have to refrain from carrying out the procedure.

Abortion has been legal in Chile since 2017 on three grounds: risk to the woman's life, fetal unviability and rape. The law was passed during Michelle Bachelet's second term, and the bill would not repeal it.

Objections also came from within the governing coalition. The president of the Unión Demócrata Independiente, Guillermo Ramírez, called the proposal ineffective and difficult to enforce. Health Minister May Chomali said last week there is no scientific basis for expecting a woman to change her decision. The World Health Organization recommends that ultrasounds not be a mandatory requirement for accessing an abortion and that information provided be objective and not aimed at influencing the decision. In late July, hundreds of women demonstrated in Santiago and about 30 other cities under the slogans “Hear my heart” and “Hear my decision.”

Kast's position drew discontent among the bill's sponsors. “We will not give up, we will keep up the fight, the battle, until we rebuild everything that former president Gabriel Boric's government tore down,” Urruticoechea said. His fellow party member Paulina Muñoz said: “The defense of innocent life has no timetable. I expected more from the president.” The head of the Partido Republicano, Arturo Squella, agreed with Kast that the debate should remain in Congress without executive involvement.

Similar measures have been in force in Hungary since 2022 and in Spain's Castilla y León region.

World.title: De la Espriella gives the first earthquake toll and entrusts Colombia to Jesus Christ
World.content:
De la Espriella gives the first earthquake toll and entrusts Colombia to Jesus Christ

10th Monday, August 2026 - 19:16 UTC Full article

The toll, as of 12:30 local time, is preliminary

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella reported 111 dead and 87 injured on Monday from the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck the west and center of the country, in an address containing extensive religious references. “I entrust our country to the Lord Jesus Christ,” he said after chairing a meeting of the unified command post set up at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit.

The toll, as of 12:30 local time, is preliminary. The president listed 1,575 homes damaged and 37 destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, 18 health centers, 52 schools and 17 community centers damaged, 18 roads affected and six airports out of service. The priority, he said, is rescuing people trapped under rubble. The government agreed to declare a national disaster situation, to be signed during the day.

De la Espriella announced he would personally lead the response and issue updates every two or three hours. He will travel to Quibdó, capital of Chocó, with the health and defense ministers, while Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara Restrepo heads to the coffee-growing region and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera to Valle del Cauca. Command posts have been set up in Bogotá, Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry will coordinate international cooperation, and the president said the country's allies had offered assistance.

“Today all Colombians, without ideological distinctions, have to unite behind a single cause: the victims of this natural disaster,” he said. He argued that those affected would recover “with the help of God,” of the government and of the international community, and asked God to “protect Colombia.” Unlike his earlier appearances, he did not close with his customary slogan, “Firm for the Homeland.”

Religious language has been a constant feature since before he took office. The president was sworn in on Friday using the constitutional formula “I swear to God,” closed a speech to troops in Cali with “Long live Christ the King,” and included an interfaith segment in the ceremony. Days earlier he had gathered his incoming cabinet at a spiritual retreat, after which he said that “God must be placed at the center of every decision.”

Those statements have opened a debate over the scope of state secularism. The 1991 constitution established a non-confessional state, and in 1994 the Constitutional Court struck down a provision requiring the president to renew annually the country's official consecration to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Senator Jennifer Pedraza walked out of the inauguration session, saying the ceremony threatened the secular character of the state. Constitutional lawyer Juan Manuel Charry has argued, by contrast, that a public official retains personal convictions while exercising office.

World.title: MND Local: Tijuana Innovadora and upcoming events in Baja California
World.content:
When businessman José Galicot Behar founded Tijuana Innovadora in 2010, the goal was to help change the narrative about the city, focusing not on crime, but rather on the city’s growing status as a business capital. In the 16 years since the first event at the Centro Cultural Tijuana (CECUT), that’s exactly what has happened — as Tijuana Innovadora has evolved from a biennial event to a continuous, year-round civic movement, with an increasing list of actionable results to its credit.

A pollution monitoring program for the Tijuana River

Toxic waste and raw sewage polluting the Tijuana River have long been an issue affecting residents on both sides of the border, and a bone of contention between the U.S. and Mexico. An estimated 35 million to 50 million gallons of contaminated water flow through the river daily, with significant impacts for local beaches and border ecosystems. The two nations signed an agreement in 2025 aimed at helping to clean up the issue, with US $93 million earmarked for infrastructure projects. But it’s not just the governments who are working to find solutions.

Tijuana Innovadora has recently announced its participation in the Río Tijuana Initiative, which brings together a binational group of 24 representatives from Mexico and the United States to establish a baseline of water quality. Trained volunteers and students, known as “River Sentinels,” will collect samples at 10 points along the channel as part of a campaign scheduled for this month. The program will measure eight water-quality parameters to identify pollution hotspots and assess their severity.

Samples will be processed in the Biotechnology Engineering laboratories at the Tijuana Institute of Technology, giving the findings an academic basis. The results will then feed into the Tijuana River Index, a platform designed to translate complex data and provide a tangible basis for measuring future outcomes.

A promotional platform to drive medical and dental tourism

Tijuana Innovadora has also joined forces with the Baja Health Cluster, a regional industry association, to help promote medical and dental tourism in Baja California.

The new agreement, announced last month at the CODET Vision Institute, is not about building hospitals or providing medical care. Tijuana Innovadora’s plan is simply to help showcase the state’s high-quality medical services and share the merits of the region’s doctors, clinics, hospitals and health workers.

Tijuana, in particular, is among the most popular medical tourism destinations in Mexico and a leader in an industry that in 2024 brought in over US $2 billion in revenue to the state. Only Sonora among Mexican states outpaces Baja California when it comes to medical tourism. However, the number of visitors was down significantly in Baja California in 2025, so an increased emphasis on promotional efforts does seem to be warranted.

As MND reported in June, the dental tourism market in Mexico is expected to quadruple over the next eight years — growing from US $527 million in 2025 to US $2.2 billion by 2033 — with Tijuana and Baja California poised to be key beneficiaries. So here, too, promotion could be an important tool in highlighting available regional services.

Fiestas de la Vendimia 2026

In terms of economic impact, no summer event in Baja California compares to Fiestas de la Vendimia, the monthlong wine harvest festival held primarily in Valle de Guadalupe, but with events also taking place in Ensenada and Tijuana. Over 90,000 visitors are expected at the 36th annual iteration of the event, slated for Aug. 5-30, 2026, with the economic value estimated at over 600 million pesos.

Among the 35 events scheduled over 25 days this month by Provino — the local non-profit winegrowers association — are tastings, pairing dinners, concerts and other experiences, including the traditional cooking contest, Concurso de Paellas. Over 80 wineries are expected to participate during this year’s festivities, which spotlights viticulture in Mexico’s most famous and productive wine region, with the state accounting for about 70% of all wine produced in the country.

Feria Nacional de Tijuana 2026

Aficionados of regional parties can also look forward to the upcoming Feria Nacional de Tijuana, an outgrowth of the previous Feria de las Californias that offers rides, regional food and culture, plus concerts featuring some of the best-known performers in Mexico at venues in Parque Morelos. This year’s event runs from Aug. 28 to Sept. 27, as part of celebrations surrounding Mexico’s Independence Day.

Access to musical performances in the open-air Teatro del Pueblo is typically included with general admission prices, while premium tickets are required to see acts like the acclaimed norteño band Los Tucanes de Tijuana (Friday, Sept. 4 at 8 p.m.) at the park’s Palenque concert arena.

Recapping Opera en la Calle 2026

Although the season’s biggest events still lie ahead, one long-time favorite has already wrapped up its 2026 edition: Opera en la Calle, a Tijuana summer institution since 2004. At its outset, the goal was to make opera and classical music more accessible to the general public through performances from talented artists. That goal has certainly been accomplished, as an estimated quarter of a million people attended the annual fête during its first two decades of operation.

This year’s free event, the 23rd annual, was held on Saturday, July 18, with approximately 300 artists and 100 support staff putting on a show for approximately 8,700 attendees during 10-plus hours of programming on Calle 11, between Avenida Revolución and Avenida Madero.

Like Tijuana Innovadora, the Feria Nacional de Tijuana and the Fiestas de la Vendimia, it’s one of the things that makes summertime special in Baja California.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Navy seizes nearly 2 tonnes of cocaine off Pacific coast, arrests 6
World.content:
The Mexican Navy last week intercepted a vessel in the Pacific Ocean found to be transporting cocaine, resulting in the arrest of six men and the confiscation of nearly two tonnes of the white powder.

During a routine maritime surveillance operation on Friday, Navy personnel spotted a speedboat with three outboard motors about 850 kilometers south of Acapulco. Initial reports suggested a little more than 1 tonne of cocaine was confiscated, but after arriving at port on Sunday, officials realized there were significantly more drugs on the boat.

“These actions combat drug trafficking, weaken the logistical capabilities of organized crime and strengthen Mexico’s security,” Admiral Raymundo Pedro Morales said on Sunday.

The specially designed speedboat was also carrying 2,450 liters of fuel in 49 drums, three satellite communication devices and two emergency beacons. The configuration of the vessel would have allowed it to cover large distances on the open sea without needing to refuel in port.

The satellite communication equipment and the radio beacons found on board suggest an operation being coordinated from land or from another vessel.

The confiscated materials were placed at the disposal of the Federal Attorney General’s Office, which will conduct the corresponding investigations and determine the legal status of the detained persons, all believed to be Ecuadorian nationals.

The interdiction earned the recognition of U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson, who commended the Navy for the bust in a Monday social media post.

We weaken cartels by striking at the operations that sustain them. The seizure of more than a ton of cocaine and 2,450 liters of fuel by @SEMAR_mx directly disrupts their drug trafficking and logistical capabilities. These decisive actions by the Government of Mexico help… https://t.co/UEKQ6pz7KS — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 10, 2026

Media reports indicate that this type of speedboat, with multiple engines and fuel reserves, appears to be gaining in popularity among cartels which have begun using smaller boats with foreign crew members.

On July 21, a speedboat was intercepted 150 nautical miles southwest of Puerto Chiapas with 1.5 tonnes of cocaine; its five crew members were identified as two Ecuadorians and three Guatemalans.

Admiral Morales has said that most of the drugs being shipped by sea to Mexico are concentrated in the South Pacific as well as the Revillagigedo Islands archipelago off the coasts of Colima and Jalisco.

Since President Claudia Sheinbaum took office in October 2024, the Navy has seized more than 80 tonnes of cocaine at sea.

With reports from El Universal, LopezDoriga.com and Infobae

World.title: Homicides down 51% since Sheinbaum took office: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🚔 Homicides down 51% in July vs. September 2024: Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 42.5 homicides per day in July — the lowest monthly average since Sheinbaum took office 22 months ago.

📉 Least violent July in more than a decade: Figueroa presented data showing July was the least violent in over 10 years, with homicides down 34.8% compared to July 2025.

📊 7-month homicide count down 30.8%: Between January and July, the daily average was 48.6 homicides, the lowest for that period since 2015.

🗺️ Nearly half of murders concentrated in 7 states: Guanajuato, Baja California, Chihuahua, Sinaloa, México state, Guerrero and Morelos accounted for just over 49% of the 10,309 homicides recorded nationwide from January to July.

⚠️ García Harfuch: “the job is not finished”: The security minister acknowledged homicides fell 51% since September 2024 but said some regions and crimes still require constant attention.

🔫 63,564 arrests since Sheinbaum took office: Authorities also seized 518.7 tonnes of drugs, 32,824 firearms, and dismantled 2,725 clandestine drug labs across 23 states between Oct. 1, 2024 and July 31, 2026.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera was significant as officials presented the national security report for the month of July.

President Claudia Sheinbaum and other federal officials frequently argue that the reduction in homicides and various other crimes is evidence that the federal government’s security strategy is working.

However, there is skepticism about the accuracy of the government’s homicide numbers, which are based on data provided by Attorney General’s Offices in each of Mexico’s 32 federal entities. Last month, Sheinbaum rejected claims that homicide figures are not accurate because some murders are classified as other less serious crimes.

“Homicide is homicide, there is no manipulation,” she said.

Homicides down 51% in July compared to September 2024

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that there was an average of 42.5 homicides per day in July, a reduction of 51% compared to September 2024, the final month of the presidency of Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

She noted that the daily homicide average in July was the lowest of any month since Sheinbaum took office 22 months ago.

Figueroa also highlighted that, on average, there were 44 fewer homicides per day in July than in September 2024, a month in which the daily murder rate was 86.9.

The least violent July in more than a decade

Figueroa presented a graph that showed that last month was the least violent July in terms of homicides of any year since 2015.

Compared to July 2025, the reduction in homicides last month was 34.8%.

Homicides decline 30.8% in first 7 months of 2026

Figueroa reported that there was an average of 48.6 homicides per day between January and July, a reduction of 30.8% compared to the same period of last year.

She noted that the daily homicide average in the first seven months of the year was the lowest since 2015, when there was an average of 48 murders per day between January and July.

Sheinbaum’s record on homicide reduction compares favorably to her predecessors

Figueroa highlighted that homicides increased during the presidencies of Felipe Calderón and Enrique Peña Nieto before falling during López Obrador’s six-year term.

The homicide rate in 2012, the final year of Calderón’s presidency, was 148% higher than in 2006, a year in which Vicente Fox was in office for the first 11 months. The homicide rate in 2018, the final year of Peña Nieto’s presidency, was 42% higher than in 2012, a year in which Calderón was in office for the first 11 months.

Homicides remained at record-high levels early in López Obrador’s presidency, but in 2024, a year in which AMLO was in office for the first nine months, murders declined 9% compared to 2018.

The daily homicide rate in the first seven months of 2026 was 47% lower than the daily rate in 2024.

Almost half of all murders this year were perpetrated in 7 states

Figueroa presented data that showed there were 10,309 homicides across Mexico in the first seven months of 2026. Just over 49% of those murders — 5,058 — were committed in just seven states.

They were Guanajuato (884 homicides between January and July); Baja California (847); Chihuahua (832); Sinaloa (735); México state (618); Guerrero (579); and Morelos (563).

Mexico City ranked as the 10th most violent entity between January and July with 488 homicides.

Seven states recorded fewer than 50 homicides in the period. They were Yucatán (15); Durango (29); San Luis Potosí (31); Baja California Sur (37); Nayarit (39); Aguascalientes (40); and Coahuila (42);

Homicides declined in 30 entities between January and July

Figueroa presented data that showed that homicides declined in 30 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities between January and July.

The five states with the biggest year-over-year reductions were San Luis Potosí (-80.5%); Nayarit (-63.2%); Quintana Roo (-60.4%); Zacatecas (-53.2%); and Baja California Sur (-51.3%).

The only states where homicides didn’t decline in the first seven months of 2026 were Oaxaca and Coahuila.

García Harfuch acknowledges there is still work to be done to combat insecurity

At the start of his presentation, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch noted that homicides declined 51% in July compared to September 2024.

“With this, we don’t want to say that the job is finished,” he said.

“We know there are still regions and crimes that need constant attention, and authorities have situations to face up to every day,” García Harfuch said.

More than 63,000 people arrested for allegedly committing high-impact crimes

According to data presented by García Harfuch, 63, 564 people were arrested between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and July 31, 2026, for allegedly committing high-impact crimes such as murder, kidnapping, extortion and violent robbery.

In the same period, authorities seized 518.7 tonnes of drugs and 32,824 firearms. In addition, the Mexican military dismantled 2,725 clandestine drug laboratories where criminal organizations produce narcotics such as methamphetamine. García Harfuch said that the laboratories were located in 23 states.

World.title: ‘The Forgotten Ones’: Mexico’s mysterious forest guardians
World.content:
Lately, I have been looking into stories and happenings in Mexico that, for one reason or another, never quite achieved the fame of other national legends. Some stories catch hold of the public imagination and refuse to let go. Others drift quietly along the margins of conversation, mentioned occasionally, then forgotten again.

It occurred to me that some of these lesser-known tales should, from time to time, be dusted off, their origins once again wandering through conversation.

Some legends age well, while others improve with neglect. Here is one such story.

‘The Forgotten Ones’

High in the mountains of El Cielo Biosphere Reserve (ECBR) in the northeastern Mexican state of Tamaulipas, there lingers a quiet legend about a group known simply as Los Olvidados, or “The Forgotten Ones.”

According to the tale, long ago, a band of shamans from the ancient Maya civilization slipped away from their communities and traveled north into these remote mountains. No one is entirely certain why they left. Still, it becomes remarkably vague whenever a group of mystics decides to walk into the wilderness and not come back.

What the stories claim is that these shamans eventually settled deep in the forests of the protected ECBR region, where mountains rise high enough to catch the clouds and hold them for a while. It is a forest where mist drifts slowly through the trees and the trails twist out of sight after a few dozen yards.

If a person wished to disappear into such a place, the forest would be more than willing to assist.

And so, according to local lore, the shamans vanished into the mountains and became the quiet guardians of the forest. Over time, they came to be known as Los Olvidados. This name, however, presents a small problem.

The mysterious stories about El Cielo’s forest guardians

Forgotten things generally stay forgotten. They do not occasionally appear on remote paths, standing silently among the trees before slipping back into the fog. Yet hikers, ranchers and the occasional birdwatcher have all reported glimpsing figures in the forest; men who seem oddly out of place, watching the land with the patience of someone who has been waiting a very long time.

Naturally, no one ever gets a very good look. This is one of the basic rules of folklore. The mysterious figure is always seen at a distance, often obscured by mist or trees. Still, the stories persist.

Admittedly, the setting does much of the work. The ECBR forests are the sort of place where imagination feels perfectly comfortable stretching its legs. The mountains are steep, the vegetation thick and the fog drifts through the trees with the deliberate pace of a stage curtain preparing to draw.

In such surroundings, even a perfectly ordinary person standing quietly on a hillside can look supernatural, if only for a moment. Add a few centuries of retelling, and the figure becomes a guardian spirit.

Who are ‘The Forgotten Ones’?

Of course, historians point out a small geographical curiosity. The great centers of the Maya civilization were located hundreds of miles to the south. For a group of shamans to journey all the way north into the mountains of Tamaulipas would require a fairly determined expedition.

But legends have never been especially bothered by geography. If a good story requires a few extra miles of travel, history generally looks the other way.

In fact, legends thrive on exactly this kind of uncertainty. A small gap in the historical record is like a loose thread on a sweater. Once someone begins pulling on it, the entire garment slowly unravels into a much more interesting story. Modern times, if anything, have helped the legend along.

In earlier centuries, a mysterious sighting might circulate among a few nearby villages. Today, it can travel across the internet before dinner. A blurry photograph of a distant figure standing among trees can revive an old legend faster than a campfire story on a cold evening.

A blurry figure on a ridge

Visitors now travel to the region precisely because of its wild beauty. Hikers arrive with cameras, binoculars and the quiet hope that they might glimpse something unusual among the trees. Most of them see nothing more mysterious than a bird, a deer or a particularly stubborn cloud of mosquitoes.

But occasionally, someone notices a figure far up a ridge, standing quietly for a moment before disappearing into the forest. And the story begins again.

Of course, there are other possible explanations. The mountains are large, and it would not be entirely surprising if a few solitary individuals had chosen to live quietly among them over the years. A hermit, a naturalist or perhaps a park ranger taking a moment to admire the view could easily appear briefly and vanish before anyone has time to ask for identification. But that explanation lacks poetry.

The idea that ancient guardians still walk the forest has a certain elegance. It suggests that someone, somewhere, is quietly keeping an eye on things, someone who remembers the forest as it once was and would prefer that it remain that way.

The legend lives on

And perhaps that is the real reason the legend of Los Olvidados survives.

In a world where nearly every corner of the map has been photographed, cataloged and given directions on a phone, it is comforting to imagine that a few places remain slightly mysterious, and where the forest, for a moment, seems to remember something the rest of us have forgotten.

Robert Santacroce is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: US border wall expansion threatens memory of Porvenir massacre
World.content:
A border wall construction project in Big Bend National Park in West Texas began last week, with a separate, nearby access road threatening the archaeological landscape of Porvenir, the site of a 1918 massacre of ethnic Mexican villagers.

Contractors began work Thursday on 17 miles of low, noncontiguous barrier fences and patrol roads, with conservationists reporting bulldozers clearing native vegetation.

One new access road appears to cut directly through Porvenir, which was a small farming community along the Rio Grande over 100 years ago.

On Jan. 28, 1918, Texas Rangers, local ranchers and apparently U.S. Army soldiers removed 15 unarmed ethnic Mexican residents (13 men and two teenage boys) from their homes and executed them, according to a lengthy report in Texas Monthly last week.

The location remains a sacred place for descendants and an archaeological site. A 2015 excavation found military-issued cartridge casings, evidence that challenged the historical narrative that the killings were carried out solely by vigilantes and Texas Rangers. The Texas Historical Commission erected a marker in 2018 after descendants campaigned for recognition.

Archaeologist David Keller told Texas Monthly that a newly built access road about 16 feet wide crosses the eastern third of the archaeological area and has been traversed by heavy machinery.

He said contractors and local officials indicated the route could eventually be widened to 100 or 120 feet.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is managing the project through Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

The CBP said the barriers, though low and not connected, are intended to prevent off-road vehicles from traveling to and from the Rio Grande, adding that the Porvenir access route is not finalized and public feedback will be considered.

DHS awarded a US $1.7 billion contract in May for the work, which has drawn widespread bipartisan opposition.

Even supporters of President Donald Trump have opposed the project for using billions of taxpayer dollars to build low fencing in a rugged, remote part of Texas where few illegal crossings have been recorded.

Podcaster Joe Rogan, who endorsed Trump in 2024, called the plan “B.S.” on his podcast, the San Antonio Current reported.

“This is the most heinous attack on an American national park in generations,” Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement posted to Instagram.

The Current reported that it was the first time in U.S. history that the federal government waived such a broad set of environmental protections for construction inside a national park.

With reports from Texas Monthly, AZFamily, San Antonio Current and Texas Standard

World.title: Mexico sends over 300 firefighters to British Columbia
World.content:
Listen to this article

More than 300 Mexican firefighters and technical personnel specializing in forest fires have travelled to British Columbia (B.C.), Canada, to support emergency efforts during the intense wildfires that have led to the evacuation of more than 20,000 people in the areas of Summerland and Peachland.

The Mexican teams arrived in separate contingents during the first few days of August, with the first group, comprising more than 100 people, arriving in Abbotsford on Aug. 3, and more than 200 crew arriving subsequently. A fourth delegation left on Sunday.

We’re beyond grateful to our friends and partners in Mexico for sending hundreds of firefighters to B.C. They’re joining a team of roughly 2,000 wildfire service personnel who are working tirelessly to get these fires under control. pic.twitter.com/5i8vFQFStr — David Eby (@Dave_Eby) August 6, 2026

Groups are deployed primarily throughout Fraser Canyon and the Thompson/Okanagan region, where they are participating in firefighting and control operations.

The contingent also features an incident management team, marking the first from Mexico to be deployed to B.C. under the mutual aid agreement between the two countries.

The tasks that the Mexican crew carry out include direct fire attack and the extinguishing of hot spots using hand tools and pumps, as well as reconnaissance and monitoring of areas where heat persists. They also participate in felling trees deemed hazardous and installing equipment to ensure a water supply during suppression operations.

B.C. Premier David Eby recognized the crew’s work and gave a welcoming speech as one of the contingents arrived at the airport.

“Mexico heard the call and, as you can see, has stepped up in a significant way,” Eby said.

Okanagan Falls park acting as base camp for over 300 wildfire firefighters from B.C. and Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

Meanwhile, Minister of Forests Ravi Parmar said that he felt proud of the firefighters’ joint work.

“I’m proud of the wildland firefighters from Canada and Mexico who are not thinking about borders but are answering the call, as we do when our neighbours need us,” Parmar said.

Mexico’s envoys are made up of experienced personnel from the National Forestry Commission (Conafor), the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (Conanp), state and municipal environmental agencies, Civil Protection, rural fire management brigades and civil society organizations.

The arrival of the firefighting crews comes as B.C. faces more than 100 active wildfires spanning 156 square kilometers. In addition to Mexico, British Columbia has received support from Australia, New Zealand and other Canadian provinces and territories.

With reports from Now Toronto, Publimetro, CBN Noticias and the CBC

World.title: Navy ramps up security presence in Mazatlán after high July homicide count
World.content:
After Mazatlán in July recorded its highest monthly homicide total of the year, the Mexican Navy on Saturday announced the deployment of more than 1,700 of its personnel to the Sinaloa port and resort city.

In a statement, the Navy Ministry (SEMAR) said that the deployment was occurring “within the framework of ‘Operation Sable’ Mazatlán” and was aimed at the “strengthening of security” in the city, the second largest in Sinaloa after state capital Culiacán.

The deployment comes after 36 homicides in Mazatlán in July, the city’s highest monthly total of murders in 2026, according to the newspaper El Sol de Mazatlán. It also follows the arrival of 900 Mexican Army troops in Mazatlán on July 23. The bolstering of the army’s presence in the city was part of a security reinforcement in response to a series of armed attacks.

In its statement, SEMAR said that the navy deployment reflects “the institution’s ongoing commitment to the well-being” of Mazatlán residents and tourists.

The ministry said that “operational actions will be focused on strategic areas … with the priority objective of reestablishing peace and public order and weakening illicit infrastructure that fuels schemes of violence and places the health of the population at risk.”

The term “illicit infrastructure” was a reference to clandestine drug laboratories and the cartel assets that support the distribution of narcotics, such as vehicles.

In its statement, SEMAR also issued what it called a “respectful call” for citizens and tourists to have “full confidence and certainty in the deployed forces.”

The ministry said that the central focus of the Mexican Navy’s operations is to “protect Mexican families while acting at all times with strict adherence to human rights, the proportional use of force and the current legal framework.”

“Its presence in the streets and on the coast has the sole aim of providing a safe and protected environment,” SEMAR said.

Violence in Mazatlán

Of the 36 people murdered in Mazatlán in July, 32 were men and four were women, El Sol de Mazatlán reported on Monday. The newspaper wrote that two cases were investigated as femicides, while two of the victims were minors.

Among the armed attacks in Mazatlán last month was one allegedly perpetrated by the “Los Chapitos” faction of the Sinaloa Cartel against marines, two of whom died from wounds they sustained. Marines returned fire and killed 10 criminals.

Much of the violence in Sinaloa is related to an ongoing battle between Los Chapitos, led by sons of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, and “Los Mayos,” a Sinaloa Cartel faction formerly led by Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada. The battle intensified in 2024 after Zambada was kidnapped by Joaquín Guzmán López and forced onto a plane that flew him to New Mexico. Both Zambada and Guzmán López, a son of “El Chapo,” were arrested by U.S. authorities at the Doña Ana County International Jetport in the U.S. border state in July 2024.

While the majority of the fighting between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos has occurred in Culiacán and surrounding areas, the battle has spilled into other parts of Sinaloa, including Mazatlán.

As Mexico News Daily reported last month, on July 17 and 18, six armed attacks were reported in Mazatlán in less than 24 hours, leaving four people dead and three others wounded. Between July 22 and 23, five more people were murdered.

El Sol de Mazatlán reported that episodes of violence in Mazatlán in July, including attacks on homes with firearms and explosives, occurred in rural and urban areas of the municipality of Mazatlán, including parts of the city frequented by tourists. Among those areas, the newspaper reported, were San Marcos, Lomas de Monterrey, Santa Fe, Infonavit Alarcón, Hacienda del Seminario, Lomas del Ébano, Zona Dorada and Pradera Dorada.

With reports from Expansión and El Sol de Mazatlán

World.title: Most avocado exports to the US have resumed after last week’s suspension
World.content:
Approximately 75% of avocado packing facilities in Mexico’s Michoacán state have been cleared for export following a pause in the avocado trade with the United States over security concerns, Julio Berdegué, Mexico’s advisor for international agri-food affairs and strategic issues under the USMCA, announced on Saturday.

The re-approved facilities handle roughly 85% of Michoacán’s avocado exports and the rest will be restored soon, according to Berdegué.

Mexico exports over 1 million tonnes of avocados a year, according to data from the Mexican Agriculture Ministry. Meanwhile, Michoacán contributes the highest avocado production of any Mexican state, with an export market valued at US $3.65 billion.

U.S. avocado imports from Michoacán were temporarily suspended on Wednesday after the U.S. Embassy issued an alert regarding a “threat to U.S. interests.” It marked the third time in just over four years that the United States has suspended avocado trade with Mexico for security reasons.

The embassy statement announcing the suspension did not reveal the nature of the threat, but President Sheinbaum has since said that the suspension followed a meeting at the U.S. embassy related to threats against some of the inspectors hired by the United States to monitor sanitary quality.

A meeting scheduled for the following day with an organization of avocado producers revealed that there had been an increase in extortion cases in certain regions of Michoacán.

In response to the news, Mexico worked to “rapidly strengthen” security in the state for the “immediate and gradual” resumption of the export program, said U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson.

Following the suspension, Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla deployed an extra 300 security operatives to Michoacán’s avocado-growing region “as a preventive measure.” Then, on Thursday morning, the federal Defense Ministry announced it had sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the state to “protect avocado producers and packing plants in the region.”

Exports resumed from the municipalities of Tancítaro, Tacámbaro and Uruapan, as well as the area between Morelia and Pátzcuaro, on Saturday.

To prevent future security issues, the Mexican government has established a permanent working group to monitor security in the region and prevent extortion of producers.

With reports from ABC Noticias and La Jornada

World.title: Chile Cuts 2026 Copper Output Forecast to 5.27 Million Tonnes on Weak First Half
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts — Forecast cut Cochilco lowered 2026 output to 5.27 million tonnes, down 2.6% from 2025.

— 2027 rebound Cochilco projects output of 5.55 million tonnes in 2027.

— Price outlook Cochilco raised its 2026 price forecast to US$5.95 per pound.

— June Escondida Output rose 45.8% year on year to 111,400 tonnes in June.

— June Codelco Output fell 4.8% year on year to 114,400 tonnes in June.

— June Collahuasi Production increased 1.7% year on year to 34,900 tonnes.

— Official comment Daniel Mas, biministro de Economía y Minería, addressed the projections.

Cochilco projects a 2.6% decline in 2026 output before a rebound in 2027.

Chile’s state copper commission cut its 2026 copper output forecast to 5.27 million tonnes, according to Cochilco. The new projection represents a 2.6% decline from 2025 output levels.

Cochilco Revises Output Forecast Lower

Cochilco, Chile’s state copper commission, revised its 2026 output forecast to 5.27 million tonnes. This marks a 2.6% fall from the previous year’s production, the commission said.

The commission cited a weak first half of 2026 as the primary reason for the revision. Lower output at state-owned Codelco and BHP’s Escondida and Spence mines contributed to the shortfall.

The revised figure represents a significant adjustment from earlier projections. Reflecting the operational realities observed during the first six months of the year.

Analysts tracking the Chilean copper sector had anticipated a possible downgrade. But the magnitude of the cut underscores the severity of the challenges faced by major producers.

Chile remains the world’s largest copper producer, accounting for roughly a quarter of global mine supply. As such.

Any fluctuation in its output has direct implications for international copper prices and the broader supply-demand balance in the global metals market. The commission’s report, released after market hours, was closely watched by traders and industry stakeholders.

The data provides a benchmark for evaluating the performance of the country’s mining sector. Which is a critical driver of Chile’s economy and government revenues.

2027 Rebound Projected for Chilean Copper

Cochilco projects a rebound in 2027, with output expected to reach 5.55 million tonnes. This forecast was reported by Reuters and Investing.

com. The projected recovery suggests a stabilization of operations after the anticipated 2026 decline.

The anticipated uptick in 2027 is based on expectations of improved operational performance at existing mines. As well as the gradual ramp-up of new projects.

Industry observers note that the recovery will depend on resolving persistent issues such as ore grade decline, water scarcity, and labor disruptions. Cochilco’s projections for 2027 also imply a return to growth that could help alleviate concerns about a prolonged copper supply deficit.

The market has been grappling with tight supply conditions. Driven by strong demand from the energy transition sector and constrained mine output globally.

The 5.55 million tonne forecast for 2027 would represent an increase of approximately 5.3% compared to the 2026 projection. This growth trajectory, if realized, would position Chile to contribute significantly to meeting the rising global demand for copper.

Particularly for use in electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, and grid infrastructure.
