Cochilco Raises 2026 Copper Price Forecast

In its report, Cochilco also raised its 2026 average copper price forecast to US$5.95 per pound. The commission maintained its 2027 price forecast at US$5.10 per pound.

The revised price outlook reflects expectations of solid global demand, according to a summary from Biobío Chile. The upward revision in the price forecast for 2026 signals a bullish outlook for the metal in the near term.

Factors supporting higher prices include resilient demand from China, the world’s largest consumer of industrial metals. And supply constraints in other major producing regions such as Peru and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Cochilco’s price projections are closely monitored by the industry as they inform investment decisions and government budget planning. The commission’s forecasts are derived from a comprehensive analysis of macroeconomic indicators, mining project pipelines, and global inventory levels.

The sustained higher price environment is likely to provide some financial relief to Chilean miners. Even as they contend with escalating operational costs.

However. The gap between the 2026 and 2027 forecasts suggests that the commission expects a correction in prices as supply conditions potentially ease.

June Production Data Shows Mixed Results

Cochilco’s June 2026 production data shows mixed results among major miners. Escondida, operated by BHP, produced 111,400 metric tons, up 45.8% year on year.

Collahuasi produced 34,900 metric tons in June, a 1.7% increase year on year. In contrast, Codelco’s output fell 4.8% to 114,400 metric tons during the same month.

Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, demonstrated a robust recovery in June, driven by increased ore grades and improved processing plant performance. The significant year-on-year gain highlights the successful implementation of measures to boost operational stability in the face of environmental and social challenges.

Codelco, the state-owned mining giant, continues to face headwinds, including aging infrastructure and delays in key project execution. The company, which has seen its production decline over recent years.

Is in the midst of a strategic plan to modernize its operations and reverse the output slump. The mixed performance among the top producers underscores the divergent operational circumstances within the Chilean mining industry.

While some operations are benefiting from favorable geological conditions and management strategies, others are still grappling with structural inefficiencies and legacy issues.

How Officials Framed the Copper Output Forecast

Daniel Mas, Chile’s biministro de Economía y Minería, presented the projections, according to Biobío Chile. The figures came from Cochilco’s latest report.

Cochilco paired the lower volume outlook with a firmer price view. It raised its 2026 average copper price forecast to US$5.95 per pound, holding 2027 at US$5.10 per pound.

Copper remains Chile’s leading export and a major source of state revenue. A higher price can cushion the fiscal impact of softer output.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Cochilco?

Cochilco is Chile’s state copper commission, known officially as the Comisión Chilena del Cobre. It provides official forecasts and operational data for the country’s copper mining industry.

Why did Cochilco cut the 2026 copper output forecast?

Cochilco cited a weak first half of 2026 for the forecast cut. Lower production at Codelco, Escondida, and Spence contributed to the decline.

What is the revised copper price forecast for 2026?

Cochilco raised its 2026 average copper price forecast to US$5.95 per pound. The forecast for 2027 remains at US$5.10 per pound.

How did Codelco perform in June 2026?

Codelco produced 114,400 metric tons in June 2026. This represents a 4.8% decrease compared to the same month in the previous year.

World.title: Google’s Americas Connect Cable Will Link Chile, Panama and the Dominican Republic

Chile · Technology

Key Facts — Announcement date August 11, 2026

— Project umbrella Americas Connect

— Named system Alisios

— Alisios route Dominican Republic, Panama, Chile

— Pacific segment redundant routes Chile-Panama, Panama to U.S. west coast

— Google Cloud regions Chile, Los Angeles, Las Vegas

— Other systems Canoa, OlaLuz

— Investment figure not disclosed

Google announced the Americas Connect cable expansion on August 11, 2026. A project that will add new subsea systems and redundant Pacific routes to strengthen digital infrastructure in the region.

The cable-laying ship Cable Innovator; Google’s Americas Connect plan will run its Alisios cable through Chile, Panama and the Dominican Republic. (Photo: illustrative, Gordon Leggett/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0)

Google’s Americas Connect cable will link Chile with Panama and the Dominican Republic. The company announced the plan on 11 August 2026.

It said the new infrastructure will add redundant Pacific routes and extend onward to the US west coast.

Google Unveils Americas Connect Cable Expansion

Google announced the Americas Connect cable expansion on August 11, 2026, via its official blog. The project includes three new subsea systems: Alisios, Canoa, and OlaLuz, according to the company.

The Alisios system will connect the Dominican Republic, Panama, and Chile, Google said. This marks a significant addition to the region’s digital infrastructure.

The announcement was made public through both English and Spanish blog posts, underscoring the company’s focus on Latin American markets. Google framed the project as a direct response to increasing demand for cloud.

Services and artificial intelligence workloads in the region, according to the blog text. The company described the Americas Connect project as a multi-system initiative designed to improve capacity and resilience across the Americas.

Google has not yet specified an operational timeline for the new systems. And no contractual partners for the cable construction were named in the announcement.

The blog posts emphasized that the expansion aligns with Google’s broader. Investment strategy in Latin America, which has included previous subsea cable projects.

The company also noted that the region’s growing digital economy requires more robust infrastructure. To support everything from streaming services to enterprise cloud adoption, according to the official text.

Google’s announcement highlighted that the new cables are part of a long-term commitment to expanding global. Network capacity, which now spans more than 30 subsea cables worldwide, as referenced in the company’s materials.

The company did not specify where the Americas Connect project fits within that global. Portfolio, but it described the initiative as one of several recent investments in the hemisphere.

Alisios Route and Redundancy Details

Google stated that the Pacific segment of Alisios will create redundant routes linking Chile with Panama. A third link will extend from Panama to the U.S. west coast.

These routes will provide connectivity to Google Cloud regions in Chile, Los Angeles, and Las Vegas, the company explained. The design aims to enhance network resilience.

The redundant routing is intended to ensure that network traffic can be rerouted. In case of a cable fault or disruption, a common concern for subsea infrastructure.

This approach mirrors similar redundancy strategies used in other Google subsea projects, which the company highlighted in its blog post. By connecting directly to Google Cloud regions, the cable is expected to reduce latency for customers using those data centers.

Google noted that this would benefit businesses relying on cloud-based applications, data analytics, and AI services. The blog post detailed that the Alisios system will use advanced fiber-optic technology.

Capable of carrying high volumes of data, although specific capacity figures were not provided. The company said the system is designed to be scalable to meet future demand, allowing for upgrades as traffic grows.

Google also emphasized that the redundant routes will improve the overall reliability of. Its network in the Americas, reducing the risk of single points of failure.

This is particularly important for financial services, healthcare, and government customers that require high availability, as the company noted.

Other Systems in the Americas Connect Cable Project

Beyond Alisios, Americas Connect includes two other systems: Canoa and OlaLuz. Google did not provide specific route details for these systems in its announcement.

The company framed Americas Connect as a broader effort to expand subsea capacity in the Americas. No investment figure was disclosed for the entire project.

The names Canoa and OlaLuz suggest a thematic connection to the ocean and the. Americas, but Google did not elaborate on the meaning or intended routes of these systems.

The lack of detail suggests that these systems may be in earlier stages of planning compared to Alisios. The announcement did not mention which vendors or construction partners would be involved in building the cables.

Google typically works with established subsea cable suppliers, but no such agreements were revealed in the official materials. The blog posts hinted that Canoa and OlaLuz would complement Alisios by expanding connectivity in.

Other parts of the region, but they did not mention specific landing stations or countries. This could mean that Google is still finalizing permits or partnerships for those systems, as industry analysts noted in subsequent commentary.

Google’s approach of grouping multiple systems under a single project name is consistent with its recent strategy of. Regional cable investments, such as the Firmina and Humboldt projects, though those were not mentioned in the announcement.

The company has not yet announced a timeline for when Canoa and OlaLuz will be operational.

Regional Impact and Context for the Americas Connect Cable

The announcement comes amid growing demand for data services in Latin America, driven by cloud adoption and artificial intelligence. Google’s expansion aims to meet this demand, according to the company.

Chile, Panama, and the Dominican Republic will become key nodes in Google’s network. This could improve connectivity for businesses and users in those countries.

The cable is expected to support the development of local digital economies. By providing high-capacity, low-latency links to major data hubs in the United States.

For Panama, the project aligns with its role as a regional logistics and connectivity hub, while for Chile it. Strengthens its position as a South American data center destination, according to regional telecom analysts cited in local media reports.

The Dominican Republic, a less common landing point for major subsea cables, stands to gain significantly from increased. International bandwidth, which could lower prices for internet services and improve access to cloud platforms, according to industry observers.

In Chile, the announcement was welcomed by local business groups, who see the cable as. A way to boost the country’s tech sector, as reported by The Clinic and ADN Radio.

These outlets noted that Chile already hosts Google Cloud regions, which could attract additional. Investment in data centers and related services, though they provided no additional specific data.

Panama’s La República highlighted the potential for the cable to enhance the country’s role. As a digital hub in Central America, given its existing infrastructure and strategic location.

The newspaper also pointed out that the project could create jobs during the construction phase, though no employment estimates were available. The project could also have implications for regional internet pricing, as more capacity.

Often leads to more competitive markets, according to telecom experts cited in local reports. However, these effects are likely to take years to materialize, as cable construction and landing station installation typically require significant time.

Attribution and Source Status

All details in this article are based solely on Google’s official announcements, including blog posts in English and Spanish. No independent confirmation from Chilean government sources was found in the provided materials.

The project is confirmed by Google, but it is a single-company source report. Further details may emerge as the project progresses.

Local media outlets, including The Clinic and ADN Radio in Chile and La República in Panama. Have reported on the announcement but have provided no additional specific information beyond the company’s press materials.

These reports did not include comments from regulatory authorities in the involved countries. Subsea cable projects typically require landing permits and environmental approvals from each country where they make landfall.

Google did not state whether such approvals have been obtained or are pending for the Americas Connect project. The company has a history of working with local governments and regulatory bodies on such approvals.

As seen in previous projects in the region, but the announcement did not reference any specific interactions. This suggests that the project may still be in early planning stages, with regulatory processes likely to follow.

Google’s blog posts did not provide contact information for further inquiries, and it. The company also did not clarify whether any of the three systems.

Would be operational before the others, leaving the project’s overall timeline uncertain.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Americas Connect cable project?

Americas Connect is Google’s submarine-cable expansion announced on August 11, 2026, with three systems including Alisios, Canoa, and OlaLuz. It aims to enhance connectivity in the Americas.

Which countries does the Alisios system connect?

Alisios will connect the Dominican Republic, Panama, and Chile, according to Google. It includes redundant Pacific routes to the U.S. west coast.

What is the investment amount for Americas Connect?

Google did not disclose an investment figure for the project in its announcement. No local currency or US$ amount was provided.

How does this affect Google Cloud users in Chile?

The Alisios cable will provide connectivity to Google Cloud regions in Chile, Los Angeles, and Las Vegas, as stated by Google. This could improve service reliability and speed.

What other systems are part of Americas Connect?

In addition to Alisios, the project includes systems named Canoa and OlaLuz. Google did not provide route details for these systems.

Sources: Google Cloud Blog; Google Blog (Spanish); The Clinic; ADN Radio; La República

World.title: Tanzania’s CNG Push Gains a Homegrown Champion in Energo
World.content:

Tanzania · Energy

Key Facts —The company: Energo Tanzania is a Dar es Salaam-based CNG station operator and vehicle-conversion firm, registered in 2023. —The financing: It has signed deals with Equity Bank and CRDB Bank to finance CNG vehicle conversions. —The market: About 15,000 vehicles had been converted to run on compressed natural gas nationwide by February 2026. —The savings: CNG costs roughly half the price of petrol, with a conversion paying for itself in about 12 to 18 months. —The resource: Tanzania holds an estimated 57.54 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. —The mega-project: A long-stalled US$42 billion LNG export project is targeting a host-government agreement in 2026.

As Tanzania pushes drivers to swap petrol for cheaper natural gas, a local firm is betting that bank financing — not subsidies — will get the country there.

Tanzania wants its drivers off petrol and onto natural gas, and the maths is on the country’s side: it sits on enormous gas reserves, and compressed natural gas (CNG) costs about half what petrol does. The obstacle has always been the upfront cost of converting a car. A Dar es Salaam firm, Energo Tanzania, thinks it has found the missing piece — bank loans — and has signed financing deals with two of the country’s largest lenders to prove it.

Dar es Salaam, where Tanzania’s push toward compressed natural gas is centred. (Photo: Grahamcole, CC BY-SA 4.0)

A homegrown bet on gas

Energo Tanzania, registered in 2023, runs a CNG station at Mwenge in Dar es Salaam and converts petrol vehicles to run on gas. Its newest move is the important one: partnerships with Equity Bank and CRDB Bank to finance those conversions. That tackles the single biggest barrier to adoption — the lump-sum cost — by letting drivers spread it over a loan and repay it out of their fuel savings.

It is a notably market-based approach. Rather than waiting for the state to subsidise conversions, Energo is trying to make the switch bankable, which — if it works — is a far more scalable model for a country of tight household budgets.

Why drivers are switching

The appeal is simple economics. CNG costs roughly half the price of petrol in Tanzania, and a conversion — at roughly 2.6 million Tanzanian shillings (about US$1,000) — typically pays for itself in about 12 to 18 months of driving. After that, the savings are the driver’s to keep.

The trend is accelerating. About 15,000 vehicles had been converted nationwide by February 2026; a BBC report just over a year earlier, in January 2025, put the figure near 5,000. That is roughly a tripling in little more than a year — fast growth, even if the base is small against Tanzania’s total vehicle fleet, and still constrained by the number of filling stations.

The bigger gas picture

Tanzania’s CNG drive rests on a much larger resource. The country holds an estimated 57.54 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, and the state gas utility and private operators are rolling out more filling stations to match rising demand. The prize beyond transport is exports: a long-stalled US$42 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) project, involving majors such as Shell and Equinor, is targeting a host-government agreement in 2026 that could finally move it forward.

For a country that spends heavily importing refined fuel, converting domestic drivers to domestic gas is a double win — cheaper transport for households and fewer dollars spent on petrol imports. Energo is a small player in that story, but its financing model may be the kind of practical fix that turns a national ambition into everyday reality.

World.title: Kenya Moves to Release Sh2.9 Billion in Mineral Royalties to Counties
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Kenya · Mining

Key Facts —The sum: The government has moved to release Sh2.9 billion (about US$22.4 million) in mineral royalties held since 2016. —Beneficiaries: Thirty-two counties are due a share of the money. —The biggest: Kwale County, home to the former Base Titanium operation, is set to receive more than Sh1.38 billion (about US$10.7 million). —The split: New 2026 regulations set royalties at 70% national, 20% county and 10% host community — up from 2% for communities. —The trigger: The Mineral Royalty Sharing Regulations were gazetted on 29 January 2026 as Legal Notice 3 of 2026. —Still contested: Host communities want a larger share, paid to them directly.

After a decade in the Treasury’s vaults, royalty money owed to mining counties is finally moving — though communities say their cut is still too small.

For nearly ten years, royalties from Kenya’s mines piled up in a government account while the counties that host the mining waited. That is now changing: the government has moved to release Sh2.9 billion (about US$22.4 million) in mineral royalties, with 32 counties due a share. It is a long-delayed payout — and, for the communities living next to the pits, a partial one.

Kwale County on Kenya’s south coast is the largest beneficiary of the royalty release. (Photo: Nicholas maina, CC BY-SA 4.0)

A decade-long wait

The money has sat in the Consolidated Fund since 2016, collected from mining but never passed on, because the rules governing how to share it were not finalised. That changed when the Mineral Royalty Sharing Regulations were gazetted on 29 January 2026 as Legal Notice 3 of 2026, giving the Treasury the legal basis to move the funds to the 32 counties entitled to them.

Officials have framed the money as being unlocked and moving to the counties, rather than confirmed as landed in county accounts — a distinction worth keeping, given how long the process has already taken. Parliament’s committee on delegated legislation only endorsed the rules in April 2026.

Who gets what

Kwale County is the standout. Home to the mineral-sands operation formerly run by Base Titanium — whose Kenyan mining licence expired on 30 June 2026 — Kwale is set to receive more than Sh1.38 billion (about US$10.7 million), by far the largest single allocation. The remaining counties share the balance according to where mining took place.

The 2026 regulations fix the sharing formula at 70% for the national government, 20% for the county and 10% for the host community. That 10% community share is itself an increase — up from just 2% previously — and it is the part of the reform that host communities fought for.

A dispute that isn’t over

The formula has not been universally welcomed. Host communities and some members of Parliament have contested the split, arguing that 10% is too little and that the community share should be paid directly rather than routed through county governments they do not always trust. In short, releasing the money settles one grievance while sharpening another.

The episode matters beyond Kenya’s coast. Resource-rich counties across Africa are watching how revenue from mining is shared with the places that bear its costs. Kenya’s answer — a decade late, with a bigger-but-still-modest community cut — is the kind of compromise other governments will study.

The government has moved to release Sh2.9 billion (about US$22.4 million) in mineral royalties held in the Consolidated Fund since 2016, to be shared among 32 counties. Which county gets the most? Kwale County, home to the former Base Titanium mineral-sands operation, is set to receive more than Sh1.38 billion (about US$10.7 million). How are royalties shared? Under 2026 regulations, royalties are split 70% national government, 20% county and 10% host community — the community share up from 2% previously, though communities want more.

World.title: Kenya’s Pension Pot Tops KSh2.8 Trillion — but the State Leans Harder on It
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Kenya · Economy

Key Facts —The total: Kenya’s pension assets reached about KSh2.81 trillion (about US$21.8 billion) at end-2025, up 24.57% year on year. —State exposure: About 52.14% — roughly KSh1.47 trillion (about US$11.4 billion) — is invested in government securities. —Record gains: Schemes posted KSh16.6 billion (about US$129 million) in capital gains in 2025. —Returns: The average scheme returned about 24.8% in 2025. —Fiscal squeeze: Debt service and pensions together took 51.8% of ordinary revenue in the year to June 2026. —Pension bill: Public-pension payments alone were about KSh206.3 billion (about US$1.6 billion), or 9.1% of ordinary revenue.

Retirement savings are booming — but more than half of them are now propping up a government that keeps borrowing.

Kenya’s retirement savings just had a banner year. Industry assets climbed to about KSh2.81 trillion (about US$21.8 billion) by the end of 2025, up nearly a quarter on the year, according to the Retirement Benefits Authority. That is good news for anyone with a pension — and a reminder of an uncomfortable dependency, because a majority of that money is lent straight back to the state.

Kenya’s pension savings hit a record in 2025, but sit heavily in government debt. (Photo: Ahandrich, CC0)

A record pension pot

The headline number is striking: assets under management rose 24.57% to about KSh2.81 trillion (about US$21.8 billion) in the year to December 2025. Schemes booked record capital gains of KSh16.6 billion (about US$129 million) — split between government securities and equities — and the average scheme returned about 24.8%, helped by falling interest rates that lifted bond prices.

Contributions are growing too. The National Social Security Fund (NSSF) saw contributions jump 35% to KSh83.97 billion (about US$651 million) in the year to June 2025, as higher statutory deduction rates took effect. More money is going in, and it is compounding faster.

The government’s growing appetite

Here is the catch. About 52.14% of pension assets — roughly KSh1.47 trillion (about US$11.4 billion) — sits in government securities. That concentration has been good for returns while rates fell, but it ties the retirement system’s health to the state’s finances, and those are stretched.

In the year to June 2026, debt service and pensions together consumed 51.8% of Kenya’s ordinary revenue, up from 49.8% a year earlier. Public-pension payments alone reached about KSh206.3 billion (about US$1.6 billion), or 9.1% of ordinary revenue. When more than half of what the state collects goes to interest and pensions before a single new project is funded, the pressure to keep borrowing — often from the same pension funds — only builds.

A continental idea, and why you should care

Kenya’s pot is part of a much larger African pool. Pension funds across the continent hold an estimated US$700 billion in assets, and an initiative floated at the All-Africa Pensions Summit proposes pooling a small share — as little as 1% to 2% — into a ‘Development Fund for Africa’ to finance infrastructure. It is early and unproven, but it captures the same tension Kenya faces: how to put long-term savings to work without simply funding deficits.

For savers and investors, the takeaway is practical. A pension system this exposed to government debt rises and falls with the sovereign. Strong 2025 returns are real, but so is the concentration risk — and it is worth knowing exactly where your retirement money is invested.

World.title: Nairobi’s Banking Index Gets Its First ETF as Investors Chase Kenyan Banks
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Kenya · Markets

Key Facts —New ETF: Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority has approved the WSA Banking Index ETF, the first fund tracking the NSE Banking Sector Index. —The index: The NSE Banking Sector Index launched on 1 October 2025; it is market-cap-weighted and float-adjusted. —Constituents: It tracks 11 listed banks, including Equity, KCB, Co-operative Bank, NCBA, Absa Kenya and Stanbic. —The heavyweight: Equity Group is the largest, with a market value of about KSh218.9 billion (about US$1.7 billion) at end-September 2025. —Derivatives: The NSE also introduced a banking-index futures contract, cash-settled at KSh10 (about US$0.08) per index point. —Why it matters: The tools let investors buy or hedge Kenya’s banking sector — its bluest chips — in a single trade.

Kenya’s banks are the anchor of the Nairobi market. Now there is an index fund that lets anyone own the whole sector in one line.

Kenyan banks have long been the reason foreign money comes to the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE). Until recently there was no clean way to buy the sector as a whole. That is changing: Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority has approved the first exchange-traded fund built on the NSE Banking Sector Index, the market-cap-weighted gauge of 11 listed banks that went live in October 2025. For investors who want Kenyan banking exposure without picking individual stocks, the wrapper has finally arrived.

Nairobi’s central business district, home to the Nairobi Securities Exchange. (Photo: Lebu Ayiga, CC BY-SA 4.0)

A banking index, now with a fund

The NSE Banking Sector Index has been live since 1 October 2025, tracking the performance of the exchange’s listed lenders on a market-cap-weighted, float-adjusted basis. On its own, an index is a scoreboard. The news that turns it into something investable is the Capital Markets Authority’s approval of the WSA Banking Index ETF — the first fund designed to mirror it. When it lists, buyers get the whole banking basket in one security.

That fills a real gap. Retail and institutional investors alike have wanted a simple, low-cost way to hold Kenyan banks as a group; an ETF does exactly that, and it gives the index a pool of tracking capital that can deepen liquidity in the underlying shares.

What is inside the index

The index carries 11 constituents: Equity Group, KCB, Co-operative Bank, NCBA, Absa Bank Kenya, Standard Chartered Kenya, Stanbic Holdings, I&M Group, Diamond Trust Bank, BK Group and HF Group. Weighting by market value means the biggest names dominate — and the biggest is Equity Group, worth about KSh218.9 billion (about US$1.7 billion) at the end of September 2025.

It is a concentrated, high-quality basket. Kenyan banks have posted some of the region’s strongest returns on equity and pay healthy dividends, which is why the sector, rather than the broad market, is where a lot of investor attention sits.

Futures, hedging and the bigger picture

Alongside the index, the NSE introduced a banking-sector futures contract — cash-settled, priced at KSh10 (about US$0.08) per index point, with quarterly expiries. Futures let investors hedge or take a view on the sector without trading every underlying share, and they round out a toolkit that now runs from the index to a fund to a derivative.

For a frontier market, this is meaningful market plumbing. Deeper, more tradable instruments make it easier for outside capital to get in and out — and easier for local savers to own the banks that already dominate their economy. The banking sector was the natural place to start.

Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority approved the WSA Banking Index ETF, the first exchange-traded fund designed to track the NSE Banking Sector Index, letting investors buy the whole sector in one trade. Which bank has the biggest weight? Equity Group, with a market value of about KSh218.9 billion (about US$1.7 billion) at end-September 2025, is the largest constituent.

World.title: Standard Bank Becomes Africa’s Gateway to China’s Yuan Payments
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

South Africa · Banking

Key Facts —First mover: Standard Bank is the first African bank to offer access to China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), live since 20 November 2025. —Volume: It had cleared more than RMB 8 billion (about US$1.1 billion) through CIPS by July 2026. —Clearing bank: In June 2026, China approved Standard Bank and ICBC as Africa’s first authorised renminbi clearing arrangement, covering 19 African countries. —Early flow: About RMB 3.39 billion (about US$470 million) moved in the first four months. —The China link: ICBC has held 20% of Standard Bank since a 2007 deal worth US$5.5 billion. —Trade backdrop: China–South Africa trade hit a record of roughly US$56.7 billion in 2022, and 2025 tariff cuts have spurred yuan use.

Africa’s biggest bank has quietly become the continent’s gateway for settling trade in yuan — and this year Beijing made the arrangement official.

When Africa trades with China, the money has traditionally taken a detour through US dollars. Standard Bank is trying to remove that step. The Johannesburg-based lender — Africa’s largest by assets — became the first African bank to offer access to China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) in November 2025, and in June 2026 it was approved, alongside part-owner ICBC, as the continent’s first authorised yuan clearing arrangement. If you move goods between Africa and China, the plumbing behind your payments is changing.

Johannesburg, home to Standard Bank, Africa’s largest lender by assets. (Photo: Hmvh, CC BY-SA 4.0)

From CIPS access to clearing bank

CIPS is China’s home-grown network for settling payments in renminbi — a rough analogue to the dollar-centric systems that dominate global trade. Standard Bank went live on it on 20 November 2025 as the first African bank to offer the service, letting clients pay Chinese suppliers directly in yuan rather than converting to dollars first.

The bigger step came in June 2026, when China approved Standard Bank and ICBC as Africa’s first authorised renminbi clearing bank, an arrangement spanning 19 African countries. A clearing role is more than access: it makes Standard Bank a hub through which yuan payments across much of the continent can be settled, deepening the currency’s footprint in African trade.

How much is actually flowing

The volumes are early but real. Standard Bank processed about RMB 3.39 billion (about US$470 million) in its first four months on CIPS, and by July 2026 the cumulative total had passed RMB 8 billion (about US$1.1 billion). Those are modest sums against total China–Africa trade, but the growth curve is what matters — and the clearing-bank status is designed to steepen it.

The relationship behind all this is two decades old. ICBC, China’s biggest bank, bought 20% of Standard Bank in 2007 for US$5.5 billion, still one of the largest single foreign investments into an African company. That stake is why Standard Bank, rather than a rival, sits at the centre of the yuan’s African expansion.

Why yuan, why now

China is South Africa’s largest trading partner, with two-way trade reaching a record of roughly US$56.7 billion in 2022. Beijing has been pushing to settle more of that trade in its own currency, and in 2025 it removed tariffs on goods from many African countries — a move that lifted trade volumes and, with them, demand for yuan settlement.

For African importers and exporters, settling directly in renminbi can cut currency-conversion costs and shorten payment times. For the broader ‘de-dollarisation’ conversation that runs through BRICS, a working African yuan-clearing hub is a concrete step rather than a talking point — which is why this quiet piece of financial plumbing is worth watching.

Frequently Asked Questions What is CIPS? CIPS is China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, launched in 2015 to settle international payments in renminbi. Standard Bank is the first African bank to offer access to it, live since November 2025. What changed in June 2026? China approved Standard Bank and ICBC as Africa’s first authorised renminbi clearing arrangement, covering 19 African countries — a step beyond simply accessing CIPS. How much has Standard Bank cleared? About RMB 3.39 billion (roughly US$470 million) in the first four months, rising to more than RMB 8 billion (about US$1.1 billion) by July 2026.

World.title: Ghana Upholds Revocation of Adamus Resources’ Gold-Mining Leases
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Ghana · Mining

Key Facts —The ruling: Lands and Natural Resources Minister Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah upheld the revocation of Adamus Resources’ mining leases on 10 August 2026. —The leases: Three concessions — Akango, Salman and Nkroful — in the Ellembelle District of the Western Region. —How it started: The Minerals Commission first revoked the leases on 26 April 2026. —The findings: A government review committee cited US$2.56 million in unpaid mineral-rights fees, GH¢86.8 million (about US$7.4 million) in royalties and GH¢290.5 million (about US$24.8 million) in tax arrears. —Capital flight: The committee said US$224 million was transferred to related parties abroad between 2020 and 2024. —What now: The Minerals Commission has been ordered to take administrative control of the mine.

The government says the company mined without approvals, subleased rights it did not own and let illegal crews onto its concessions. After hearing the company’s appeal, the minister agreed.

Ghana has drawn a hard line with one of its Western Region gold miners. On 10 August 2026, Lands and Natural Resources Minister Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah upheld the revocation of Adamus Resources’ mining leases, rejecting the company’s petition and confirming a decision the Minerals Commission first took in April. For anyone watching how Accra now polices its mining sector, the ruling is a clear signal: paperwork and compliance are no longer optional.

Gold mining in Ghana, where regulators have tightened enforcement on licence holders. (Photo: EITI, CC BY-SA 2.0)

What the minister decided

The case reached the minister’s desk after Adamus Resources, through chief executive Angela List, petitioned against the Minerals Commission’s 26 April 2026 revocation of three concessions — Akango, Salman and Nkroful — in the Ellembelle District. A ministerial review committee examined that petition and recommended the revocation stand. On 10 August, Buah confirmed it and ordered the Minerals Commission to take administrative control of the operation, with an orderly transition.

The legal basis is the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703), which requires ministerial approval for transfers of mineral rights and lets the state revoke leases for breaches. This was a final ruling on appeal, not a preliminary notice — the distinction that makes it stick.

The findings behind the revocation

The government’s review committee laid out the numbers. It found US$2.56 million in unpaid mineral-rights fees, GH¢86.8 million (about US$7.4 million) in outstanding royalties and GH¢290.5 million (about US$24.8 million) in tax arrears — a combined GH¢377 million (about US$32 million) in royalties and tax owed. The committee also said US$224 million had been moved to related parties abroad between 2020 and 2024. These are the state’s own findings, not third-party allegations.

The compliance breaches went beyond money. Regulators cited unauthorised subleasing and assignment of mineral rights without ministerial approval, mining without approved operating plans, missing environmental and forestry permits, and the presence of Chinese nationals running illegal ‘galamsey’ pits on the concessions. Taken together, they formed the case the minister upheld.

An ownership dispute in the background

Adamus Resources’ ownership is itself contested. The structure has been described as 90% held by an Australian parent and 10% by the Government of Ghana as a carried interest — but a purported sale of the majority stake, now claimed by Nguvu Mining, has been challenged in court, and a High Court earlier installed an interim management committee. The Minerals Commission’s takeover adds a state hand to an already tangled situation.

For investors and operators across West Africa, the message is blunt: Ghana is willing to pull leases from a producing mine, not just junior explorers, when it concludes the rules were broken. That raises the compliance bar — and the political risk — for anyone holding Ghanaian gold ground.

Frequently Asked Questions What did Ghana’s minister actually decide? On 10 August 2026, Minister Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah upheld the Minerals Commission’s revocation of Adamus Resources’ three mining leases and ordered the commission to take administrative control of the mine. Why were the leases revoked? A government review committee cited unpaid fees and tax arrears totalling roughly GH¢377 million (about US$32 million), unauthorised subleasing, missing environmental permits, and illegal galamsey mining on the concessions. Where are the concessions? They are the Akango, Salman and Nkroful concessions in the Ellembelle District of Ghana’s Western Region.

World.title: New York Lawyers Group Raises Alarm Over Costa Rica Court Budget Cuts
World.content:
One of the oldest and largest bar associations in the United States has asked two international bodies to keep watch over Costa Rica’s judiciary, citing budget reductions imposed by the Executive Branch and the Legislative Assembly’s failure to appoint enough substitute justices to the Constitutional Chamber.

The New York City Bar Association published the statement on Monday, August 10. It calls on the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Independence of Judges and Lawyers to monitor developments here.

Founded in 1870, the association counts more than 20,000 members across the United States and in over 50 countries, among them judges, prosecutors, defense attorneys, government lawyers and academics. The statement was prepared by its Cyrus R. Vance Center for International Justice, with Jaime Chávez Alor and Cuitlahuac Castillo Camarena named as authors alongside Christopher Ferguson of the association’s Task Force on the Independence of Lawyers and Judges.

The document addresses two matters that have run in parallel since May. The first is the announced reduction of roughly ₡27 billion (about $59.5 million) to the judiciary’s budget, which Finance and Presidency Minister Rodrigo Chaves Robles set out as part of a 5% cut applied across public institutions for the second half of the year.

The Costa Rican Association of the Judiciary, known as ACOJUD, has said the measure “compromises every citizen’s right to receive a timely, impartial, and effective response” and would reach criminal investigations, victim assistance, public defense and court operations nationwide. The association’s statement quotes that warning and treats the reduction as a matter of judicial independence rather than ordinary fiscal policy.



On that point the arithmetic deserves a closer look than the statement gives it. The ₡27 billion figure was an announced modification that required budgetary processing and could not be applied unilaterally by the Executive Branch. On June 29 the Corte Plena, the full 22-member Supreme Court, agreed to make ₡13.242 billion (about $29.2 million) available and rejected the remainder.

The Ministry of Finance subsequently applied a retention of roughly ₡3.053 billion (about $6.7 million), bringing the total the judiciary says it will not receive or execute to approximately ₡16.3 billion (about $35.9 million). The judiciary has calculated that retention as close to 42% of the operating spending it had planned for the remainder of 2026, a category covering fuel, per diems, forensic examinations, maintenance, technology licenses, translation, transport and victim services.

The second matter concerns the Constitutional Chamber, the branch of the Supreme Court that decides constitutional questions including habeas corpus and amparo actions. Sitting justices must step aside from certain cases for disqualification, incapacity or conflict of interest, and without substitutes available the panel required to decide those cases cannot be assembled.

The association states the Chamber requires 12 substitutes to function normally and that only three have been appointed. It notes that 123 case files were left unresolved as a result, involving pensions, health, public employment, tax reform and municipal questions. Among the matters stalled by the lack of quorum is the request to lift the immunity of former President Rodrigo Chaves over allegations of irregular financing of the 2022 electoral campaign.

The judiciary submitted a slate of 18 candidates for the substitute positions on June 15. The governing party declined to endorse it, citing a lack of consensus, after initially indicating it would review the list. The operational picture has since shifted. On July 23 the Constitutional Chamber provisionally extended the appointments of substitute justices whose terms had expired, until the Legislative Assembly names replacements.

President Laura Fernández described that ruling as a coup d’état against the Assembly, and on August 3 Assembly President Yara Jiménez and governing-party lawmakers filed a criminal complaint against the four justices in the majority. The Chamber rejected the characterization, saying its decision fell within its authority to protect access to constitutional justice.

The association measures both matters against the United Nations Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary, adopted in 1985 and recognized within Costa Rican law. It points in particular to Principle 7, which requires states to provide the judiciary adequate resources, and Principle 10, which requires that judicial appointment methods guard against improper motives.

The statement is careful on one point. It does not dispute a state’s authority to set budget priorities, and it says a finding of improper effect does not depend on proving an intent to weaken the courts. Costa Rica is not the first country to draw the association’s attention this year. It issued a similar statement in May on reprisals and attacks against judges across Latin America, and a July statement in support of the bar associations of Morocco.

Concern from outside of here had already been voiced before Monday. The UN Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, Margaret Satterthwaite, raised the budget question publicly on July 23, and the Latin American Federation of Women Judges issued its own statement the same day urging that budgetary decisions affecting the courts be adopted through transparent, technical dialogue.

Inside Costa Rica, the tension between the Executive Branch and the courts has been building for months, and last week thousands filled the plaza in San José in support of the judiciary. Fernández and Chaves have rejected the suggestion that their administration intends to close, control or dismantle the judiciary, arguing that spending reductions follow from the government’s fiscal position and that the justice system requires significant reform.

Over the weekend Fernández announced she intends to resume periodic meetings among the heads of the three branches of government, and Supreme Court President Orlando Aguirre Gómez welcomed the proposal while asking for a clear agenda and respect for each institution’s competencies.

The association makes four requests of the Executive Branch and the Legislative Assembly. It asks them to refrain from using budget allocation as a mechanism of pressure, to open technical dialogue with the judiciary on its actual needs, to establish legal mechanisms guaranteeing a stable minimum allocation subject to accountability, and to approve enough suitable substitute justices to restore the Constitutional Chamber’s full operation.

Whether either body responds is now the open question, and the answer will be visible in the Assembly’s appointment calendar and in the 2027 budget rather than in any statement issued abroad.

World.title: New Coral Species Found Off Costa Rica Gets a Name From Tolkien’s Elvish
World.content:
A bright yellow coral that grows like a small tree on the flanks of Costa Rica’s underwater mountains has turned out to be so unlike anything else in the ocean that scientists had to build a new branch of the coral family tree to hold it. The animal has been named Laurinque elenya, and its formal description does something researchers rarely get to do in a single paper. It establishes a new species, a new genus and an entirely new family, Laurinqueidae, all at once.

The study was published in the open-access journal ZooKeys in late June and announced by the publisher this week. It was led by Odalisca Breedy, an octocoral specialist at the Universidad de Costa Rica, working with an international team that included researchers from the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Natural History.

The colonies grow to more than a meter (3.3 feet) tall and were collected between 360 and 529 meters (1,180 and 1,735 feet) below the surface. That is far below the reach of any recreational diver, in a stretch of the Pacific that has been surveyed only a handful of times. Specimens came up during two expeditions, in 2019 and 2023, using the remotely operated vehicle SuBastian deployed from the research vessels Falkor and Falkor (too), both operated by the Schmidt Ocean Institute.

The dives covered seamounts off the insular shelf of Isla del Coco and three geological features along Costa Rica’s Pacific margin. What the cameras found on those rocky outcrops is the reason for the coral’s unusual name. The rock was almost completely carpeted in brittle stars, and the golden colonies rose out of that shimmering layer like lit-up trees.

Breedy and her co-authors turned to Quenya, the Elvish language J.R.R. Tolkien invented for The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion. The genus name comes from Laurinquë, meaning golden tree, for the colonies’ color and branching shape. The species name, elenya, means stellar or of the stars, a reference to the brittle star fields the coral was growing in.

Placing the coral in the tree of life proved considerably harder than naming it. The team sequenced three genes routinely used to sort octocorals into families, and each one pointed to a different, unrelated family, an unusually stark disagreement. To break the tie, the researchers ran a phylogenomic analysis using hundreds of genes at once. That result was unambiguous.

The coral sits in its own lineage, closest to the family Eunicellidae but different enough in both genetics and anatomy that neither that family nor any other could accommodate it. Breedy said she first saw the octocoral garden in 2019 and was struck by the beauty of the landscape, which later inspired the Elvish name. Her early look at the specimens’ physical structure told her something was off.

She said “it was something very different that I could not match” against known groups, and only the molecular work done after the 2023 collection settled where it belonged. The expeditions were supported by the Schmidt Ocean Institute and a National Geographic Society research grant. The find lands in waters that already carry heavy conservation weight.

Isla del Coco is a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the government significantly enlarged the protected area around it at the end of 2021. Deep coral gardens like this one are classified as vulnerable marine ecosystems. They build complex three-dimensional structure on otherwise bare rock, which becomes habitat for a wide range of other deep-sea animals, and they recover very slowly from physical damage such as bottom contact from fishing gear.

The discovery adds to a lengthening list of species being pulled out of Costa Rican waters for the first time. In June, researchers described a new deep-sea ghost shark from the Pacific, and in May a jaguar-patterned marine worm was named from a beach in Santa Rosa National Park.

On land the pace has been similar, with a new frog described from the streams of the Los Santos coffee region and a new tree species added to the national record from the Guanacaste mountains.

Roughly two-thirds of the planet’s surface lies under deep ocean, and the overwhelming majority of it has never been looked at directly. For a country that has built much of its international identity on biodiversity, the coral is a reminder that a significant share of that biodiversity sits hundreds of kilometers offshore and hundreds of meters down, in places almost nobody has seen.

World.title: Cabinet receives presentations from Acquisition Stakeholders
World.content:
Cabinet receives presentations from Acquisition Stakeholders

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize noted that as part of the process to determine its position on the proposed acquisition of Smart/Speednet Communications Ltd. by Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL), Cabinet invited stakeholders to make presentations on the proposed acquisition.

At today’s meeting with the Belize Social Security Board, the Public Utilities Commission and BTL will present to Cabinet.

On Thursday, August 13, 2026, the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the National Trade Union Congress of Belize (NTUCB) will be invited to make presentations to the Cabinet.

Cabinet said that following these presentations, cabinet will deliberate at its meeting on August 18 and inform on its position on the matter.

World.title: International News: Alleged murder plot against Messi revealed in police report
World.content:
International News: Alleged murder plot against Messi revealed in police report

By Zoila Palma: Football superstar Lionel Messi was reportedly the target of multiple serious threats during the 2026 World Cup, including an alleged plot to kill him inside a stadium, according to a police report reviewed by Spanish newspaper Marca.

The report detailed security threats investigated by U.S. authorities during the tournament, with Messi reportedly receiving more death threats than any other footballer named.

One alleged threat involved plans to enter a stadium with homemade explosives and an AR-15 rifle, while another suspect reportedly threatened to attack Messi during Argentina’s group-stage match against Jordan.

Ahead of Argentina’s match against Egypt, another suspect allegedly posted online that he planned to enter Atlanta Stadium and kill Messi using explosives.

Authorities reportedly took the threat seriously and searched the stadium with sniffer dogs, including checks of bins and other areas, but no explosives were found.

Messi was not the only football star reportedly targeted during the tournament.

Cristiano Ronaldo also faced security concerns, while French referee François Letexier reportedly received more than 6,000 hate messages following the controversial Argentina-Egypt match.

World.title: When the pendulum swings
World.content:
When the pendulum swings

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

Dr. Philip Castillo: In any two party democracy, the pendulum eventually swings. Key word…eventually. But what makes it swing?

Focus on the comparatively more recent “Pendulum Swing” General Elections and recall the tremendous outpouring of pure national joy that accompanied such elections in Belize. Mr. Said Musa and the PUP won the pendulum swing General Elections in 1998 with a national total of 59.3% of votes and was the first to repeat in 2003 with a national total of 52.8%. In the subsequent five year span from 2003 to 2008, the pendulum again swung such that the PUP lost badly in 2008, when they obtained only obtained 40.9% of the votes. What made the pendulum swing? Was it one issue? A combination of several issues? American pollsters coin the phrase “wedge issue” to focus on a defining issue that motivates single issue voters or brings out less motivated and occasional voters. Was there a wedge issue in 2008 that “moved the needle”? This is another phrase used by pollsters to describe a seismic shift in political fortunes.

Mr. Dean Barrow and the UDP won the pendulum swing national elections in 2008, with 56.3% of the national vote and kept wining for three consecutive elections until defeat in 2020. The same questions need to be asked. What made the pendulum swing? Was it one issue? A combination of several issues? Was there a wedge issue in 2020?

Table 1

Election Year % PUP votes % UDP votes % alternate party votes Voter Turnout (%) Comments Possible Reason for Pendulum Swing 1993 51.2 48.7 .06 71.6 1998* 59.3 39.2 0.9 90.1 Pendulum Swing to PUP. Note INCREASE in % votes for PUP, DECREASE in % votes for UDP & massive INCREASE in voter turnout. Retrenchment?? Introduction of VAT?? Economic Citizenship Programme?? 2003 52.8 45.2 1.3 79.5 Start of 2nd term for PUP 2008* 40.9 56.3 2.1% 77.2 Pendulum Swing to UDP. Note double digit DECREASE in % votes for PUP & double digit INCREASE in % votes for UDP. Corruption/Malfeasance?? PUP infighting – Gang of Seven?? Superbond?? Privatization of national assets?? BTL issues?? Ministerial misconduct?? 2012 NA NA NA 73.2 Start of 2nd term for UDP 2015 47.3 50.0 1.7 72.7 Start of 3rd term for UDP 2020* 58.9 38.3 1.5 81.9 Pendulum Swing to PUP. Note double digit INCREASE in % votes for PUP, double digit DECREASE in % votes for UDP & INCREASE in voter turnout. Corruption/Malfeasance?? UDP infighting & succession squabbles?? Covid Restrictions?? Ministerial misconduct?? 2025** 66.6 28.9** 2.5 65.0 **The UDP % represent the combined totals of the Tracey & Shyne factions of the party .

Source: https://elections.gov.bz/general-election-results/

In general, while there are many issues that motivate a typical Belizean voter, my polls have found that generally high on their list — in no particular order are their economic situation, perceptions of corruption/malfeasance in government, candidate quality, party loyalty and family connections. Money is important because, among other things, it is needed to motivate the base, entice the less committed and dole out favours, including outright bribery. Note the report from BelPri on money in Belizean politics. https://heyzine.com/flip-book/8bd36f9fb4.html

Incumbency does confer advantages and in our politics, one such advantage is that it allows the incumbent to use public resources for partisan electoral advantage. We are also now aware of chicanery in the electoral process whereby voters form one constituency are transferred to another constituency. Both parties have safe houses where many voters officially reside. Both parties also activate bacon houses where benefits are doled out to partisan supporters. Money, in multiples of thousands, is required to undertake these activities.

But money also has its limitations due to what economists refer to as diminishing returns. After all, cash rich incumbent governments and cash rich individual politicians have lost, sometimes badly. In Belize, Opposition politicians are known to advise voters to “Take dem money and still vote dem out.” This is tacit acknowledgement that incumbents have money and resources, which voters are encouraged to take accept, while simultaneously voting against said incumbent. Rinse and repeat when governments change.

Fast forward to Mr. John Briceno and the PUP’s pendulum-swing victory in 2020. A victory that was repeatedly on a similar scale in 2025, facing a divided Opposition. The next set of elections that will serve as a referendum on Mr. Briceno’s government are the municipals slated for next year 2027, then the village councils slated for the following year 2028. But will the pendulum swing? Will the needle move? Voter turnout may provide a guide.

But Approval Ratings would likely provide a more reliable guide. My polling revealed an approval rating of 21.8% for the PM in Dangriga in February 2026. A month later in March my polls revealed an approval rating of 39.1% for the PM in Belmopan. Admittedly approval ratings are time and location specific, but I daresay, in the absence of actual elections, approval ratings polls of the Prime Minister, if regularly undertaken and countrywide in scope, would definitely provide an excellent indicator of any pendulum swing. And reasons that may cause any such swing?

Listen to the UDP talk shows. Their big issue is corruption/malfeasance in Government. Then listen to the PUP talk show, and be regaled with the corruption/malfeasance issues that doomed the UDP in 2020 and be reminded that some players are still around. Is corruption/malfeasance a wedge issue and will it cause any pendulum swing?

It is glaringly obvious, that for its own survival, the PUP must meaningfully address the burgeoning stench of the corruption/malfeasance issue surrounding government’s procurement and payment processes. Particularly distressing is the report of unsuitable guns to our soldiers. One indicator that the PUP has effectively dealt with this issue is actually ensuring transparency, due process and enhanced governance such that any leaks in any procurement and payment processes are no longer necessary.

But until then, expect the UDP to keep riding the corruption horse for as long as they can. But will that cause the pendulum to swing? Will that move the needle? And if so, would the movement be sufficient to make a meaningful difference?

At this time, focusing on Belmopan is most appropriate because both election and polling data exists. In 2020, then novice politician Mr. Oscar Mira won 60% of the votes to defeat veteran incumbent Mr. John Saldivar. Five years later, Mr. Mira again defeated Mr. Saldivar, and this time Mr. Mira’s voting percentage had upped to 65%. Exactly one year later in March 2026, Castillo Poll # 2 recorded an approval rating of Mr. Mira at 67.5%. Fast forward couple months later to June 2026 and Mr. Mira is among the central figures in the procurement debacle and has officially obtained a leave of absence from his Cabinet duties as Minister of Home Affairs.

The above are all known and undisputed facts. There are many other known and undisputed facts regarding questionable procurement and associated payment practices involving other senior government officials. Now adding to the above, it was announced last week that the national telecoms company (BTL/Digi) is purchasing its rival (SMART) thus re-creating a de facto monopoly in the all-important telecommunications sector. Several sectors of society have mobilized in opposition.

But focusing specifically on future political outcomes, the questions are: Can any of the above be regarded as wedge issues? Has the pendulum swung? Has the needle started to move? And if so, by how much? Would issues that are of intense interest to popular media outlets, talk show hosts, political operatives, the business and social sectors and the trade unions register as major concerns to actual voters? Or as an ephemeral blowing over of a “lee breeze?”

The President of Belize’s largest and most powerful commercial entity, Mr. Giacomo Sanchez of the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry, when questioned specifically on the BTL acquisition mentioned the high degree of political apathy with the following statement:

Giacomo Sanchez, President, BCCI

“Well, the public should push back. However, there’s only a few people in the know that will feel the way we feel. However, I mean, just about 90% of Belizeans could care less.” https://www.7newsbelize.com/index.php#story8

Reverting back to Mr. Mira, from a objectively polled approval rating of 67.5% in March, for his electoral fortunes to be jeopardized, his approval rating would have to fall by at least 18 percentage points to hover below 50%. But possibly even more than 18%, to account for what is regarded as the statistical margin of error. A national Approval Rating for the Prime Minister is unknown.

And so then, while the political capital of the incumbent Government has diminished, to what extent has the pendulum swung? Has the needle moved sufficiently to make a difference? These are prime examples of known unknowns.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Dr. Philip Castillo is a development economist and an independent pollster. Send comments to [email protected]

World.title: Taiwan opens applications for 2026 Global Pathfinders Initiative
World.content:
Taiwan opens applications for 2026 Global Pathfinders Initiative

By Zoila Palma: The Taiwan Embassy in Belize is inviting young Belizeans to apply for the 2026 Taiwan Global Pathfinders Initiative, a flagship program aimed at strengthening youth exchanges and creating opportunities for Belizean participants to gain international exposure.

Selected participants will travel to Taiwan for a fully sponsored one-month program in October 2026. The initiative, launched by Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Education, will provide participants with an opportunity to explore areas of cooperation and develop ideas connected to Belize’s future development.

Applicants are invited to submit proposals under one of two themes: Sustainable Tourism or New Energy and Carbon Credit Cooperation. Preference will be given to applicants who have not previously travelled to Taiwan or abroad, with up to six Belizean candidates expected to be selected for this year’s program.

The deadline for applications is August 20, 2026.

Applicants must submit all required documents in person at Taiwan Embassy.

World.title: Scarlet Macaws released back into wild in Cayo
World.content:
Scarlet Macaws released back into wild in Cayo

By Zoila Palma: Fifteen scarlet macaws were released into the wild in the Cayo District on August 10, 2026, following a rehabilitation and monitoring effort led by Friends for Conservation and Development (FCD) in collaboration with the Forest Department.

The parrots had been rescued and placed at a rehabilitation facility, where they remained for approximately 100 days before being prepared for release.

According to FCD, the macaws were placed at the facility because of the high risk of being poached or dying when three chicks are found in a nesting cavity. The birds were cared for under a strict protocol established by the Forest Department. After being rescued, they were fed and eventually transferred to a flight cage, where they developed their flying skills and prepared for survival in the wild.

On Monday morning, the cage was opened and the macaws were allowed to return to their natural environment. The birds initially gathered to feed on fruits and nuts before gradually flying out of the flight cage. While some flew longer distances, others remained closer to the release site as they adjusted to their surroundings.

FCD said its Research Unit has also been conducting biological monitoring of scarlet macaws since early March. The monitoring focuses on the species’ natural cavities and helps researchers maintain a presence around nesting sites while ensuring that chicks are developing safely until they are ready to leave the nest. Personnel presence also helps deter poachers, although FCD reported that two chicks were lost to poachers this year.

FCD noted that illegal wildlife trade remains a significant threat to scarlet macaws.

FCD and the Forest Department maintain a binational task force that shares information and coordinates interventions to address wildlife trafficking. However, the organizations say it remains difficult to determine the exact number of macaws lost to the illegal trade each year, with some poached birds reportedly taken into Guatemala by Guatemalan “guauqeros,” or macaw poachers.

The release of the 15 macaws marks another important milestone in ongoing efforts to increase Belize’s scarlet macaw population, which FCD says has now surpassed 500 individuals.

During the last national survey, approximately 350 individual parrots were known to be present in the country. FCD says that while the population appears to be expanding, continued monitoring, protection and conservation efforts remain essential to safeguard the species.

World.title: World Meteorological Organization: July among hottest on record as extreme weather intensifies globally
World.content:
World Meteorological Organization: July among hottest on record as extreme weather intensifies globally

By Zoila Palma: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says July was marked by extreme weather conditions around the world, with record ocean temperatures, intense heat, drought, wildfires and flooding continuing into August. The latest assessment highlights the growing impacts of a warming climate across several regions.

July was the second-warmest July ever recorded, tied with July 2024, with global temperatures reaching 1.47°C above the pre-industrial average. Western Europe experienced its hottest June-July period on record, with four heatwaves recorded since May, according to the Copernicus EU Climate Change Service.

Ocean temperatures also reached unprecedented levels, with global sea surface temperatures recording their highest July levels on record. Exceptionally warm conditions were reported across the tropical Pacific as El Niño strengthens, while record-high sea temperatures and widespread marine heatwaves affected coastal communities and ecosystems in the Atlantic and western Mediterranean.

Meanwhile, drought conditions intensified across Western Europe, where major rivers including the Seine, Rhine and Danube recorded exceptionally low water flows.

Drier-than-average conditions were also reported in parts of North America, Africa, Asia and South America, while Western Europe experienced exceptional wildfire activity. Major fires were also reported in parts of the western United States and Canada.

At the same time, intense monsoon rains triggered flooding across parts of West Africa and South and Southeast Asia, with India and other countries facing increased risks of flash floods and landslides.

Typhoon Dolphin, an unusually long-lasting storm that formed in late July, also prompted mass evacuations and emergency response efforts in China ahead of its landfall on August 7, highlighting the continuing threat of extreme weather as August unfolds.

World.title: Patient praises NHI clinic experience at La Loma Luz in Santa Elena, Cayo
World.content:
Patient praises NHI clinic experience at La Loma Luz in Santa Elena, Cayo

By Zoila Palma: A patient who recently visited the National Health Insurance (NHI) clinic at La Loma Luz in Santa Elena Town shared a positive experience with Breaking Belize News journalist Zoila Palma, describing the facility as different from other healthcare institutions.

The patient said he was impressed by the welcoming staff, noting that healthcare workers took vital signs and explained each step of the process.

After waiting for his turn to see the doctor, he said he was charged just $2 for the consultation and $2.39 for medication.

The patient encouraged other Belizeans who have not yet registered for NHI to do so, noting that registration only requires a Social Security card.

“NHI is really for the people of Belize,” he said.

“This is the part of Plan Belize I want to see.” he said that the experience demonstrated how accessible healthcare can make a meaningful difference for patients.

World.title: International News: China, Indonesia to hold naval drills East of Taiwan
World.content:
International News: China, Indonesia to hold naval drills East of Taiwan

By Zoila Palma: China and Indonesia will conduct joint naval exercises in waters east of Taiwan later this month, China’s Defence Ministry announced Tuesday, in an area where Beijing has been increasingly asserting its sovereignty claims over the island.

The ministry said a Chinese naval warship will conduct a joint “navigation exercise” with an Indonesian navy vessel in mid-August.

The exact location was not disclosed. The drills are expected to focus on communication exercises and at-sea replenishment, with China saying the activities are intended to strengthen the two navies’ operational capabilities, expand practical cooperation and promote regional peace and stability.

According to Reuters, the planned exercise comes as China continues to increase military and coast guard activity around Taiwan. Beijing considers Taiwan part of its territory, while Taiwan maintains that its future can only be decided by its people.

In June, China began coast guard patrols off Taiwan’s east coast, prompting concern in Taipei and among the United States and other Western governments.

Indonesia, like most countries, does not maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, although more than 300,000 Indonesian migrant workers live in Taiwan.

World.title: Committing to CCJ would be reckless, says Tavares-Finson
World.content:
Tom Tavares Finson

President of the Jamaican Senate, King’s Counsel Tom Tavares-Finson says it would be extremely reckless for Jamaica to commit to the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) as its final appellate court given the turmoil currently gripping the institution.

The Trinidad Express reported earlier this week a series of allegations made by judges of the CCJ, including allegations of dictatorial tendencies in the running of the court and a series of inter-personal conflict.

Tavares-Finson says no less than a public enquiry is required to deal with the issues facing the CCJ.

While acknowledging that inter-personal conflicts is not unusual for a court, he said the allegation surrounding the convening of panels to achieve pre-desired outcomes is troubling and must be treated seriously.

Tavares-Finson says the Opposition People’s National Party, whose insistence that Jamaica must accept the CCJ as its final appellate court has stalled the island’s constitutional reform process, should state clearly whether it maintains its position despite the turmoil which has gripped the regional court.

World.title: WATCH: 20 families homeless after early morning demolition in Trelawny
World.content:
Flattened structures in Coopers Pen, Trelawny after a demolition crew tore down 20 housing units in the area on Tuesday, August 11, 2026. (Photo: Horace Hines)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Some 20 families in Coopers Pen, Trelawny, have been left homeless after a demolition team reportedly tore down about 20 housing units in an early-morning operation Tuesday.

The residents say they have been before the courts since 2009 for the parcel of land that some say they have occupied for more than three decades.

Residents said the demolition crew arrived on the parcel of land shortly after 3:30 am, catching them off guard and leaving little time to save their belongings.

The team reportedly arrived with two excavators, sledgehammers, pickaxes and other equipment, and was accompanied by a strong contingent of police personnel.

Residents said they received no prior warning before the demolition began.

They also claimed that, before leaving the area, members of the demolition team warned that they would return in the coming weeks to continue the operation.

World.title: Tougher water fines
World.content:
Water level in the Mona reservoir last week.

SEVEN parishes will face a water prohibition from Monday, August 17 as the Government moves to tighten restrictions amid worsening drought conditions.

At the same time, Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda is set to approach the executive and legislature to punish violators with stiffer fines.

“As we had to do after the first incident that took place with Rio Cobre, where we had to shift the fine, we now have to take the same approach with fines in relation to water prohibition,” Samuda told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“Because of the present forecast and warning associated with El Niño, we will have to move with unprecedented speed, and we will have to engage first the Cabinet and then Parliament in the coming weeks to facilitate this,” Samuda added.

On Monday, Samuda’s ministry, through the National Water Commission (NWC), announced that the water prohibition orders will apply to Kingston, St Andrew, St Thomas, St Mary, Portland, St Ann, and St Catherine and will remain in force until further notice.

“Under the orders, no person shall use or cause water supplied by the NWC to be used for non-essential or unusual purposes. Prohibited activities include:

• irrigation or watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms;

• refilling or supplying of ponds or swimming pools and/or for use other than normal domestic services such as drinking, cooking, washing, bathing, and sanitation;

• washing of vehicles by the use of a hose;

• watering or washing of roadways, pavements, paths, garages, or out-rooms;

• any activity requiring excessive or unusual quantities of water,” the ministry release stated.

The ministry said the decision followed a high-level stakeholder meeting earlier Monday with the NWC and the Meteorological Service, which confirmed that rainfall levels remain critically low and temperatures continue to soar.

Underscoring the necessity of the measure, Samuda said, “We understand that there is some disproportionate economic impact on commercial operations, such as car washes, and we have not taken this decision lightly. Ultimately, our priority is to maintain supply to critical services, especially schools, as we prepare for the September reopening.”

He further advised that sanctions will be applied to individuals and entities found in breach of the prohibition order, noting “these penalties are intended to ensure compliance and protect the integrity of Jamaica’s water supply during this critical period”.

The current fine for breaching an NWC prohibition order is $1,000. Failure to pay the court-ordered fine results in imprisonment for up to 30 days.

Samuda’s reference to the Rio Cobre was the action taken by the Government after chemical spills that resulted in fish kills that affected several species and impacted other aquatic organisms four years ago.

In January 2025 he successfully piloted a Bill in the House of Representatives which approved amendments to the Natural Resources Conservation Authority (NRCA) Act and the Wild Life Protection Act to allow for significant increases in fines and related custodial sentences.

Under the Acts, depending on the severity of the offence, as adjudicated by the Supreme Court, corporate bodies may now be subject to a fine of approximately $10 million, individuals in breach of the Acts may face a fine of up to $5 million or serve a term of imprisonment up to five years, subject to the jurisdiction of the parish courts.

On Monday, Samuda told the Observer that the request he will be taking to Cabinet and Parliament is to “move the fines in line with what was done for bodies corporate and individuals under the NRCA Act breaches.

The naturally-occurring El Niño climate pattern, which began in June and is expected to peak later this year, has already amplified unprecedented temperatures across the world.

Some 33 countries recorded their hottest July since records began, according to a detailed analysis of billions of data points from Copernicus’s ERA5 climate model.

The severe drought has triggered food security concerns worldwide.

Last week, the United Nations World Food Programme said that Central America is expected to be the region hardest hit in terms of the relative increase in food insecurity.

Including the Caribbean, the agency estimates that an additional 16 million people could face food insecurity by the end of 2027.
