World.title: How to Find a GP in Prague When Practices Aren’t Accepting New Patients
World.content:
Finding a general practitioner in Prague can look simple until the first calls begin.

One practice does not answer. Another says it is full. A third can offer an appointment, but not in English. Your insurer’s list may not show who is accepting new patients today or what kind of visit is available.

If registration is blocked, first clarify whether you need long-term GP care, a one-time consultation, a specialist, an urgent route, or a private self-paid visit.



Decide whether this is really a GP problem

A GP is often the right first contact for common health concerns, preventive care, prescription questions, basic tests, and referrals. In Czech, this doctor is called a praktický lékař.

Not every situation should wait for GP registration. For a sudden and serious health problem or a possible threat to life, call 155 for the medical emergency service or 112 for the European emergency number.

If the issue clearly belongs to a dentist, gynaecologist, or specialist, ask that provider whether direct booking is possible or a referral is required. Patients in Czechia can generally approach a specialist without a GP referral, but an individual provider, insurer, or procedure may have its own requirements.

Tell the provider if you already have results, imaging, a hospital discharge report, or a specialist recommendation, because those documents may affect the next step.

Ask your insurer for help finding a provider

If you have Czech public health insurance and cannot find a GP, contact your insurer directly. Czech health insurers are responsible for helping their members access contracted care under the applicable rules on geographical and time availability.

Ask for practical information:

• Which contracted GPs in my area should be available to new patients?

• Which providers can communicate in English?

• Does the provider have a contract for my care?

• Do I need a referral, approval, or particular documents?

Availability can change, so confirm the details with the practice before travelling there.

If you have commercial insurance, check the provider network and approval process in your policy or contact the insurer. Do not assume that a clinic visit is covered simply because the clinic appears in a search result.

Understand why a practice may say no

A practice may lawfully refuse to accept a patient into care for reasons such as capacity, operational limits, distance that prevents home visits, or the absence of a contract with the patient’s public insurer.

If a provider refuses to accept you as a patient, ask for written confirmation with the reason. This gives you something concrete to show your insurer when requesting another available provider.

Clarify whether the refusal covers long-term registration, all appointments, only publicly insured care, the requested language, or a service the practice does not provide. A limited “no” does not necessarily close every route.

Separate registration from a one-time appointment

Registration and a medical appointment are related, but they are not identical.

Registration creates a long-term relationship with a primary-care doctor. It matters for continuity and for services whose public-insurance reimbursement is linked to the registered GP.

A provider may also offer care without registering you, particularly through a one-time, self-pay appointment. The scope and payment conditions vary, so never assume that a single consultation also means registration or that public insurance will cover it.

Before booking, ask whether the offer is long-term registration, a one-time consultation, a preventive check-up, an urgent appointment, specialist care, or a self-paid visit. Do not leave a clinic assuming that one consultation means you are registered there.

Prepare the information the provider needs

Share only enough information for the provider to understand the request, and use its approved secure channel for medical documents.

Prepare:

• the main reason for the appointment;

• how long the issue has been present;

• whether the request is routine, worsening, urgent, or preventive;

• your insurer or intention to self-pay;

• your preferred language;

• current medicines and allergies;

• relevant reports, results, imaging, or referrals.

A concise request helps the provider determine whether it can help and which appointment type is appropriate.

Make sure the visit has a clear ending

Getting an appointment is only the first part of the process.

A doctor may order tests, issue a referral, prescribe medication, or recommend another consultation. It should be clear who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Before leaving, ask:

• What happens next?

• When should I expect the results?

• Who will explain them?

• Do I need another appointment?

• Should I send anything to another doctor?

A useful appointment should leave you knowing what comes afterwards.

When coordination support can help

OpenMedical helps patients find suitable English-speaking GPs and other medical specialists in Prague, confirm current availability and appointment conditions, and coordinate the booking process. The service also helps prepare documents, communicate with selected providers, and keep follow-up steps clear.

Quick checklist when GP registration is blocked

• Decide whether the situation is an emergency or can wait for a planned appointment.

• Ask your public insurer to help identify an available contracted provider.

• Ask the practice whether its refusal applies to registration or to all appointments.

• Request written confirmation if a provider refuses to take you into care.

• Confirm language, payment route, referral requirements, and whether a one-time appointment is available.

• Keep copies of medical reports and results.

• Before leaving an appointment, confirm who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Finding a GP in Prague can take patience. A blocked registration does not mean there is no possible way forward. It means the next route needs to be identified more precisely.

Questions to ask before confirming a GP appointment

• Are you accepting new registered patients?

• Is this a registration visit or a one-time consultation?

• Can the appointment be handled in English?

• Do you have a contract with my public health insurer?

• What is the price if the appointment is self-paid?

• Do I need a referral or prior approval?

• Which documents should I provide, and how should I send them securely?

• How will results and further steps be handled?

World.title: Prague Plans 1.9 Billion Crown Reconstruction of Kasárna Karlín
World.content:
Prague plans to invest around CZK 1.93 billion, including VAT, to transform Kasárna Karlín into a mixed-use complex with shops, offices, student housing and space for cultural and artistic activities.

The city acquired the former military complex in 2023 and has since been working on plans for its long-term redevelopment.

Prague City Council has now approved the next step, allowing the city-owned Trade Centre Prague (TCP), which manages the site, to launch a tender for the preparation of the reconstruction project.



Construction is scheduled to follow between 2027 and 2032, with the investment financed from Prague’s municipal budget.

The first stage will focus on the complex’s main building. A separate building in the courtyard, currently used by the Karlín Barracks Cultural Center, will be addressed in later phases.

Deputy Mayor for Territorial and Strategic Development Petr Hlaváček said the reconstruction should open the site to the surrounding neighborhood while preserving its historic character and protected architectural elements.

One of the main changes will be to improve access to the courtyard, which currently has just one entrance and is largely hidden from the surrounding streets.

Adam Zábranský, Prague’s councilor for property, transparency and legislation, said new passages from the street would lead into the complex, with shops and services occupying the ground floor. The arcade running alongside these commercial spaces would form part of the new circulation system through the site.

The upper levels could eventually accommodate student housing, studios and offices. Zábranský also mentioned the possibility of using some of the space for businesses such as a technology park.

The exact future use of many of the rooms has not yet been decided. According to Zábranský, the project should therefore prioritize flexible layouts that can be adapted for different purposes over time.

The initial investment will focus in particular on replacing and upgrading essential infrastructure, including water, electricity and waste systems, as well as preparing the commercial areas on the ground floor. Work on the upper floors is expected to come later.

World.title: Czechia Sees Lyme Disease Surge With 90 New Cases a Day
World.content:
Lyme disease cases are rising sharply across the Czech Republic, with more than 8,000 infections recorded since the beginning of the year.

Health officials warn that the summer peak may not have arrived yet.

A total of 8,108 cases were reported through the end of July, according to data from the Czech State Institute of Health (SZÚ). July alone accounted for 2,792 infections, meaning that roughly one in three cases recorded so far this year occurred during the month.



Doctors registered an average of about 90 new cases each day in July.

The figures are significantly higher than those seen in previous years. Between January and July, the Czech Republic typically recorded between 1,500 and 2,000 Lyme disease cases.

Part of the increase may be linked to a change in the way infectious diseases are reported.

The number of tick-borne infections depends on several factors, including tick populations and seasonal weather conditions. Climate change is also playing an increasingly important role.

The highest numbers of Lyme disease infections have so far been reported in the Central Bohemian and South Moravian regions.

The risk is not limited to forests and countryside. Prague’s parks and wooded areas can also provide suitable conditions for ticks.

“Prague’s parks and forest parks create a specific microclimate where ticks thrive, so the risk of infection is real for residents even during an ordinary walk,” said Martina Marešová, head of the anti-epidemic department at the Prague Hygiene Station.

Early treatment can prevent complications

One of the most recognizable signs of Lyme disease is an expanding red rash that develops around the site of a tick bite and may have a paler area in the center.

Anyone who develops such a rash should seek medical attention rather than waiting for it to disappear.

The most common form initially affects the skin. If left untreated, the infection can progress and cause further skin problems. More serious complications can involve the nervous system, heart or eyes.

World.title: Shella Radio Visualizes Struggling Culture Scene At National Gallery
World.content:
A radio tower installation at Prague’s National Gallery is showcasing local efforts to preserve alternative culture as the Czech government seeks to cut funding to the arts and other public sectors.

Created by members of Prague-based Shella Radio, the tower is adorned with fabrics and relics of previous parties hosted in Ankali & Planeta Za, a nightclub that has faced closure due to financial problems.

“We believe in the idea of this radio as an amplification of voices that are often neglected in other spaces,” Shania Rodriguez, a Prague-based DJ and Shella radio host, said in an interview. “Here, they can be vocal about the issues and problems within our system and also share ideas of change.”



Many artists and curators say the environment for cultural organizations has grown more challenging due to financial cuts by the new right wing government led by Andrej Babiš.

The planned budget for this year shrank by 3.9 billion crowns – an almost 20 percent decrease from the previous year, according to the Czech Ministry of Culture. The cuts sparked widespread backlash across the country in April, and many took to the streets.

Shella, an Egyptian Arabic slang word meaning “a group of friends who do things together,” hosts political talk shows, electronic music club nights, and summer markets featuring local artists.

“The idea behind our installation was to be able to transmit parts of our identity that have been fundamental in Shella Radio’s trajectory,” Rodriguez said. “This DIY approach gives us the freedom to customize and handcraft our installation and studio space using materials from our temporary home: Ankali.”

The installation is part of the Necessary Wishes exhibition at the National Gallery which brings together more than 50 collectives and artists.

The event is free of charge and ends on September 13.

By: Lili Anna Lempek, Adam Pohořilský, Milena Gevorgyan, Isabella Fattore

World.title: Where to See the Partial Solar Eclipse in Prague and Across Czechia
World.content:
Skywatchers in the Czech Republic will have two reasons to look up on the night of August 12.

A partial solar eclipse will be visible in the evening, followed by favorable conditions for watching the annual Perseid meteor shower.

The eclipse will be visible across Czechia shortly before sunset, with the Sun low over the western and northwestern horizon. In Prague, the partial eclipse is expected to begin at about 7:19 p.m., reach its maximum at 8:12 p.m. and end around 8:27 p.m.



At the height of the eclipse, the Moon will cover about 86 percent of the Sun’s disk in Prague, making the event particularly noticeable if skies are clear.

The eclipse will look different depending on where observers are located. The farther east they are, the later the eclipse will begin and the less of it will be visible. In eastern Czechia and much of Slovakia, the maximum phase will take place after sunset, when the Sun is already below the horizon.

The event will be a partial eclipse in Central Europe, while a total solar eclipse will be visible in parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain. Astronomers and eclipse enthusiasts are expected to travel to those areas to experience totality.

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking part or all of the Sun from view. In Czechia, the eclipse will be especially low on the horizon, so observers will need an unobstructed view toward the west and northwest.

Several Czech observatories are preparing public observing events. A list of locations and other information about the eclipse is available through the Czech astronomical website astro.cz.

Perseid meteor shower will follow

The same night will also offer good conditions for watching the Perseids, one of the most prominent annual meteor showers.

The shower will reach its peak during the early hours of August 13, when the Moon will be only a few hours past its new-moon phase. With virtually no moonlight in the sky, faint meteors should be easier to spot.

The Perseids are active from July 17 through August 24, but the best opportunity this year will come during the night of August 12-13.

Under dark skies and favorable weather, observers away from cities could see between 50 and 80 meteors per hour.

Light pollution will be the main obstacle for anyone hoping to see large numbers of meteors. The best locations are well away from major cities, ideally several dozen kilometers from strong sources of artificial light.

World.title: Non-Alcoholic Beer Sales Rise by More Than 25% in Czechia
World.content:
Beer remains a staple of the Czech shopping basket, but new sales data from online supermarket Rohlík shows that drinking habits are gradually changing.

Traditional lagers still dominate, while non-alcoholic beer is recording the fastest growth among the main beer categories.

The category has grown by more than a quarter over the past year, with Birell among the brands driving the increase. Birell sales alone are up by almost 20%.



Together with flavoured beers and radlers, non-alcoholic beer now accounts for close to one-third of all beer sales on Rohlík.

Beer from small and regional breweries is also gaining ground, with sales increasing by more than 11%.

The biggest decline is being recorded among craft beers grouped by style, including IPA and APA. This is currently the only major beer segment experiencing a year-on-year drop.

Czech brands continue to dominate the market. More than nine out of every 10 beers sold through Rohlík are from domestic brands.

Imported beers, however, are growing at a faster rate. Their sales have increased by 18% year-on-year.

Beer sales peak at the weekend

Friday is the busiest day for beer sales, with roughly twice as much beer sold as on Monday. Friday and Saturday together account for almost two-fifths of the category’s weekly sales.

Orders containing beer also tend to include significantly more items than orders without beer, suggesting that customers often buy it as part of a larger meal or weekend shop rather than as a standalone purchase.

Seasonal patterns have also shifted. Beer sales during this year’s summer months have reached levels comparable with the December Christmas peak.

World.title: Explore Holašovice: A UNESCO-Listed Gem with Its Own Stonehenge
World.content:
For over 20 years, the South Bohemian village of Holašovice has held a place on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Located approximately 16 kilometers west of České Budějovice, this village is famed for its picturesque houses, built in the distinctive Peasant Baroque style.



The first recorded mention of Holašovice dates back to the late 13th century. The village has a rich and storied history, marked by events such as the Hussite wars and a devastating plague in the 16th century that significantly reduced the local population.

The iconic houses that now define Holašovice were constructed in the latter half of the 19th century, reflecting the Baroque, Rococo, and Classical influences prevalent in South Bohemian architecture of that era.

The village’s ethnic composition underwent significant changes during and after World War II. Following the establishment of the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, the Czech residents were forced to leave Holašovice, and the village was annexed to the Third Reich.

After the war, the German population was expelled, once again altering the village’s demographics.

Lada’s Pond and the Czech Stonehenge

Despite its turbulent past, Holašovice has retained a unique atmosphere that continues to attract visitors.

In addition to its charming houses, tourists can explore the local chapel and the picturesque Lada’s Pond, which, along with a statue of a water sprite, seems to be straight out of a painting by Josef Lada.

Just outside the village lies a unique stone circle, often referred to as the “Czech Stonehenge.” This site was designed to channel negative energy away from the human body, offering visitors a chance to experience its reputed healing properties.

World.title: Prague 7 Plans Floating Swimming Pool on the Vltava in Holešovice
World.content:
A floating swimming pool could be built along the Vltava River in Prague’s Holešovice district, near U Vody Park.

Prague 7 City Hall is considering using a section of the waterfront near the Port 7 development for the project.

The municipality hopes the pool could be ready within three years, although the cost has not yet been determined.

The project is still in its early stages. The district is currently looking into whether it could obtain older or unused pontoons and adapt them to create the swimming facility.



One of the main questions is where the pool water would come from. Prague 7 is considering both the Vltava and the municipal water supply.

The aim would be to use this data to determine when swimming in the river is considered safe. Čižinský has suggested introducing a simple traffic-light system similar to those used in cities such as Copenhagen and Amsterdam, allowing swimmers to see whether conditions are suitable.

According to Čižinský, the Vltava generally has good enough water quality for swimming, although conditions can deteriorate after heavy rainfall.

Recent measurements support this concern. Prague hygiene officials have been monitoring the water at Branická beach since the beginning of this year. The water has generally received a rating of two on the five-level scale used by hygienists.

The Holešovice proposal is not the first plan to introduce a floating swimming facility on the Vltava.

A similar idea was included in an earlier proposal to transform Prague’s riverfront. The project near Vyšehrad envisaged a large floating structure measuring 69 by 7.5 meters, with a swimming pool and a smaller paddling pool. A second connected vessel would have provided facilities for visitors.

The proposal was later put aside. In 2025, Prague property councilor Adam Zábranský of the Pirates said the investment was not among the city’s priorities.

World.title: New, thrilling – but deadly – routes emerge in drought-stricken Hungary
World.content:
Drought-stricken Hungary is opening up a series of intriguing new, but deadly routes even for fit and experienced hikers. Several people have already found themselves in trouble, and the latest incident came perilously close to ending in tragedy.

She almost sank into the mud

A few days ago, it was reported that a 35-year-old woman from Dunaújváros nearly disappeared into the vast expanse of mud at the shrinking Lake Velence after deciding to cross it. An off-duty police officer and a local resident eventually pulled her to safety, after which paramedics took her to hospital for further examination, the Hungarian police wrote.

The incident is a stark illustration of the dangers facing drought-stricken Hungary. As lakes and rivers recede, previously inaccessible areas are opening up, creating what may appear to be exciting new opportunities for walks and excursions. In reality, most of them are extraordinarily hazardous. Had no one nearby heard the woman’s cries for help, she would almost certainly not be alive to recount the experience as a warning to others.

Lake Velence drying out, but the mud can be extremely dangerous. Photo: Facebook/Élhető Velence Egyesület

Record-low water levels are also exposing places that had previously remained hidden, prompting magnet fishers and collectors to set out in search of discoveries. Most recently, a German Second World War motorbike was found on the banks of the Danube in Budapest, alongside various other items of equipment and human remains. Elsewhere, warships, bombs and other objects have emerged from the water – all of which may pose a danger to virtually anyone other than trained specialists.

New, but deadly routes in the Danube riverbed and in Lake Velence

Walking along the exposed banks of the shrinking Danube, or attempting to wade across Lake Velence, may seem tempting. But the receding waters have created dangers that have never previously been encountered. Experts warn that a single wrong step could put someone’s life at risk.

Entering the lakebed at Lake Velence remains prohibited, and the area becomes particularly dangerous beyond 100 metres from the shore. Although the surface may look completely dry, cracked and hard in many places, this is merely a thin crust. Beneath it, the mud may still be wet, soft and sticky.

Gábor Kürti, alias Kükü, the chairman of the Hungarian Bicycle Club, crossed the lake with special equipment he dragged with him after he studied carefully his route from the air. Photo: Facebook/Kürti Gábor Dezső

The lakebed may also contain so-called mud wells, which can be as much as two or three metres deeper than the lake’s average depth, according to Blikk.

Panic can make you even more vulnerable

Several people have already had to be rescued from the mud at Lake Velence this year. A young woman and a man from Budapest both got into difficulty; the latter was freed by water police before receiving medical attention.

One of the greatest dangers posed by the mud is the vacuum it can create around a person’s legs. The harder someone struggles and tries to move their feet, the deeper they may sink. Decomposing organic matter can also release dangerous gases, including methane and hydrogen sulphide, while the lakebed may contain shards of glass, rusty metal objects and fishing hooks.

If you missed: Did the Danube run dry in Budapest and Paks because the Slovaks diverted it?

Rescue operations are far from straightforward. Lifeguards do not approach those in trouble on foot, but use boats, ladders, planks, ropes and other equipment. Panic and unnecessary movement can make the situation even worse.

It may look dry and shallow at first

The Danube’s unusually low water level can be just as deceptive. Wide stretches of riverbank have been exposed at several points, attracting walkers and even cyclists. But the clay banks are being eroded from below by the river’s current, creating apparently solid ledges of earth that may collapse without warning, infostart.hu wrote.

The German WWII motorcycle that emerged from the record-low Danube last week. Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

This is particularly dangerous because someone standing in water only a few centimetres deep could suddenly plunge into several metres of fast-flowing water. The cold can cause cramp, while the current may sweep a person away – or carry them beneath a collapsing section of riverbank.

The danger at both locations lies precisely in the false sense of security created by ground that appears dry or water that seems shallow. Experts therefore warn that exceptionally low water levels do not make a river or lakebed safer. On the contrary, they can expose hidden hazards that remain invisible under normal conditions.

Deadly new routes emerge fromt the Danube. Photo: Anadolu/Németi Róbert

World.title: Sziget Festival kicked off – West European police help Hungarian colleagues
World.content:
British, French, Slovak and Dutch police officers are assisting the work of the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) at this year’s Sziget Festival, a BRFK spokesperson said on Tuesday.

“We are cooperating with the Civil Guard, the Standby Police and the Metropolitan Municipality’s Law Enforcement Directorate to provide external security for the event,” Soma Csecsi told a press conference held at K-bridge which is the entrance to the festival grounds.

“Plainclothes police detectives are also involved in internal security, and if they detect any offences or criminal acts, they will take the necessary measures,” he said.

He added that police presence will be maintained also on the River Danube throughout the festival.

A police “Prevention Point” is operating on the island, providing information on crime prevention and accident prevention through interactive programmes, he said. This year’s programmes focus on sport, drug prevention and cyber security, he added.

World.title: Shock as young man joins women taken ill en masse at Budapest concert and recounts his ordeal
World.content:
One moment he was partying with his friends; the next, he was walking towards the toilets. After that, his next memory was of lying on a bed with a doctor standing beside him, a number marked on his stomach. This was not the opening scene of a horror film but a real-life ordeal – and it happened the day before yesterday at a Budapest on the Hajógyári Island, the site of the Sziget Festival. No one yet knows exactly what happened: were the young people drugged, or was something else behind the incidents?

Many fell ill at Budapest concert

The concert did not form part of the Sziget Festival, although it was held on the festival’s main stage, where the illnesses occurred.

Sziget organisers issued a statement on Sunday condemning what had happened, but stressed that they had nothing to do with the DJ OTI – Balázs Sebestyén – concert, which was not included in the Sziget Festival programme. The concert was nevertheless held on Sziget’s main stage, and at one of the high points of the party Balázs flew in front of a Sziget logo, leading many people to associate the two events.

Both Sziget and Balázs expressed their regret and stressed the importance of human life. Károly Gerendai, Sziget’s lead organiser, added that he and his colleagues would try to investigate exactly what had happened more thoroughly. He said he knew of 20 cases among the 100 people who had received medical attention, while tens of thousands had attended the event.

Balázs Sebestyén, alias DJ OTI, on the main stage of Sziget Festival. Source: Facebook/DJ OTI

Hours missing from his life

An affected man told Index on Tuesday how he had experienced the events. The man, who is in his thirties, said he had not drunk much alcohol, yet had ended up in a condition for which he still has little explanation: three or four hours had disappeared completely from his memory.

One moment he was partying with his friends; then he set off for the toilets and remembers nothing after that. His next memory was of lying in a room with a doctor standing beside him. He does not know how he got there, nor who helped him reach the medical facility. He assumes that, when he regained consciousness, someone may have explained what had happened to him, but none of that information remained with him.

One of the most shocking details only became clear to the man later. Once he had recovered further, he noticed that a huge number had been written on his stomach in marker pen. His pockets had been emptied, and his phone and identity documents were returned to him in a transparent plastic bag.

Professional care, followed by illness

According to Index, the number written on the skin is an identification method used at mass events. If someone is unconscious or unable to communicate, the number is used to link the patient to their medical records and to the belongings found on them.

Our previous article concerning the issue – Young women collapse one after another at Budapest concert: police investigate as victims recount same story

The man came round in the detoxification unit operating at Sziget. This is the observation area where people who are severely intoxicated or under the influence of psychoactive substances are kept under medical supervision until their condition stabilises. The festival has a fully equipped medical centre, including a triage unit, internal medicine and surgical treatment rooms, a resuscitation unit, an inpatient area and a detoxification unit, supported by an emergency team of around 50 people.

All victims received professional medical care. Photo: depositphotos.com

But the ordeal did not end with the night. The man said he felt extremely unwell throughout Sunday, adding that he had never felt so ill in his life.

Following the incident, the Budapest Police Headquarters launched an investigation on suspicion of drug possession and questioned witnesses. However, no toxicology results have yet been made public to prove that the man or anyone else was given a psychoactive substance without their consent. Many people suspect GHB – commonly known in Hungary as “gina” – but the substance leaves the body quickly, although it can be detected in hair at considerable expense.

World.title: Breaking – New Hungarian President elected: “Hungary’s future cannot be built on revenge” – read his full message below
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament elected András Baka, the former head of the Supreme Court, as President of the Republic on Tuesday. Baka, the candidate of the ruling Tisza Party, was elected head of state with 140 votes in favour and 6 against in a secret ballot. Orbán’s Fidesz and the KDNP did not participate on the vote. Baka will assume office on the eighth day following the announcement of the election result.

Hungarians cannot avoid confronting the past at the beginning of a new era, Baka, the president-elect said in a speech to parliament on Tuesday. In his address after his election, Baka emphasised the need to understand “how the nation reached this point”. The president-elect said Hungary had “wasted a generation’s worth of time, slipping from a model student during the time of the democratic transition to the ranks of lagging nations”.

He said that he had accepted the nomination “because I think that Hungary has arrived at a point in its history when it needs to seriously contemplate the operation of the state, constitutionality and the country as community.” Baka, who was the sole candidate for the post, said the National Assembly’s decision to elect him was “a great honour, recognition and exceptional trust. The candidacy itself was also unexpected, overwhelming and an honour,” he said.

Photo: MTI

Past regime failed to meet basic democratic rule-of-law requirements

Baka said that before 2026, the Hungarian state had failed to meet one of the most fundamental requirements of a democratic rule-of-law system: the genuine separation of powers and a functioning system of checks and balances.

Baka said Hungary had developed a system in which a single party had captured the state and its institutions, culminating in years of governance by decree that largely bypassed parliament. “It is the responsibility of us all to ensure such a system never emerges again in Hungary,” he said.

Expressing national unity means political neutrality, but never neutrality on values

Expressing the unity of the nation first and foremost means political neutrality, but it must never mean neutrality on values, he said. Baka said that a modern, democratic society was inherently diverse, with coexisting worldviews, political convictions, lifestyles and interests. “There may even be deep, sometimes irreconcilable divisions among them,” he said.

Here are some photos from the Parliament:

As president, Baka said, he must represent this diverse community and always acknowledge the legitimacy of differing views, as well as the right of both majority and minority positions to be heard. The president’s role, he said, was not to manufacture consensus where none exists, but to represent the idea that “citizens with differing views are equal members of the same nation.“

A democratic institution’s authority is defined by its ability to remain true to its function, even in situations of conflict, he added. A democratic institution’s authority did not come from operating without conflict, but from its ability to stay true to its mission even amid disputes. He added that he intended to uphold this principle as president.

New President Baka could stand up firmly to PM Magyar – so why is the opposition attacking him so viciously?

Constitution’s stability hinges on broad societal ownership

A constitution’s stability rests on its being regarded as belonging to the broadest sections of society, Baka said. He warned that once again drafting a constitution “solely as the document of a temporary majority” would result in repeating the mistake the consequences of which Hungary was now attempting to rectify.

Drafting a constitution required more than mere parliamentary legislation, he said. “A wide-ranging societal and expert debate, genuine political consensus, and a process that in itself reflects the democratic culture the new constitution will later be tasked with upholding” was also necessary, he said.

World.title: Budapest in deep trouble: more threatening individuals on streets, cheap drugs becoming increasingly widespread
World.content:
The mayors of Budapest’s inner districts have united in warning the government that it must immediately begin filling vacant police posts, saying local authorities can no longer cope with the large numbers of threatening people and groups arriving in the capital from the countryside. They also said that some of these people exchanged empty bottles for cash before using the money to buy cheap, extraordinarily harmful drugs and alcohol. At present, the authorities are virtually powerless to deal with them.

They come from the countryside to make money and buy drugs

Dávid Vitézy, now the Minister for Transport, proposed – when he was still a Budapest council member and the MOHU bottle-return scheme was being introduced – that the Budapest municipality install bottle-collection bins in the inner districts. Not everyone, he argued, would seek out a redemption point where they could receive 50 forints for an empty mineral-water or soft-drink bottle.

The proposal was implemented, and the yellow bins still accept bottles today. However, while the initiative may have led to the collection of bottles, it may also have given a further boost to the presence of threatening individuals and groups on the streets.

The mayors of Ferencváros, Erzsébetváros, Józsefváros and Terézváros, as well as Újlipótváros, have joined the initiative launched by Imre László, the Democratic Coalition mayor of District XI. Among other demands, they are calling for more police officers, broader powers and additional funding to tackle the problem. According to the mayors, at least 3,000 police officers are missing from the streets, and they cannot be replaced with overtime payments or municipal resources, Blikk reports.

Meanwhile, Budapest as a whole is facing an increasingly serious social, mental-health and public-order crisis on its streets. The problem is particularly visible around railway stations and major transport hubs. In District XI, for example, complaints from residents have increased in recent months. The district says the bottle-return scheme is bringing increasing numbers of people to Budapest from the countryside in an attempt to make money by collecting bottles.

More drug users on the streets

The problem, however, is not confined to bottle collecting. District mayors say that more and more drug users are appearing on the streets, including people whose behaviour may be influenced by severe mental-health problems. Some spend the money earned from collecting bottles on alcohol or drugs, further undermining residents’ sense of safety.

The leaders of the inner districts say the emergence of cheap, new types of drugs is particularly alarming because they can trigger serious psychiatric problems among users. Keleti and Nyugati railway stations, Népliget, Blaha Lujza Square and several other busy transport hubs therefore require special attention, but there are not enough police officers to resolve the problems.

The Nyugati railway station in Budapest. Photo: Daily News Hungary

Long-term solutions are impossible through temporary redeployments. In an overstretched system suffering from staff shortages, any worker taken from one location will sooner or later be missed at their previous post. In addition, an effective support system is needed to address the social problems underlying homelessness and addiction.

Gergely Karácsony, the Mayor of Budapest, recently highlighted this point, noting that the problem has implications not only for public safety but also for health and social services. Most people cannot afford to pay the fines imposed on them in any case, and instead “convert” them into detention or community service.

Joint proposals submitted to the Government

The mayors have also drawn up a joint package of proposals. Among other measures, they would introduce a 30 per cent Budapest allowance for police officers serving in the capital to make the postings more attractive, while calling for a continuous police presence at problematic transport hubs.

If you missed: Aggressive ‘zombies’ everywhere: Is a new drug claiming victims in Budapest? Inner-city leaders sound the alarm

The municipalities are also seeking greater influence over the regulation of national tobacco shops and want to expand the scope for holding people accountable on the basis of CCTV footage.

The mayors further reported that municipal wardens and civil-guard patrols funded by district budgets have extremely limited powers. For example, they cannot even check people’s identities, meaning they have no way of knowing whether they have encountered someone who is wanted by the authorities.

Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai. Photo: Facebook/TISZA Párt

The district leaders say that, alongside reinforcing the police, access to night shelters must also be made easier. They believe Budapest’s municipalities are no longer able to tackle the simultaneous problems of homelessness, addiction and public disorder using their own resources, and are therefore calling for immediate state intervention.

World.title: Hungarian Parliament clears fiscal reforms to unlock additional EU funds
World.content:
The Hungarian Parliament cleared amendments to budget rules to comply with commitments made to unlock the country’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) funding in a vote on Tuesday. The bill was approved with a vote of 140 for and 44 against, with 5 abstentions.

The law approved by the Hungarian Parliament contains provisions to improve fiscal sustainability, including ones to harmonise rules on the Fiscal Council with a constitutional amendment removing the body’s right to veto budget drafts, to require justification for expenditures that are not earmarked for specifically defined purposes, and to require disclosure and transparency for reallocations and extraordinary government measures, MTI wrote.

The law also limits the period during which the government may submit the budget bill to lawmakers to the month of October. The law revokes the government’s right to issue ad hoc resolutions on expenditures exceeding thresholds contained in the budget.

Have Orbán’s former allies abandoned him? He may be seeking international posts that offer protection

MPs roll back discretionary power to designate battery recycling sites

The energy minister’s discretionary power to designate sites for battery recycling plants was rolled back in a vote in parliament on Tuesday, MTI wrote.

The measure, which also ends the discretionary power for applications for designation already submitted, was cleared with a vote of 145 for and 44 against, with no abstentions. The bill’s author noted that three such applications had been submitted to the predecessor of the Economy and Energy Ministry.

World.title: Hungarian State Treasury hacking scandal: Is the Russian connection merely a cover story?
World.content:
Hackers did attack the Hungarian State Treasury’s IT system from Russian servers, according to Népszava, but the operation was not carried out by any Russian intelligence service. Instead, it is alleged to have been the work of an organisation believed to be linked to an Algerian man. The newspaper suspects that the Russian connection is being emphasised merely in an attempt to downplay the authorities’ own serious information-security failings.

Hackers may have penetrated deeply and obtained vast amounts of data

The consequences of the attack on the Hungarian State Treasury’s IT system may have been far more serious than initially suspected. According to information obtained by Népszava, the attackers may have gained access not only to agricultural subsidy data, but also to the pension and family-support systems.

The Treasury has yet to disclose the extent of the damage or whether an attempt was made to extort money. Although the successful attack does not mean that the hackers could move public funds, they may have obtained huge amounts of data on Hungarian pensioners and citizens receiving various family-support payments. Such information could later prove extremely valuable in carrying out a range of fraudulent operations.

According to the newspaper, the hackers may have exploited a known security vulnerability that had not been properly closed. They reportedly gained entry through an outdated web server before acquiring administrator privileges for the central authentication system. From there, they may have been able to access other parts of the network.

The reason was that the central databases were protected by weak, outdated password security. The attackers were therefore able to break into them virtually in a single step and obtain whatever they wanted.

During the attack, databases containing confidential personal and financial information were also encrypted. The Hungarian State Treasury is currently attempting to restore the affected systems from earlier backups, but so far it has achieved only limited success.

The IT infrastructure is therefore operating only on a restricted basis. Damage limitation and the investigation are being conducted by the National Cybersecurity Institute of the National Security Special Service, working alongside Treasury specialists. The data-protection breach has also been reported to Hungary’s National Authority for Data Protection and Freedom of Information, although that alone will not resolve such a complex problem.

Interestingly, the new government has done nothing yet regarding this issue, although there is still much work to do in order to detect and close all backdoors in the system.

Underage hackers who threatened bomb blasts and murders arrested in Hungarian-Romanian operation – video

Stolen data could easily be abused

The incident is particularly alarming because the compromised credentials may, in theory, have provided access to data connected with the assessment and payment of pensions, as well as the system used to manage local authorities’ bank accounts.

An expert said, however, that this did not mean the attackers could directly access or transfer state funds. The greater danger lies in the abuse of the stolen data – through targeted phishing attacks, for example – and in the disruption of the operation of IT systems.

There are also unanswered questions surrounding the origin of the attack. The Hungarian State Treasury said that the operation had originated from Russian servers, while an analysis by a cybersecurity company pointed to a group known as ByteToBreach, which is believed to be backed by an Algerian man.

Cyberattack hits Hungary’s State Treasury as experts trace attack to Russian servers

According to the newspaper, the group had previously offered for sale on the DarkForums forum data that may have indicated a breach of the State Treasury’s systems.

The case also highlights the significance of an earlier finding by Hungary’s State Audit Office. As long ago as 2019, it warned that data-protection vulnerabilities remained in systems inherited from the former Central Administration of National Pension Insurance. Despite this, the vulnerable components were left in place, allowing the hackers to “walk straight in”.

Does blaming the Russians sound better?

Népszava suggests that the Russian connection may therefore be nothing more than a cover story. No one expects the Hungarian State Treasury and its experts to be able to thwart a Russian intelligence operation, but citizens would be entirely justified in holding those responsible to account if it emerged that an Algerian national had simply walked into the system by exploiting its vulnerabilities – as a result of failings on the Hungarian side – and stolen vast amounts of data about them.

Moreover, criticising Russia on this issue fits more neatly with the current government’s preferred narrative.

World.title: Was a EUR 275 million fraud uncovered in connection with Gondosóra emergency alert device for the elderly?
World.content:
The science and technology ministry has filed a criminal complaint alleging misuse of funds and budget fraud exceeding 100 billion forints (EUR 275,000) in connection with the “Gondosóra” programme that hands out and manages an emergency alert device for the elderly, Zoltán Tanács, the minister, said on Monday.

Huge fraud in connection with the emergency alert device for the elderly?

The scheme is a government initiative launched in 2022 to provide elderly Hungarian citizens aged 65 and over with a free GPS-enabled emergency alert device, enhancing their safety and enabling them to call for help in emergencies, MTI wrote.

Responding to a question from Tisza MP Éva Görögh Bocskai in Parliament, Tanács called the Gondosóra programme a “typical phenomenon” of the previous government’s NER system of national cooperation where “a good initial idea was stolen, distorted and overpriced before being forced on society“.

Elderly couple receives their new Gondosóra devices. Photo: Facebook/Gondosóra

Tanacs said that authorities had already launched investigations and filed reports in connection with the scheme. On Monday, the ministry added its own report, citing suspicions of misappropriation of funds and budget fraud worth over 100 billion forints.

If you missed: New President András Baka could stand up firmly to Péter Magyar – so why is the opposition attacking him so viciously?

He said that more than 6,500 documents, invoices, contracts and financial statements were reviewed, uncovering over 12,500 suspicious cases, including more than 1,500 flagged as critically high-risk.

Tanacs also said that the head of the Government Service Centre Nonprofit, the body responsible for the programme, along with several members of its leadership, are being dismissed effective today, and an interim leadership will be appointed to ensure uninterrupted service.

World.title: Romania’s sole nuclear power plant prepares to shut down due to low Danube flow
World.content:
Romania’s Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant has initiated the technical procedures preceding the controlled shutdown of its second nuclear reactor, the so-called Unit 2, due to the very low flow of the Danube. The river water was essential for the cooling of the pumps used by the plant.

The shutdown of Unit 2, scheduled for Thursday, August 13, represents the complete closure of the facility in Cernavodă. The nuclear power plant, operated by Bucharest Exchange-listed company Nuclearelectrica (BVB: SNN), shut down Unit 1 in late July for the same reason, as drought persists in the Danube basin.

Sorin Rândașu, deputy general manager of Romanian Waters, said that the critical threshold of -230 cm water level had been reached at Cernavodă. “In the coming period, the plant will be shut down; it is inevitable. It will be shut down for about two weeks, as an estimate. In the next five days there will be no rain at all in the Danube basin, according to the data we have,” Rândașu told Digi24.

Previously, the state secretary in the Ministry of Energy, Cristian Bușoi, also stated that Unit 2 at Cernavodă will not be able to remain in operation throughout August.

To compensate for the loss of energy, the Rovinari 4 energy unit of the Oltenia Energy Complex will be restarted and integrated into the national power grid.

However, without nuclear energy, which ensured roughly 20% of Romania’s consumption, the country will have to reduce consumption and increase expensive energy imports, especially in the evening. The phased limitation of consumption for certain large industrial consumers, in the 7 PM and 11 PM interval, is the last measure in the order of priority and could be applied, according to the authorities. Household consumers are not targeted by the consumption limitation mechanism, the same source added.

However, Romania’s Energy Ministry again appealed to the population, public institutions and economic operators to limit their energy consumption between 7 PM and 11 PM. A similar call had been issued last week and echoed by prime minister Ilie Bolojan.

Separately, through a stock exchange announcement issued on Tuesday, August 11, Nuclearelectrica drew attention to a series of Notices of the Existence of a Force Majeure Event by the Constanța Chamber of Commerce, Industry, Navigation and Agriculture (CCINA), applicable in the case of electricity supply contracts. This means that the company may not be able to fulfill contractual obligations.

“Nuclearelectrica will send to its contractual partners an estimate regarding the duration of the period during which it will not be able to fulfil its obligations. Nuclearelectrica will make all commercially reasonable efforts to minimise the effects of the Force Majeure Event,” the company stated.

World.title: Storia: Apartment prices in Romania’s large cities fairly stable, Cluj-Napoca and Brașov most expensive
World.content:
Apartment prices in Romania’s most important cities remained largely stable in July relative to the previous month, according to Storia’s analysis cited by Economedia, with a slight 6% increase in both new and old one- to three-room apartments.

Cluj-Napoca remains the most expensive city among those analyzed, with an average cumulative price of EUR 3,298/sqm, followed by Brașov with EUR 2,342/sqm and Bucharest with EUR 2,160/sqm. The analysis is based on the average asking prices requested by sellers in listings published on Storia in July 2026, compared with the same month last year and with the previous month, June 2026.

In the new apartment segment, the largest annual percentage increase in prices was recorded in Constanța (+14%), followed by Sibiu (+11%), Iași and Oradea (+10% each). In the case of old apartments, the largest annual percentage increases were observed in Timișoara (+12%), Sibiu (+11%) and Craiova (+10%).

Regarding the average asking prices for new apartments, Cluj-Napoca remains the most expensive city, with EUR 3,340/sqm, followed by Brașov with EUR 2,331/sqm and Constanța with EUR 2,257/sqm. World.title: Cinemascop: Festival in Eforie Sud kicks off this weekend
World.content:
The ninth edition of the festival Cinemascop brings a program of European films, creative workshops, community meals, and a silent disco party to the Cinemascop Garden in Eforie Sud, on the Romanian coast of the Black Sea.

The festival opens on August 14 with the Hungarian film Orphan, directed by László Nemes, the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind Son of Saul. Set in Budapest in the aftermath of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, the film follows a 12-year-old boy trying to uncover the truth about his family’s past in a society still scarred by war and violence. The film is presented by the Liszt Institute – Hungarian Cultural Center Bucharest.

On August 16, the Polish documentary The Godmothers, directed by Emilia Śniegoska, follows the friendship between Hanka and Bronka, two women from the village of Pleșa in Bukovina. As the world around them changes, they retain their independence, sense of humor, and the bond they have built over a lifetime. The film is presented by the Polish Institute in Bucharest.

On August 17, the Italian crime comedy Agata Christian: Murder in the Snow, directed by Eros Puglielli, turns the relaunch of a game into a real murder investigation after a murder and an avalanche leave guests stranded in a mansion in the Aosta Valley. Inspired by the novels of Agatha Christie and the success of the Knives Out franchise, the film is presented by the Italian Cultural Institute in Bucharest.

On August 18, the French film Jim’s Story, by Jean-Marie and Arnaud Larrieu, follows nearly two decades in the life of Aymeric, who becomes a father figure to the child of a former colleague. Screened in the Cannes Première section in 2024 and earning Karim Leklou a César Award for his performance, the film is presented by the French Institute in Romania.

On August 19, the Romanian film Catane, Ioana Mischie’s feature-film debut, focuses on a community that has found an ingenious way to avoid paying taxes by declaring people with disabilities in almost every household. When the authorities launch an investigation, the entire community is forced to confront a truth it has been trying to conceal. The film is presented by the Romanian Cultural Institute.

The festival ends on August 20 with the Czech-Danish documentary Mr. Nobody Against Putin, winner of the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. It follows teacher Pavel Talankin, who captures from the inside the transformation of his school into an instrument of war propaganda. The film is presented by the Czech Centre Bucharest, with the screening organized in partnership with KineDok Romania as part of this season’s selection.

At the 1M² Gallery, the former cinema ticket booth that has been transformed into an art gallery, visitors will be able to see a video work by artist Loredana Bardaș. The ETAJ on Wheels space at the entrance to the garden will host an exhibition by Sergiu Chihaia exploring the resilience of nature. A collective installation created by Alexandra Dumitrescu and Emil Cristian Ghiță at the beginning of the summer will continue to collect messages from visitors wishing to share a thought or memory. The exhibitions Eforie Unframed and The City with Four Names will remain accessible on the seafront. The garden will also feature areas for table tennis and LEGO.

Meanwhile, Mini Cinema will present a selection of British short films curated by the British Council, including BAFTA-winning animations and thematic programs focusing on climate change, communities and identity.

The Cinemascop Garden opens daily at 6 p.m., and admission to all activities is free.

World.title: Romania’s Green House program to focus exclusively on batteries
World.content:
Romania’s government-run Green House program, designed to encourage the use of home heating and energy systems based on renewable energy, will be modified this year and will finance only energy storage systems, not the installation of photovoltaic panels, according to environment minister Diana Buzoianu.

In an interview for Euronews Romania on Monday, August 10, the official explained that the current problem of the Romanian energy system stems from the fact that in recent years, significant funds have been allocated for energy production through photovoltaic panels, while investments in storage batteries have been almost non-existent.

“Things got stuck because, over time, exponentially large amounts of money were allocated for panels and almost EUR 0 for batteries. We will change that,” she said.

As such, this year, the program will exclusively fund batteries that allow for the storage of energy.

Buzoianu estimated that after the completion of the project, the capacity installed through the program will allow the storage of at least 200 MWh. The energy accumulated in the batteries is expected to be used during peak consumption intervals, especially in the evening, when photovoltaic production decreases, and Romania ends up importing energy.

The official also criticized the system based on the “first come, first served” principle, in which beneficiaries have to access the platform within a very short time in order to obtain funding. Instead, the authorities want to introduce additional criteria for competitiveness so that funding is granted to beneficiaries who present the most competitive offers.

In the case of batteries, one of the criteria being considered is co-financing. “How much you are willing to co-finance; the more you are willing to co-finance, the more priority you will have,” the minister explained.

Romania is currently experiencing an energy crisis driven mainly by the severe drought and the sharp reduction in the Danube's flow, which has reached its lowest level in the last 40 years, reducing energy generation at Nuclearelectrica (BVB: SNN) and Hidroelectrica (BVB: H20). The drought is set to continue, with no short-term improvement, according to the most recent forecasts.

World.title: Five beaches in Romania get Blue Flag label, another one preparing for 2027
World.content:
Romania has five beaches included in the Blue Flag program this year, the Ministry of Economy, Digitalization, Entrepreneurship and Tourism announced on Tuesday, August 11.

The beaches that have received the Blue Flag label are: Axxis Nova – Năvodari; Phoenicia – Năvodari; Azur – Eforie Sud; Citadel – Eforie Sud; and Phoenicia Blue View – Olimp.

Thirty-three criteria are assessed for the certification, covering four areas: environmental education and information, water quality, environmental management, and safety and services.

“A new candidate is preparing for the 2027 edition. Dharma Beach in Eforie Sud is currently in the pilot phase of the program, where it needs to work to meet the criteria required for certification,” the ministry said.

The Blue Flag program was launched in 1987 by the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), with the aim of recognizing beaches, marinas and recreational boats that promote sustainable tourism.

In Romania, the program was introduced in 2004. The criteria are assessed annually by a national jury, with the participation of central public authorities and representatives of tourism industry associations.

The Blue Flag program was present in 52 countries in May of this year. The list of countries is available here.

World.title: Russia kills civilians every day, Romanian Foreign Ministry spokesperson says
World.content:
The spokesperson of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Andrei Bogdan Ţărnea, stated on Monday, August 10, that Russian officials should not comment on the national identity of a country while their own country is waging “a brutal war of conquest.”

The statements came in reaction to comments made by Yuri Pilipson, director of the Second European Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry. The Russian official stated in a recent interview with the Russian state-owned news agency TASS that Romania was providing direct military aid to Ukraine through the Moldovan port of Giurgiuleşti, which it bought this year.

“Romania is already involved in providing direct military and logistical support to the regime in Kyiv,” said Pilipson.

According to him, the port of Giurgiulești, whose operator was acquired by Romania, has long been transformed “into a transit hub for the delivery to Ukraine of various goods, including those intended for the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”

During the same speech, the Russian official criticized Greece for offering support to Ukraine and said that the majority of Moldovans reject the prospect of unification with Romania.

"Any Russian official speaking about the national identity of a country is in an obvious contradiction. While spreading this kind of Stalinist propaganda, Russia is engaged in a brutal war of conquest. Russia kills civilians every day, while denying the sovereignty and national identity of a neighbor. How can one take seriously any statement on such subjects coming from Moscow?" the spokesperson of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Andrei Bogdan Ţărnea, said on Monday, August 10, in reply, cited by Agerpres.

According to him, in Tsarist Russia and later in the Communist Soviet Union, the official policy was one of forced Russification of occupied peoples. "National identities and national aspirations do not respond to Moscow’s demands, neither when it comes to language nor when it comes to economic decisions and investments. The times when Moscow chose by force for these nations or imposed on them what to do have passed," the Romanian official said.

In April of this year, the National Company Administration of Maritime Ports (or CNAPM), the port authority for the Romanian seaports Constanta, Midia, and Mangalia, completed the acquisition of Danube Logistics, the operator of the Republic of Moldova’s sole seaport, Giurgiulesti, from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

World.title: Spanish fashion group Tendam brings Cortefiel brand to Romania with store in Rivus Cluj-Napoca
World.content:
Spanish fashion group Tendam will bring three of its brands to Rivus Cluj-Napoca, the real estate project currently under development.

Cortefiel, the fashion group’s original brand, will open its first store in the country in Cluj. The other two units will operate under the Springfield and Women'secret brands. The three brands will take up a total area upwards of 1,000 sqm, Rivus said.

Tendam recently opened two stores under the Springfield and Women'secret brands in Iulius Town Timișoara.

Tendam, Spain’s second-largest apparel group by market share, has been majority-owned by the Abu Dhabi-based investment holding company Multiply Group since last year. It operates more than 1,800 points of sale and runs digital loyalty programs in over 80 markets, including Spain, Portugal, France, the UAE, and Latin America. The company manages 13 fashion brands: Women'secret, Springfield, Springfield Kids, Cortefiel, Pedro del Hierro, Hoss Intropia, Slowlove, High Spirits, Dash and Stars, OOTO, HI&BYE, Milano and Fifty.

Rivus Cluj-Napoca is a EUR 550 million investment by Iulius and Atterbury Europe. Spanning 14 hectares, the complex will integrate a diverse mix of uses: cultural, educational, sports, entertainment, events, park, shopping, and office. Its leasable retail area amounts to 142,000 sqm, with more than 70% already pre-leased, according to the developers.

The project is supported by a EUR 400 million syndicated green loan, the largest of its kind granted to a new real estate development in Romania. The financing is tied to meeting international sustainability standards, including LEED Platinum and EDGE Advanced certifications.

World.title: Bucharest Court of Appeals gives reasoning in Bihor unauthorized care homes case
World.content:
The Bucharest Court of Appeal rejected the accusations of human trafficking and organized criminal group made against Viorel Pașca, the owner of an authorized care homes network in Bihor County, western Romania, when it ruled against his detention back in July.

The information emerged from the reasoning of the judge, now made public, who decided on July 16 that Viorel Pașca and his family members should be investigated while at liberty, an opinion contrary to that of the other magistrate from the Bucharest Tribunal who considered that “there are reasonable suspicions” against Pașca.

“At least at first glance”, the manner in which the injured persons were treated in Pașca’s nursing homes “does not present characteristic elements of keeping persons in a state of slavery or subjecting them to procedures similar to deprivation of liberty or servitude,” the Court of Appeals judge said, according to Digi24.

DIICOT prosecutors had said that the victims were treated improperly, and that money intended for their care did not serve the stated purpose.

However, the judge rejected DIICOT’s accusations. The sums of money were not appropriated by Pașca and his family, according to the evidence presented.

The Bucharest Court of Appeal also maintained that “the accommodated persons benefited from basic medical assistance.” Those in the care homes had “periodic medical consultations, including psychiatric specialist consultations, from prescribed and monitored treatments, from recreational activities and from assistance in carrying out current activities.”

The judge further mentioned that “persons with mental illnesses were involved in various activities carried out within the community and benefited from bodily hygiene services - haircuts, washing, shaving, as well as clean clothing and linen.”

Among deficiencies, the Court noted the fact that the persons dealing with the care of the sick and the administration of medicines had an extremely low educational level. Some did not have the ability to read and write.

Similarly, several accommodated persons did not benefit “in all situations” from “the medical treatment corresponding to the illnesses they suffered from.” Moreover, some of the patients contributed to the administration of medicines. The staff dealing with the care of the elderly was insufficient;

However, these shortcomings, the judge of the Bucharest Court of Appeal maintained, are due to “the lack of financial resources, and not at all to the fact that the defendants appropriated the money from which the patients benefited from the received donations.”

At the same time, the judge further said that the aid received from the state by vulnerable persons (such as a pension or any other form of social assistance) would not have allowed them to live in better conditions than those ensured by Viorel Pașca’s family.

The Bihor illegal care homes case broke at the end of June, uncovering similarities with another, more serious case from 2023. Unlike the latter, however, the situation of the care homes in Bihor is not as clear, leading many to argue that Viorel Pașca and his association were doing their best with the available resources, taking care of patients who had been abandoned by state institutions.

Ever since then, Viorel Paşca defended the activity of his association, which housed vulnerable people despite the fact that it lacked a license to do so.
