But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: National leader or problem rediscoverer? The issue with Malinauskas's AI royal commission
World.content:
You would be hard-pressed to find a state government in Australia that loves describing itself as "nation-leading" as much as the current South Australian one does.

A quick "ctrl + F" of the inbox throws up more than 50 Malinauskas government media releases that use the phrase over the last 18 months — some up to four times in the one email.

The social media ban for kids and outlawing of political donations were only the tip of the iceberg; there were also nation-leading knife laws, a nation-leading tobacco crackdown, nation-leading civics education and a nation-leading "freight management framework".

That's not to mention nation-leading sensory buses, nation-leading "spaces" within SA's new sports centre, and a nation-leading textile event to donate your unwanted clothes.

Renmark's creek system recently got a new canoe channel and pedestrian bridge. A nation-leading design? You bet.

Why SA is holding a royal commission into AI South Australia pioneered the global push to restrict children's access to social media. Could the state's royal commission into AI also lead to national policy

Even Labor's intervention to stop paid parking at Tea Tree Plaza shopping centre — an issue that would struggle to register beyond Adelaide's north-eastern suburbs, let alone the country — copped the "nation-leading" treatment.

A national first, but why?

Lest anyone think the term was becoming devalued, Premier Peter Malinauskas announced a genuine national first on Monday.

SA's royal commission into artificial intelligence will be the biggest Australian public inquiry yet into the policy problems posed by AI.

Its terms of reference are yet to be drafted, but it's expected to examine the impact of AI on education, skills, work, health and infrastructure — almost everything except data centres (SA's already got a "nation leading strategy" for those).

Mr Malinauskas made the announcement shortly after a business trip to the United States where "70 per cent" of his meetings were about the emerging technology. This included discussions with the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and Apple.

Mr Malinauskas with Apple CEO Tim Cook at Apple Park in California. (Supplied: Facebook)

Speaking to journalists on Tuesday, Mr Malinauskas said: "Maybe I've got the bug, I don't know, but once you really start reading about AI and getting into the depths of what this is going to mean, you can't help but feel a weight of responsibility to do something about it."

"To do nothing about it I think would be completely reckless and foolhardy," he said.

But the SA royal commission has critics, as well as questions about its utility.

Those questions are less about whether it warrants the nation-leading title, but more around why is South Australia leading. Shouldn't this be the federal government's domain? And will the royal commission's findings still be relevant by the time it's finished?

The University of Sydney's Rebecca Johnson, who has a PhD in AI evaluation and safety, was among those with doubts.

Dr Johnson said researchers had been studying AI's risks for years and a royal commission could be useful "if we can uncover evidence that the rest of us can't access".

"But if we spend a year re-discovering that AI creates risks to jobs, privacy, security and accountability, well we already know that," she told 891 ABC Radio Adelaide.

" So, the challenge now is to stop rediscovering the problem and to start using the expertise we already have here in Australia, before we start spending millions of dollars asking questions that we already know the answers too. "

Rebecca Johnson says the cost of the royal commission could be better spent on practical steps. (Supplied)

The royal commission would cost $3 million, which Mr Malinauskas argued was "chicken feed" compared to the cost to society if the AI transition is managed poorly.

Asked why he didn't float the possibility of a national inquiry with the prime minister beforehand, Mr Malinauskas said: "When it comes to our record as a state, we've got no reservations about acting as leaders in this area."

"My responsibility is to the people of South Australia — now, I care about outcomes for the nation as an Australian, but I want South Australia to have a position of leadership," he said.

He also credited Anthony Albanese for creating an office for AI within the prime minister's department, arguing he had shown "more leadership on AI policy development than I've seen other national leaders around the world".

Counting in AI years

The inquiry's three commissioners are yet to be appointed, but they will have a tight turnaround to meet a July 1 deadline.

But even by then, some of their findings could be out of date, Dr Johnson argued.

"I don't understand why we would spend a year — which is, in the development of AI, that's like five years — wasting time asking questions that people have already asked," she said.

" That $3 million could also be spent actually enacting some of the guardrails and the changes that need to happen now. "

The inquiry will consider the consequences of AI for education, skills, work, health and infrastructure. (Unsplash: Steve Johnson)

The premier hit back when asked about Dr Johnson's criticisms, arguing this was a challenge that "will be enduring not just for this government but the 10 that follow it".

"There's a lot of professors that think they know the answers to everything when the truth is there are far more questions sitting around the future of AI and how it informs the work than there are answers," he said.

"We don't announce a royal commission to win the universal applause of academics. We announce a royal commission because we accept our responsibility to embrace the opportunities this technology provides but also accept our responsibility to do something about the risks."

The social media ban model

Of the Malinauskas government's "nation-leading" reforms that have garnered attention outside of South Australia, there have been mixed results.

For example, the state-based First Nations Voice to Parliament was meant to dispel fears about the federal Voice before the national referendum. That clearly didn't happen, and the state Voice still has its own share of problems.

AI just had its Sarah Connor moment Australia's government and experts are taking the OpenAI hack seriously.

SA also continued to stand alone on its political donations ban. While the Albanese government has taken up some electoral funding reform, they go nowhere near the Malinauskas government's move to outlaw them.

But the teen social media ban provided a compelling counterargument.

Mr Malinauskas announced in May 2024 his government's intention to ban under-14s from social media. The idea took off so much that by December of next year it was being implemented nationally for under-16s, albeit with serious questions about its effectiveness.

A similar scenario could play out with the AI royal commission, according to British computer scientist Toby Walsh.

"I would expect perhaps we will end up in the same place here with artificial intelligence that the ideas put forward, the proposed legislation, the guidelines, rules, might be ones that then be picked up for national use," said Professor Walsh, who is also chief scientist at UNSW Sydney AI Institute.

" If this is a way of getting the government to move faster, I welcome the idea that South Australia can again help us to get to a good place. "

Professor Toby Walsh says the state-based commission could prompt national responses. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Mr Malinauskas announced the AI royal commission this week in the same room he announced the teen social media ban in May 2024.

He suggested having the commission's AI recommendations adopted nationally or by other states would be a sign of success.

"I think this is far broader and more consequential frankly," the premier said.

"I think AI gone bad will make social media look like a walk in the park.

"All the more reason to have the highest level of inquiry examine it."

World.title: Calls to address hidden pain of regional pregnancy loss
World.content:
Psychologist Heidi Lynn Welsh knows the pain of pregnancy loss only too well.

Warning: This story contains content relating to pregnancy loss and neonatal loss, which some readers might find distressing.

She has had several miscarriages and endured the stillbirth of her daughter Ellie at 38 weeks in 2017.

"It's one of those pivotal moments you won't ever forget; you just realise it's the end and it's not going to happen," Ms Welsh said.

" There's no hierarchy to loss; people can be just as devastated in early loss as they can be in stillbirth. "

Psychologist Heidi Lynn Welsh started a support group in the regional city of Bunbury after the stillbirth of her daughter. (ABC South West WA: Harriet Dash)

Researchers say a lack of regional access to perinatal bereavement support is compounding trauma for families in the bush, and data remains inadequate.

'People don't talk about it'

After leaving hospital, Ms Welsh, who is based in the regional WA city of Bunbury, said she received no meaningful support for her grief.

"I left empty-handed apart from a bunch of pamphlets," she said.

"They said, 'what you need to know when you want to get pregnant again'; it was just not sensitive."

A St John of God Bunbury Hospital spokesperson said while it could not comment on individual cases, every effort was made to support those affected by perinatal loss.

The hospital no longer provides maternity services.

After her experience, Ms Welsh took matters into her own hands, starting pregnancy loss support group My Little Luv.

"I wanted to reach out to people to let them know they're not alone," Ms Welsh said.

"People don't talk about loss because they're worried about upsetting someone, but it's actually more upsetting to not talk about it."

Heidi Lynn Welsh started the group My Little Luv to offer support to families dealing with pregnancy loss. (Supplied: Heidi Lynn Welsh)

She was frustrated by a lack of pregnancy loss support in the Bunbury region, which is about 200 kilometres south of Perth.

"I don't want to have to travel two hours to Perth when I've just lost my baby to get the support I need," she said.

Midwife and perinatal loss bereavement care researcher Skye Stewart said access to bereavement care was the biggest barrier facing regional families.

"We need to make sure the families are receiving care from someone who has an understanding of not just the clinical side but the mental wellbeing side," she said.

Researchers say there is inadequate bereavement support for regional women after pregnancy loss. (Supplied: Heidi Lynn Welsh)

Ms Stewart said improving access to support could help reduce lasting trauma that included increased rates of anxiety and depression.

Gaps in understanding

The full picture of pregnancy loss across the country is not fully understood, according to a recently released study by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

"Substantial gaps remain in understanding the prevalence of pregnancy loss in Australia, affected populations, access to care, quality of care and approaches to early intervention and management," the report states.

There is also no consistent national reporting on pregnancy loss before 20 weeks.

Ms Stewart said routine collection of data would help make the case for more support where it is needed.

There is no national reporting system for pregnancy loss before 20 weeks. (ABC News: Lisa Mctiernan)

"Consistent data would capture the strengths in what's happening currently, where the gaps are and how we can better support families in a time that is really critical," she said.

" When families feel their experience matters and that they are being listened to, they can come out of that with a trajectory of healing. "

Ms Welsh hopes sharing her story will ensure families in the future avoid what she went through.

"We don't have very good rule books in our culture about how to support people," she said.

"I've experienced and lived through loss, and there's wisdom that comes with it."

More help coming

More help is on the way for those struggling with pregnancy loss.

The WA Country Health Service last month launched a Perinatal Loss Service pilot in the South West, offering holistic care for families.

"The way we talk about and care for families experiencing perinatal loss continues to evolve and improve so no one should have to process their grief alone," a WA Government spokesperson said.

The pilot program will be assessed next year, to see if it can be rolled out across regional areas.

Emma McBride, the federal assistant minister for mental health and suicide prevention, said options were being explored for nationally consistent miscarriage data collection.

A federally funded perinatal mental health centre is also planned for Bunbury, as part of a national network.

"(The government) recognises the profound and lasting impact that stillbirth and pregnancy loss can have on individuals and families," Ms McBride said.

World.title: Inner Melbourne council walks away from plan for key worker housing
World.content:
An inner Melbourne council has halted plans to build new affordable housing for local workers priced out of the private market due to a lack of available funding for the project.

The Yarra City Council project had already completed an initial expression of interest campaign for the building, which would transform a Collingwood car park into at least 50 discounted rental apartments.

However, councillors unanimously voted to stop work on the project on Tuesday night after a panel reviewing the proposals identified "significant funding and delivery constraints".

Councillor Evangeline Aston said they were "disappointed", but that council was always "very clear" it would not use ratepayers' money to fund the project.

"We were … [not going] to get into a field that we have no obligation to be in and to sign us up to ongoing operating and maintenance expenses," Councillor Aston said.

" The market reality determines the situation here and the reality is that the money is just not there. "

s for the project showed the affordable rentals were to be built on a car park beside Collingwood Town Hall in Abbotsford. (Supplied: City of Yarra)

Limited funding options

Tenants in the eight-storey building would have had their rent capped at 75 per cent of the local rate, but had to be working in the municipality to be eligible.

To realise the project, the council had resolved to lease a 2000-square-metre parcel of land behind the St Philip's Anglican Church to a delivery partner, but no further funding was guaranteed from the council itself.

Council staff reviewing proposals from potential delivery partners found the project could not be delivered under the proposed model.

"There is currently limited funding available within the sector and no clear state or federal government mechanism that enables local government to effectively deliver an affordable housing project of this type without significant external funding," they wrote.

At the meeting, Councillor Aston said council would continue to support social and affordable housing, and would reconsider the project if market conditions changed in future.

"We will continue to advocate for funding, and if the conditions change," she said.

"We've done all the work, got all the preparation, we can pick this up and hit the ground running again to try and make the most of those conditions."

Sarah Toohey is calling on the Victorian government to provide more funding for affordable housing. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

Community Housing Industry Association Victoria said of 13 Victorian council-led affordable housing projects over the past 20 years, all of them required state or federal funding to get off the ground.

"Councils are on the front line of the housing crisis in their communities and they're doing the heavy lifting to find solutions, but they can't do it alone," CEO Sarah Toohey said.

"Whether providing land, opening housing trusts, or facilitating planning agreements, no council-led housing project has been delivered without a funding contribution from the government, and projects often involve multiple funding partners."

She said it was critical the state government committed to an annual funding pipeline so councils could deliver the social housing.

She urged the City of Yarra not to abandon the project.

The land is currently being used as a car park. (Supplied: City of Yarra)

The proposal marked a second bid to redevelop the Collingwood Town Hall precinct off Hoddle Street after a larger proposal with a mix of housing types was voted down by a previous council in 2021.

It came in the midst of a significant uptick of approvals for affordable housing projects, partly driven by schemes that offer incentives for developments with below-market housing.

Luxury apartments greenlit under affordable housing scheme Property developers are using an affordable housing scheme to bypass normal planning requirements and win fast-tracked approval for contentious projects across Melbourne.

However, the model has attracted criticism, including for income requirements that can lock prospective tenants out of the scheme.

By contrast, the City of Yarra — which has been critical of some developments fast-tracked under the state government's affordable housing scheme — proposed setting higher income limits, a move that would have broadened eligibility for the Collingwood building.

Project documents said market housing would only be considered if the project was unfeasible without it.

Locals consulted on the project were split on whether council land should be sold or leased, but those who were supportive said housing affordability was a key issue.

Others believed council assets should not be leased or sold.

The council said it would reconsider the proposal if funding or market conditions changed.

Growing feasibility gap

The Urban Development Institute of Australia is a non-profit advocacy and research body for developers.

CEO Linda Allison said there was a growing feasibility gap in Victoria for such projects.

Linda Allison says developers need to be offered incentives to build affordable housing. (Supplied: Urban Development Institute of Australia)

She said developers were struggling to get loans because of global economic and supply chain uncertainty and the higher costs of finance and taxes.

She said new apartment completions were at a 15-year low, pushing Victoria further behind on its housing targets.

"If at-market housing isn't feasible, affordable housing is even more challenged," she said.

"The next Victorian government must remove these roadblocks and make the delivery of homes easier, more affordable, and more certain."

A state government spokesperson said the Collingwood Town Hall Affordable Housing Project was a matter for the City of Yarra.

They said the government had invested $8 billion in social and affordable housing which was delivering more than 16,000 homes across Victoria.

"We also recently changed rent settings in the Homes Victoria Affordable Housing Rental Scheme to make it more accessible for Victorian families."

World.title: Women coaches have almost tripled, but 'misogynistic and abusive' behaviour remains
World.content:
If you asked generative AI to create an image of a sports coach, it would likely serve up a middle-aged white man.

And while rooted in stereotypes, it would not necessarily be inaccurate.

The picture is slowly changing in some sports, although not substantial enough yet to disturb the algorithm.

The Australian Institute of Sport found the number of female head coaches in funded sports has nearly tripled since starting its Women in High Performance Coaching project in 2021.

The number now sits at more than 25 per cent, but AIS Director Matti Clements told ABC Sport that is still not good enough.

"Maybe we've had a history where we've just had male coaches coaching our best athletes," she said.

"We want to make sure the right people are coaching our athletes at the right time, female or male coaches."

AIS director Matti Clements says many female coaches still face key barriers. (ABC News: Peter Healy)

The AIS report found many women coaches have experienced bad behaviour, which was "in some cases appalling, misogynistic and abusive," as well as challenges managing careers alongside having a family, and difficulties even getting a foot in the door, let alone climbing the ladder.

It highlighted the need for leaders within the sporting sector to drive cultural change to address the barriers.

"As a system, we've had a real focus in the last couple of years of wellbeing being fundamental to high performance sport in this country," Clements said.

"If you look at wellbeing as a sustainable high-performance lever, that will encourage all different types of people to stay in our system, female coaches included.

"Perhaps historically, high-performance sport in this country has not been as welcoming for female coaches as it has been for male coaches."

Clements pointed out some of the strategies which have helped deliver positive results over the past four years include visibility of high profile coaches, having conversations at the highest levels, re-evaluating recruitment practices, and targeted development.

Sauvage leading the way

Louise Sauvage is one of Australia's most decorated Paralympians, and since retiring in 2004, has established herself as a leading coach in para wheelchair track and road racing.

She has noticed an evolution over the past 20 years.

Louise Sauvage has been an elite coach for more than 20 years. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

"It's been really good to see that infrastructure and also the investment into women's coaching," she told ABC Sport.

"Our athletes are almost 50-50 male, female, so to have that balance is perfect.

"And I think women bring something a little different to the male coaches as well. So I think it's important that we encourage them to continue on in those roles and to show the identity and what we can bring as female coaches."

Sauvage is also one of very few elite coaches with disability across the Australian sporting landscape, and acknowledged it has not always been an easy path for her.

"I think some of the barriers were definitely identifying what you could or couldn't do or how the workarounds would work," she said.

"And also talking with your national sporting organisation and how you can get past them or what help you might need and then you can just be as effective as any other coach.

"I think it's about communication more than anything and not just looking at something [and saying] 'oh, I can't do that.'

"[You should ask] how can you do it? How can we make it work for you so that you can progress as a coach?"

She added having coaches with shared lived experiences was a valuable asset for athletes.

"They already know that I know how they're feeling or what they need because I've been there and I've done that," she said.

"But things evolve all the time, so I need to keep learning as well. But I really do think a lot of the athletes do appreciate that the understanding is already there."

The professional picture

The AIS report focused on sports it funds, largely rooted in the Olympic and Paralympic arena, but many of the issues raised prevail in the professional codes too.

Four of the 18 of AFLW head coaches are women, one of 12 in the NRLW, one of 11 in the A-League Women and two of eight in the WBBL (last season).

The WNBL is close to parity with four of the nine coaches women, and as the country's number one female participation sport, five of Super Netball's eight coaches were female last season.

Like the dearth of disabled coaches, there are also very few First Nations, or culturally diverse head coaches, across men's and women's sports.

Clements said diversity in coaching simply makes sense.

"The sports are seeing the value of it in terms of performance outcomes. So this is not just a nice to have, we're doing it because it feels good," she said.

"It absolutely is a competitive advantage and that's what's going to engage our sports to continue to focus on this because we want to have the best games ever in Brisbane and in order to do that we have to make sure we've got the best people coaching."

World.title: Wait times, cost barriers to ADHD testing in Tasmania, report finds
World.content:
Tasmanians are waiting too long for ADHD assessments and turning to interstate and telehealth services because of a lack of support in Tasmania, a parliamentary report has found.

The report also acknowledged that since its hearings concluded, the government has authorised general practitioners (GPs) to diagnose ADHD, "which should improve access to diagnosis, treatment and support".

The 250-plus page report — titled Inquiry into the assessment and treatment of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and support services — was tabled in parliament on Tuesday, making more than 100 findings and 31 recommendations.

It found that there was currently limited capacity to receive an ADHD diagnosis through Tasmania's public health system, with most people accessing assessments through a private psychiatrist; a more costly process.

Nearly 3,000 Tasmanian children were waiting to be assessed for ADHD through the public system at the start of 2026. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

In its submission to the standing committee, the Royal Australasian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) said there were "significant financial barriers to receiving a diagnosis", which disproportionately affected those on lower incomes.

"With patients often paying significant out-of-pocket costs and many patients needing to travel long distances, sometimes interstate, to see a specialist with availability," it said.

" This cost barrier means that people on low incomes are unable to access care and are disproportionately affected by poor access to care. "

The committee heard from the Australasian ADHD Professionals Association (AADPA), that the cost of an assessment can range between $500 and $3,000.

One of the report's many recommendations was for the state government to advocate for an increase in Medicare-subsidised sessions under mental health treatment plans. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

Scott Wynands, who provided evidence on his lived experience with ADHD diagnosis and treatment, told the committee he was worried about his ability to afford future appointments.

"It was about $1,200 for the initial assessment, and it would be lower with follow-up appointments, but I can't actually afford the follow-up appointments," he said.

"I am concerned [for] the next year now, when I need to reapply for my medication.

" Will I be able to access it? Because I cannot afford to see a psychiatrist. "

'Excessive' wait times hinder early assessment

Another barrier for people seeking diagnosis for suspected ADHD was the wait times, which paediatric respiratory physician Associate Professor Heinrich Weber described as "excessive".

"We obviously know the morbidity associated with late diagnosis of ADHD," he said.

" It's advisable that diagnosis is made early. "

The committee heard that 48 Tasmanian GPs had undertaken training to diagnose, treat and manage ADHD for both children and adults. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

But he said early diagnosis could be a "significant challenge", with barriers to accessing diagnostic services and subsequently support services, such as allied health.

Committee chair Ella Haddad wrote that Tasmania's services "are so stretched that often young children suspected of having ADHD miss out on assessment in the early years and can start school without having received the support they needed prior".

As of January this year, there were nearly 3,000 Tasmanian children waiting to be assessed for ADHD through the public system.

The wait time for children to see a public paediatrician (category 2 or 3) ranges from about six months to almost a year, depending on the category and where in the state they live.

Tasmanian Labor MP Ella Haddad chaired the standing committee. (ABC News: Rani Fletcher)

Paediatrician Natasha-Ann Laidler told the committee wait lists were "incredibly long".

"We often have children who, by the time they get to us, have already suffered significant blows to their self-esteem and educational trajectories," she said.

"Particularly in the north-west, there are [also] high rates of family violence and other socio-economic impacts.

" These are often disadvantaged children who are being further disadvantaged by not accessing care. "

AADPA said wait lists for adult assessments exceeded two years.

Interstate telehealth 'only option' for some

The long waits have left many Tasmanians turning to interstate services for assessments.

That was the path Madeleine O'Keeffe took.

"[There are] no avenues for assessment for adults whatsoever in the public system in Tasmania," she said in her submission.

" My only options were all telehealth assessments costing more than $1,000, to be paid in advance, and waitlists were more than six months long. "

But experts told the committee they held concerns about the quality of care offered by some "quick fix" telehealth providers.

Tasmanians have increasingly turned to telehealth providers, the report said. (Supplied: iStockphoto/jacoblund)

The Tasmanian Adult ADHD Support Group said telehealth providers were filling a void.

"A considerable number of telehealth providers have begun to operate in this space in Tasmania, and for most adults seeking a diagnosis this is the only option currently available," it said in its submission.

" Prices are often very high and the quality of care varies, according to feedback from our members. "

The AADPA warned about quick assessments not being followed up by proper treatment plans.

"Unfortunately, there are also reports that the assessments being offered by some new clinics, many of which operate via telehealth, do not meet the quality standards set out in the ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline.

"AADPA does not support increased access that comes at the cost of reduced quality."

Increased access to services needed

The report made a significant number of recommendations, including that the Tasmanian government increase investment in treatment and support in the state's public system for people with ADHD.

The neighbourhoods where ADHD rates are skyrocketing ADHD diagnoses in adults have exploded across Australia since 2017. For the first time, we have the data that shows where it is — and isn't — happening.

It recommended the state investigate options to provide access to ADHD diagnostic services in child and family learning centres and increase supports through them.

It also said there was more of a role for the federal government to play, and recommended the state government advocate for an increase in Medicare-subsidised sessions under mental health treatment plans, and called on it to fund GP training in ADHD diagnosis and management.

The report also acknowledged a number of recent government initiatives that it hoped would increase access to services.

In a statement, Minister for Health, Mental Health and Wellbeing Bridget Archer said the government was taking steps to deliver better access to health services.

"That is why we are delivering our 2025 election commitment to enable Tasmanian GPs to diagnose, treat and manage ADHD for both children and adults," she said.

"Forty-eight GPs have undertaken the training so far, and we expect to see this number increase over time.

"This will mean faster access to medication, reduced costs for patients, and better continuity of care."

World.title: 'People are losing everything': Ukraine's drones could crash Russian banks
World.content:
For Ukraine's drones buzzing over the border, they have been lucrative targets.

On the outskirts of Russian cities, enormous warehouses belonging to the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries, have been struck systematically over the past four weeks.

The company is often compared to Amazon and sells everything from clothing and electronics to books, groceries and cosmetics.

Kyiv has accused Wildberries of helping supply President Vladimir Putin's military and says it must be stopped.

But there's another reason this business is being attacked, and experts say it could affect Russia's entire financial system.

Over the past four weeks, Ukrainian drones have struck at least 22 Wildberries facilities. Some have been destroyed while others have been shuttered or had their operations disrupted due to the damage.

Kyiv describes the strategy as "long-range sanctions". They are part of an intensive 40-day campaign designed to strangle Russia's already stalling economy.

Oil refineries and other critical infrastructure has been hit. But Wildberries, which is estimated to be responsible for around 2 per cent of the country's GDP, could be the juiciest prize of all.

Many Western companies left Russia after Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Since then, Wildberries has capitalised, and embarked on a massive expansion which meant debt surged too.

In 2023, the company's capital expenditure increased by 85 per cent year-on-year to 52.6 billion rubles ($903 million). In 2024 it rose sharply again to 150 billion rubles and last year it was 310 billion rubles.

Russian and Ukrainian media outlets claim Wildberries took out its biggest loans with VTB Bank and Sberbank, both of which are more than 50 per cent owned by the Kremlin.

It means any financial trouble at Wildberries would likely set off a chain reaction that affects its creditors, and ultimately, the Russian government.

This Wildberries warehouse near Moscow was destroyed by a Ukrainian attack. (Reuters)

Russian officials deny Wildberries is selling military equipment, despite the fact its website advertises dual-use items like night-vision goggles and body armour.

The commander in charge of Ukraine's drone strategy, Major Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, this week claimed ordinary Russian consumers were "addicted" to the convenience the company provided.

"It turned out to be a sensitive sensor of the comfort of Russia's massive population — people who consider themselves completely untouched by the actions of the aggressor country," he told AP.

Major Brovdi said Ukraine would continue attacking Wildberries "until it becomes impossible for it to recover quickly".

Ukrainian presidential advisor Mykhailo Podolyak told German broadcaster DW last month Russia's economy would suffer "severe defiscalisation" due to Kyiv's attacks on Wildberries.

'Every morning it's terrifying to open the news'

Russia's banking system is already in crisis, according to International Monetary Fund (IMF) metrics.

Analysts also warn the country's economy is already in, or on the brink of, a recession and weighed down by Western sanctions and by funding the prolonged war.

They say the Kremlin can ill afford to bail out its banks if Wildberries goes under.

Even Russia's censored media outlets have reported on the warehouse fires, warning the country's business sector would face challenges like rising logistics costs.

Loading...

Stephen Hall, an assistant professor in Russian and post-Soviet politics at the University of Bath, told the ABC there were several reasons Wildberries is a lucrative target.

"Of most importance is simply bringing the war home to Russians. Ukraine has been doing this already with their strikes on oil refineries, which has made people queue for petrol," he said.

"Wildberries is the Amazon of Russia; next-day delivery and all that. Huge distribution centres. If it's targeted, the average Russian is going to notice and be affected by it.

"But Wildberries is also heavily indebted to two major banks in Russia.

"That has ramifications. If Wildberries fails, then the loans won't be paid back to those banks, which will start to bring down the economic sector."

Wildberries is the largest online retailer in Russia, and one of the country's biggest companies. (Reuters: Anastasia Barashkova)

Shortly before Ukraine's attacks started, Wildberries updated its contracts to say sellers would be liable if stock in its warehouses was destroyed due to "terrorism".

Angry small-business owners have taken to social media to vent.

"Every morning it's terrifying to open the news. People are losing everything. There are probably many people who were injured in the warehouse fires as well. It's horrifying," one man posted last week.

"Today our main Wildberries warehouse is on fire. This is where most of our products were stored so we could fulfil your orders quickly and efficiently.

" Independent brands simply can't survive under the current marketplace conditions, when they take half of your revenue and then either don't respond or try to avoid questions about compensation. "

Amid mounting criticism, Wildberries founder Tatyana Kim, who is also Russia's richest woman, delivered a video address last month in which she described Ukraine's campaign as a "terrorist attack".

"We will do everything we can to help businesses cope with this difficult situation," she said. "I thank everyone for their support. Together, we are stronger. Because Wildberries is you."

The attacks on Wildberries have killed some of the company's employees and left others injured.

In response to Ukraine's barrages, Russia has also escalated its aerial bombardment of Ukraine's infrastructure and cities in the past month.

The attacks have been among the most deadly for Ukrainian civilians since Moscow's full-scale invasion was launched in February 2022.

World.title: A year on, this human skull mystery at Mildura may never be solved
World.content:
A human skull found on the banks of the Murray River in Victoria's north-west more than 12 months ago is being sent for carbon date testing.

In July 2025, a man was walking along the river's edge near the entrance of Apex Riverbeach Holiday park in Mildura when he made the discovery of the partial skull.

NSW Police said the remains were found partially buried and that early indications suggested the remains were not historic.

After the discovery, the skull was sent to Newcastle for special forensic investigation.

NSW Police Detective Inspector Matt Sippel said given authorities were dealing with a partial skull, the tests had come back inconclusive.

"We haven't been able to identify the origin of that skull and the date or the age of the skull," Detective Inspector Sippel said.

"What we'll do [now] is have that sent to the Australian National University where radiocarbon data testing is to occur."

He said a number of inquires had been made including searching through missing person databases.

However, he said there was a lack of evidence.

"We don't know how long this skull had been there and how it got to that location," Detective Inspector Sippel said.

"Obviously, examinations were conducted at the time, nothing further was located and that's pretty much where it sits.

"But, we are very hopeful that we'll be able to get some further answers in relation to the radiocarbon data testing that the partial skull is about to undertake."

He confirmed historic remains were ruled out by an anthropologist.

"Hopefully, we can build a sufficient amount of evidence… [that] can lead to other inquires, our missing persons databases and all those of things and hopefully we will get a result," he said.

"But, ultimately that will all be put before the Coroner."

How investigations of this nature unfold

Former Victoria Police homicide detective Charlie Bezzina said the investigation into the mystery skull could take years.

"Your first point of call certainly is missing persons records, given [the length] of the Murray River, [it] makes it quite difficult," he said.

"So, you'd have to really expand it to the whole direction and length of the Murray River and establish any age.

"If you're able to determine any gender, and then any distinguishing factors, more specifically in the teeth … if there is some specific work that's been done on the teeth … they would take X-rays and distribute it to dentists in Victoria and New South Wales [who] may recognise their work if there is something significant in their teeth.

"They may try and extract DNA, depending on the age of it, but that's another avenue of identification."

Former Victoria Police homicide detective Charlie Bezzina says investigations like these could remain a mystery forever. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

Mr Bezzina said given it was a partial skull, "very little" could be extracted from an identification point of view.

"Because you've only got skull or part of the bone, you might be lucky enough to get some DNA if there's any teeth left there, but it [comes down] to the age of it, how long has it been in the water, has it been buried," he said.

"So it becomes difficult … that's why I say this is a scientific investigation as opposed to a criminal one.

"[You're] dealing with scientific stuff, you're not dealing with door knocks or interviewing witnesses, apart from if the missing persons reports come back as negative," he said.

"Then you're relying on science quite significantly through an anthropologist to try to determine the gender of the skull, the dental records and any DNA."

He said given the circumstances it would not be unusual for the skull to never be identified.

"It may remain a mystery forever and a day but they might be lucky enough to identify the skull and hopefully have some respite for the family," Mr Bezzina said.

World.title: VIP gambling perks targeted as Labor, Coalition edge toward deal
World.content:
The Coalition is seeking a targeted crackdown on VIP gambling inducements offered to high rollers and a simplified option to curb ads on streaming services amid ongoing "constructive" gambling bill talks with the federal government.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met early Tuesday evening for a second time in as many days to hash out details of an expected agreement to amend Labor’s proposed gambling ad restrictions.

Major changes such as an "opt-in" system for online advertising or a total ban on so-called gambling inducements are not on the table from either side, with Mr Albanese having previously indicated he would not entertain a wholesale rewrite of the draft legislation.

Albanese returns to a gambling debate ready to ignite Drugs, sex and multi-million dollar high rollers are themes more often featured in a Hollywood film than a parliamentary hearing, but this week's gambling inquiry has been the exception.

Instead, the asks put forward by Mr Taylor and Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson have focused on stronger protections for children and vulnerable people from exposure to advertising or predatory industry tactics.

With a modest deal seeming increasingly likely, gambling harm reduction advocates within the Coalition are calling for the bill to include an automatic independent review of the measures in the future.

It is hoped this would eventually expose what they believe are flaws in the legislation and create the case for further changes in the next term of government.

Labor is seeking to pass the legislation through the Senate by the end of the fortnight, which Mr Taylor is understood to be open to though is not in a rush this week as he has committed to take a final proposal back to the full Coalition party room for sign off.

Coalition asks for focus on high-end inducements

Rather than a broader crackdown on so-called gambling inducements, such as bonus bet offers, the Coalition has instead asked Labor for amendments focused on vulnerable and high-spending gamblers.

This included creating some type of cooling period preventing gambling companies from sending any inducements to Australians immediately after they remove themselves from the government’s self-exclusion register Betstop.

Loading...

The Opposition has also suggested targeting VIP offers extended to high rollers, such as access to exclusive events, game day tickets or large bonus-bet offers.

More common inducements pushed out to the average customer, such as deposit or bonus bet deals in the $25 range, are not the focus of the Coalition’s negotiations with Labor.

This is in part due to a view that the Liberals and Nationals must remain the parties of "personal responsibility" where individuals are expected to make their own decisions.

Coalition wants to give streamers option to comply with TV ad laws

The Coalition has also proposed a workaround for concerns among what has been dubbed a "triple lock" requiring all online platforms to restrict gambling ads to logged-in users who are aged over 18, while also giving every adult user a simple way to "opt out".

Harm advocates are unhappy with this proposal, because if a streaming service, social media or other online platform has a triple lock in place, they can show as many gambling ads as they want to over-aged, logged in viewers who have not opted out.

Streamers have also expressed concerns about the complexity of the proposed system.

The Coalition has also proposed a potential workaround for restrictions aimed at targeting gambling advertising loopholes. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

The Coalition has therefore suggested streamers be given the option of either enforcing a triple lock or adopting the far more restrictive advertising rules for TV.

Under the bill, gambling ads are limited to three per hour between 6am and 8:30pm and banned during live sport broadcasts within those hours.

Liberal MP Simon Kennedy used a speech in parliament on Tuesday to attack the "two glaring problems" with Labor’s bill, which he said "did nothing" on inducements and allowed “unlimited advertising online” for adults who had not opted out.

"There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more," he said.

Inducements up for negotiation in ‘unusual’ leader talks

Coalition sources acknowledged it was "unusual" for Mr Taylor and Mr Albanese to meet twice to discuss legislative issues, attributing it to the prime minister's interest in being involved in negotiations.

Both leaders were on annual leave last week when a two-day Senate inquiry heard shocking evidence about the efforts VIP account managers at gambling companies went to strengthen relationships with high-rolling clients.

Gambling companies deny drug claims Sportsbet and TAB have denied explosive claims they offered customers access to illicit drugs.

Allegations of offers to provide access to illicit drugs dominated media coverage of the hearings, but advocates also warned of harmful legal examples of so-called gambling inducements.

This included things like big spending gamblers being offered travel, accommodation and access to exclusive events linked to race days or football games.

Advocates also warned about the targeting of gamblers with inducements such as bonus bets, which the wagering sector described as “promotions”.

Last month Labor members unanimously voted to adopt a pledge to tackle these inducements into the party's 2026 national policy platform.

More than three years ago the You Win Some, You Lose More report into online wagering harms, which was authored by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, recommended a total ban on all inducements.

Multiple Labor backbench MPs have gone public with their push for the party to address inducements since the government’s draft bill did not deal with the issue.

Industry expects 'unscrupulous' VIP account manager crackdown

Sources in the wagering industry said one of the issues discussed between the Coalition and Labor was a crackdown on the "payment" of VIP account managers offering gambling promotions.

At the Senate hearing last week, ACT independent Senator David Pocock was visibly shocked by evidence account managers at some wagering companies were paid on commission based on customers’ losses.

Gambling company offered addict drugs Luke Bateman says gambling company employees unofficially offered him illicit drugs.

A wagering source said they believed Labor's bill could be amended to stop "unscrupulous" account managers being paid in this way.

This would not impact every company however, as the ABC reported last year that Sportsbet and Tabcorp no longer pay commissions to VIP account managers.

Any deal between Mr Taylor and Mr Albanese would still have to be signed off by the Coalition party room, which meets weekly when parliament is sitting.

Five backbenchers using the regular meeting on Tuesday to push for tougher reforms, while four cautioned against over-regulation.

Greens communications spokeswoman Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said Labor always intended to make a deal with the Coalition on the gambling reforms, to get away with doing the "bare minimum" on the issue.

Loading

Senator Hanson-Young said she met yesterday with Communications Minister Anika Wells, who indicated the government was willing to amend the bill to limit inducements.

"Last week, we were told the government wouldn't move at all and now they're saying they're prepared to move. The question is how far?" she said.

"The government has always intended to put this piece of legislation through with the opposition because they want to do the bare minimum.

"I have no faith that Angus Taylor is up to the job of negotiating the best outcome for people here."

World.title: ‘Stranger things have happened’: Trump coy on calling midterm-elections emergency
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS election ‘Stranger things have happened’: Trump coy on calling midterm-elections emergency Michael Koziol August 12, 2026 — 6:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump delivered a cryptic response when asked whether he would consider calling a national security emergency ahead of the midterm elections, giving oxygen to calls from right-wing pundits for an unprecedented intervention. The US president was asked on the Real America’s Voice network – a conservative media platform that includes former Trump strategist Steve Bannon – about the prospects of him declaring such an emergency within the next month. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office this week. Bloomberg “Let me just say this, stranger things have happened. I’ll leave it at that,” Trump replied. The host, Wayne Allyn Root, one of the prominent advocates for the idea, agreed to leave the subject there. The comments mark the first time Trump has engaged with the specific proposal for a national security emergency ahead of the November midterms – an idea pushed by Bannon, Root and other influential pundits in recent months.



It comes amid the US Senate’s refusal to pass the SAVE Act, a bill that would compel prospective voters to show documentary proof of American citizenship in person when registering to vote and present photo ID at the polling booth. Currently, voter ID requirements differ from state to state. Root said the emergency declaration would deliver photo ID and proof of citizenship requirements, plus restrictions on mail-in ballots, which Trump has also advocated. Later, when he described it as “the SAVE Act on steroids”, Trump said: “Yep.” Journalist John Solomon, right, has been made a special government employee in the White House examining election integrity and alleged weaponisation. Bloomberg Chuck Schumer, the leader of the Democrats in the Senate, noted the remarks. “Donald Trump wants to take over American elections,” he said. “Senate Democrats are prepared to combat his unprecedented, illegal efforts at every turn.” Last month, in a much-hyped prime-time address to the nation, Trump unveiled what he said was evidence of widespread election meddling and influence by China, including the alleged harvesting of 220 million Americans’ data.



“Members of the deep state” within the US intelligence system actively worked to suppress and downplay the seriousness of this activity, Trump claimed on national television. The allegations attracted scepticism throughout the American media and were generally seen as lacking evidence or rehashing known vulnerabilities in the electoral system. Steve Bannon, a former Trump adviser, has been one of the key voices calling for a national security emergency. Bloomberg But they were immediately used by Trump’s conservative media backers as justification for the president to intervene in the democratic process. Bannon told this masthead that same evening: “The damning evidence unearthed from the ‘deep state’ intelligence agencies sets the predicate for President Trump to declare a national security emergency regarding this November’s elections.”



Later, he said Trump’s televised address was the beginning of the process, and more evidence of election fraud would be presented. “I believe we will have a national emergency declared by late August.” Over the past week, the White House has attempted to focus attention on declassified documents showing the FBI opened a criminal probe into Trump in May 2017 to examine whether he acted – wittingly or unwittingly – as a Russian asset when he fired then FBI director James Comey. Trade counsellor Peter Navarro, a loyal Trump ally, spoke at length about the allegations at the White House on Tuesday morning. Bloomberg It is part of a broader investigation by the White House into election integrity and the alleged weaponisation of the federal government against Trump by the so-called “deep state”. That probe is being run by John Solomon, founder of right-wing news site Just The News, who has been brought into the White House temporarily as a special government employee.



Related Article Opinion

Steve Bannon Trump will declare a ‘national emergency’ before midterms: Bannon Peter Hartcher Political and international editor On Tuesday morning (US time), the president’s loyal trade counsellor, Peter Navarro, spoke to reporters at the White House at length about the allegations, and called for Republicans in US Congress to immediately issue subpoenas. “These people need to be held to account,” he said. “This was nothing more than an attempted coup d’tat.” Navarro – who went to jail in 2024 for refusing to co-operate with a congressional probe into the January 6, 2021 riots at the US Capitol – declined to talk about his discussions with Trump on the matter, citing executive privilege. “If you look at the president’s statements, he wants, as Steve Bannon said, action, action, action,” Navarro said. “There’s nothing more important than election integrity.”

World.title: Too big for Sydney: This massive work signals Opera Australia’s comeback
World.content:
CultureMusicPerforming arts Too big for Sydney: This massive work signals Opera Australia’s comeback Nick Galvin August 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After several years plagued by management volatility and financial strife, Opera Australia is pitching its 2027 season as one of stability and renewed ambition with a varied slate of productions for Sydney and Melbourne. The new season ranges from a new David McVicar production of Wagner’s Tannhäuser to a family-friendly, steampunk Magic Flute, two major Australian operas and the return of Gilbert and Sullivan to the Sydney Opera House. Amy Lane and Ruth Thomas. James Brickwood This will be the first season for newly appointed director of opera Amy Lane, who is presently serving out her time as artistic director of the Copenhagen Opera Festival. She will join OA full time after delivering her final event in Denmark this month and said she was excited for the company’s future. “It does feel strangely like, after a slightly bumpy period, that the ground is kind of fertile for us to go, ‘OK, what are we planting and what are we going to see in our five-year round?’” she said. Lane joins Alex Budd (CEO) and music director Andrea Battistoni in a revamped leadership team, wiping the slate clean from the revolving-door era of Jo Davies and Fiona Allan.



The big-ticket item for 2027 will be staged not in the Sydney Opera House but at Melbourne’s State Theatre, which will come as a relief to the city’s opera fans, who have suffered slim pickings for the past three years while the venue has been closed for renovations. Performers in the steampunk take on The Magic Flute by Scottish Opera. Tannhäuser is a monumental work requiring an orchestra too big for the pit at the Opera House’s Joan Sutherland theatre – not to mention the massive off-stage brass ensemble scored by Wagner. OA will be hoping fans from Sydney and beyond will make the trip to Melbourne to see Scottish director McVicar’s vision for Tannhäuser. “His take on it is so extraordinary,” said Lane. “Only David’s mind could work in this brilliant way to find a pathway through this piece to make it enticing, not just for those who love Wagner, but for those who want to be in the theatre.” Leah Purcell with composer of The Drover’s Wife, George Palmer. Sam Mooy



She described initial meetings with McVicar, where he outlined his vision for Tannhäuser as “exhilarating”. In Sydney, OA is pitching the Australian premiere of Scottish Opera’s well-reviewed Magic Flute as a show for all ages in its continuing bid to capture young opera fans. Opera Australia hopes a steampunk take on Magic Flute will excite younger audiences. James Glossop “We’re trying to program family operas and build on that,” said planning and program director Ruth Thomas. “We had Hansel and Gretel earlier this year and last year we had Cendrillon [Cinderella] so we want to try and keep that [going].” Sydney’s season opens with the local premiere of perhaps the world’s best-loved opera, Puccini’s La Boheme, which has its world premiere in Melbourne in November. Sydney audiences also get a return of Simon Phillips’ production of Donizetti’s frothy comic opera The Elixir of Love, complete with ocker-ised surtitles.



Also coming to Sydney is an intriguing double-bill of one-act French works. Ravel’s L’enfant et les sortileges will feature much-loved Australian mezzo soprano Margaret Plummer. La Voix humaine, by Francis Poulenc, is a one-woman opera in which the woman makes a final phone call with her faithless lover. Leah Purcell at Opera Australia’s headquarters. Sam Mooy “You hear her side of the conversation as we as an audience have to imagine what she is hearing,” said Lane. “It is painfully intimate and so vulnerable.” Sydney’s winter season features a return of McVicar’s lush production of Faust plus Stuart Maunder’s knockabout Pirates of Penzance and a Sydney premiere of Verdi’s A Masked Ball. Melbourne also gets that city’s premiere of Ann Yee’s Turandot, the Magic Flute and Leah Purcell’s stunning The Drover’s Wife. And in a left-field programming decision, Melbourne fans will get a one-off performance of Beethoven’s 9th Symphony with the Opera Australia Chorus and Orchestra Victoria.

World.title: Shut down by algorithm: Small businesses suffer online nightmare
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCompetition Shut down by algorithm: Small businesses suffer online nightmare David Swan August 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Small businesses’ online shops are being switched off by computer algorithms with no warning or apparent human oversight, the small business ombudsman’s office says, as digital platform disputes become its biggest source of complaints. These disputes have quadrupled to 48.3 per cent of all new cases managed by the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman in the June quarter, up from 12 per cent a year earlier. Businesses built over a decade or more, with millions of dollars a year in sales running through their online accounts, can now be closed off in seconds by a system nobody has to explain, the agency warns. Jack Nekhala, inventor of the Bed Scrunchie. Sellers increasingly report their accounts being switched off entirely, rather than the isolated problems that once dominated: a hacked login, a withheld payment, a single listing pulled down. “Small businesses seeking our assistance describe how a ‘community standards’ algorithm has taken down their account without any apparent human oversight,” the ombudsman’s office told this masthead.



Last month, at least five Melbourne and Sydney queer venues were locked out of Facebook and Instagram accounts they had spent more than a decade building, with the stated reasons ranging from human exploitation to a review over alleged drugs and guns. Meta later said the accounts had been flagged in error. A suspension freezes a company’s account on such platforms, cutting sellers off from customer details and product photographs. The ombudsman’s office has urged digital platforms to provide human contacts, specific reasons and structured appeal paths before taking such action. Nekhala has lodged a complaint against Amazon with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC). AP One of the disputes has recently been taken to the competition watchdog: US inventor Jack Nekhala has lodged a complaint with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) against Amazon Commercial Services, the online giant’s local arm, after his amazon.com.au seller account was deactivated on April 11, 2025. He says there had been no Australian investigation or notice, and is asking the ACCC to establish whether anyone in Australia had assessed the decision or if it automatically followed a US block.



Nekhala invented the ‘Bed Scrunchie’, a sheet fastener business that turned over about $US6 million ($8.5 million) a year, almost all through Amazon. Trouble began in September 2024, when Amazon accepted two patent infringement complaints against the product. Nekhala’s listing was disabled for nine days and took 19 calls to Amazon support. The fix, which he eventually found in a two-year-old Reddit post rather than from Amazon, was to formally retract a complaint he says he never lodged. Then, on October 30 that year, Amazon deactivated Nekhala’s US, Canadian, Mexican and Brazilian accounts over alleged review rule breaches - the platform’s guidelines for consumer feedback, testimonials and online ratings, with nine European marketplaces following days later. Related Article Social media Queer venues locked out as Meta suspensions hit Melbourne and Sydney Weeks later, a man on LinkedIn offering Temu sales support connected Nekhala to a woman calling herself Jenna, who said she was a bedding seller with contacts inside Amazon. She was not an Amazon employee, and Nekhala says he never dealt with one directly. Over four calls, Jenna showed him internal Amazon material about his account, including enforcement classifications and investigator notes invisible to standard sellers. The records described his account block as final with an instruction not to disclose the investigation’s reason to the seller. This masthead has reviewed Nekhala’s complaint records, correspondence with Amazon and his submission to the ACCC.



Jenna offered to have an internal contact release roughly $US90,000 in frozen funds for a 20 per cent fee. Nekhala says he refused to pay, but kept the conversation going to understand the offer. “If confidential account information can leave Amazon, or if intermediaries can sell supposed influence over suspensions, complaints, reviews, listings, or frozen funds, honest Australian sellers may be competing in a marketplace where the official rules are not the only rules,” he said. Amazon said the account was permanently suspended following multiple enforcement actions for policy violations. Asked about the case by Bloomberg in June, Amazon confirmed the employee who leaked Nekhala’s information had been sacked for unrelated misconduct. A spokesman said employee involvement in fraud is very rare, and Amazon invests heavily in prevention. Nekhala says Amazon has never named the employee, provided access logs, or said whether other sellers were affected. Contacted by this masthead, Amazon confirmed that Nekhala’s account had been suspended for policy violations, without providing further details. It rejected the entrepreneur’s account that it was because it found his warranty cards, which offered customers a free accessory in exchange for registering and leaving a review, amounted to review manipulation. Nekhala says the reviews were published on his own website, weren’t linked to Amazon and never required a positive rating.



Independent sellers account for more than 60 per cent of Amazon’s global sales and thousands of Australian businesses, most of them small and medium-sized, sell in its stores, according to the online retail behemoth. Professor Jeannie Paterson of Melbourne University Law School University of Melbourne Australian sellers have several routes to support, Amazon says, including phone, email and live chats, with access to Selling Partner Support and account health specialists. Email support runs around the clock, while phone and live chat are handled between 9am and 6pm. Whether local consumer law can protect Nekhala’s contract is contested. A seller’s account being immediately deactivated due to a platform’s own risk assessment, with financial consequences and no disclosed reason, could be unfair under the Australian Consumer Law, according to University of Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson. “A service provider can terminate at will, but generally needs sound reasons for doing this and ideally criteria for when it will take place,” she said.



Nekhala’s Australian revenue was modest, at $US31,444 in 2023. After the shutdown, about 650 stranded bed scrunchies were handed to a distributor. The product now reaches Australian shoppers through that distributor at $99.99, up from Nekhala’s direct $79.99 price. University of Sydney academic Rob Nicholls said complaints of this kind hinge on whether they reveal a systemic problem. “If this problem has also affected a number of other, likely Australian, small businesses, then the ACCC will be concerned,” he said. The ACCC said it does not comment on complaints it receives, or on individual businesses. A spokesman said obligations under the Australian Consumer Law applied equally to every business trading in Australia, whether based here or overseas, and that whether particular conduct breached the law depended on the circumstances. “The ACCC has consistently been advocating for adequate mandatory minimum standards for digital platforms’ internal dispute resolution, and an independent external dispute resolution body for digital platform services,” a spokesman said.
